lesson_text:
Gone but Not Forgotten
Scientists estimate that more than 99% of species that have
existed on Earth are extinct. Still, it’s rare when more than half
of living species disappear at the same time. Such events have
occurred, though, and they are known as mass extinctions.
Here are the top five mass extinctions in Earth’s history. The
circle graphs show what percentage of species went extinct.
Collection 1
Earth’s Long
Life Story
1
Picturing the
Fossil Record
2
Gone but Not
Forgotten
3
Carbon 14’s
Disappearing Act
4
Living
Things
End-Ordovician Extinction:
440 million years ago
At the end of the Ordovician era, Earth’s climate
cooled. The sea level fell as glaciers spread over
the land. Many small ocean-dwelling species
disappeared, including most of the trilobite
species.
Trilobite
Vocabulary
mass extinctions, n. events
in Earth’s past during which
large percentages, usually
about 75%, of species
became extinct during short
periods of geologic time
End-Devonian Extinction:
365 million years ago
It’s not clear what changes on Earth caused
this mass extinction, and it wasn’t quite as
disruptive as the other events. Nevertheless,
many tropical ocean species disappeared,
including fish called placoderms.
Placoderms
6
End-Permian Extinction:
250 million years ago
Triggered by volcanic eruptions
and followed by wildfires, this
most massive of the mass extinctions wiped out
many species of trees, ocean corals, amphibians,
and ancestors of mammals called pelycosaurs.
End-Triassic Extinction:
210 million years ago
As the super-continent
Pangaea began to break apart
and volcanic eruptions increased,
these events may have led to climate change.
Many species of animals with backbones
perished, including reptiles and fish called
conodonts.
End-Cretaceous Extinction:
65 million years ago
Sixty-five million years ago, a
huge asteroid crashed into Earth
and sent a dust cloud into the
atmosphere that blocked sunlight.
Wildfires, volcanic eruptions, and a fall in sea level
may have also been culprits in a mass extinction
that wiped out all the dinosaur species except
those that were the ancestors of birds.
Pelycosaur
Conodont
Tyrannosaur
Dig into Data
The fossil record doesn’t show all the species that have lived
and gone extinct. Not all species form fossils. For example,
most microscopic, bacteria-like species never became
fossils. Also, creatures didn’t always die in places such as
muddy swamps where fossils could form. For these reasons,
counts of extinct species are always broad estimates.
7
summary: Over 99% of Earth's species are extinct, with rare mass extinction events wiping out large percentages (around 75%) of species in short geological periods. Five major mass extinctions include the End-Ordovician (climate cooling, sea level fall), End-Devonian (tropical ocean species loss), End-Permian (volcanic eruptions, wildfires, most massive), End-Triassic (Pangaea break-up, volcanism, climate change), and End-Cretaceous (asteroid impact, dust cloud, wildfires, volcanism, sea level fall, ending dinosaurs). The fossil record provides only estimates of extinct species due to incomplete fossilization.

Have you ever wondered how old something

ask them their age. If you want to know how
old a tree is, you can count the rings on its
trunk. For fossils, scientists use radiometric

Word to Know
Radiocarbon dating is a process in which
scientists study the ratio of carbon 12 to
carbon 14 atoms in a fossilized organism
to tell how long ago the organism was
alive. Scientists can tell how old a fossil
is by analyzing the remaining amounts
of carbon 14 atoms, but this process is
limited to going back about 50,000 years.
Radiometric dating, studying isotopes that
decay over longer periods of time, is used for

summary: Scientists use radiometric dating, specifically radiocarbon dating, to determine the age of fossils. Radiocarbon dating analyzes the ratio of carbon-12 to carbon-14 atoms in a fossilized organism, with its effectiveness limited to about 50,000 years. For older materials, general radiometric dating, which studies isotopes decaying over longer periods, is employed.

topic: Characteristics of Living Things and Taxonomy
lesson_text:
Living Things
What makes something alive? Humans have
wrestled with this question for thousands
of years. Today, scientists’ definition of living
centers on several defining abilities:
Collection 1
Earth’s Long
Life Story
1
Picturing the
Fossil Record
2
Gone but Not
Forgotten
3
Carbon 14’s
Disappearing Act
4
Living
Things
The ability to react to stimuli
A bat uses its large ears to hear mosquitoes in the air.
The ability to reproduce and grow
Bacteria can reproduce very quickly.
The ability to maintain homeostasis
A turtle suns itself to gain thermal energy and make its
internal environment more stable.
The ability to acquire energy
A shark preys upon fish.
Word to Know
Homeostasis is a stable internal environment.
10
Fungi, animals, plants, protists, archaea,
and bacteria are all considered living things
because they have the four abilities listed on
the opposite page. Each of these large groups,
or taxa, can be further divided into other taxa.
Each taxon farther out on a branch of the tree of
life has organisms that are more closely related.
Organisms that can reproduce with each other
and produce offspring that are also capable
of reproducing are part of the same species.
Within a species, scientists sometimes identify
types that have distinguishing characteristics.
These are known as subspecies.
Taxonomy is now guided by genetics. When the
genomes of organisms are analyzed, scientists
can determine that two organisms that look
the same on the outside are distinct species. In
2013, biologists in South Carolina determined
that some of the scalloped hammerhead sharks
they had sampled from coastal waters were
genetically distinct from most of the others and
also had ten fewer vertebrae. Otherwise, it was
impossible to tell the two types apart. Sharks
that would’ve been lumped in with others
of the species Sphyrna lewini are now called
Sphyrna gilberti, named after a scientist, Carter
Gilbert, who first noticed the difference in the
number of vertebrae among some scalloped
hammerheads years earlier.
Vocabulary
taxa, n. plural of taxon, a group of related
species
species, n. a group of living organisms
consisting of similar individuals capable of
exchanging genes or interbreeding
11
One goal of taxonomy and
DNA analysis is to develop
a phylogenetic tree. This
is a diagram that shows
how different life-forms are
associated with each other.
In this tree, which shows
many kinds of vertebrate
animals, you can see that
all the land vertebrates can
be traced back to common
ancestors that are fish. By
following the branches of
the tree, you can tell which
animals are more closely
and less closely related
to one another. Genetic
analysis shows that humans
and other animals known as
tetrapods are more closely
related to bony fishes than
bony fishes are to sharks
and rays. This comes as a
surprise to many people,
because sharks and rays
are usually lumped in with
other fish and their physical
features and behaviors
make them seem closely
related.
Word to Know
Phylogeny, or phylogenesis,
is the evolutionary history
of organisms. The word
phylogeny comes from the
Greek phylon, which means
“race” or “tribe,” and genesis,
which means “origin.”
12
13
summary: Living things are defined by their abilities to react to stimuli, reproduce and grow, maintain homeostasis (stable internal environment), and acquire energy. Taxonomy, now guided by genetics, classifies organisms into taxa, with a species being a group that can interbreed to produce fertile offspring, and subspecies having distinct characteristics within a species. Phylogenetic trees, constructed using DNA analysis, illustrate the evolutionary relationships among life forms, showing common ancestry and degrees of relatedness, like the unexpected close relation between tetrapods (including humans) and bony fishes compared to sharks and rays.

lesson_text:
It’s All in the Genes
Cells are the building blocks of life, and all living things are
made of them. Your cells are responsible for many functions,
one of which includes carrying the instructions that determine
how you become the unique organism that you are.
Collection 2
Genes, Species,
and Change
1
It’s All in
the Genes
2
Hunting for
Mutations
3
Variation Within
Species
4
Convergence
5
Evo-Devo
The instructions for determining how a
person forms and what they look like are
found within a cell’s nucleus. The nucleus
is an inner part of a cell that contains
chromosomes.
Chromosomes are materials located
within a cell’s nucleus. They are made
of proteins and deoxyribonucleic acid,
or DNA. Each chromosome is a single
molecule of DNA wrapped up tightly
around proteins so that the DNA fits
within the cell and is isolated from many
cell activities. However, if the number or
structure of chromosomes changes as
new cells are formed—such as if some
chromosomes break or go missing—
this can cause offspring to have certain
diseases or disorders.
DNA is a molecule that carries
genetic information and is known
for its double helix structure. A DNA
molecule is made up of sugars and
phosphates, and each sugar has a
base attached to it. There are four
bases that can attach themselves to
a sugar—adenine, cytosine, guanine,
and thymine—and the bases are
organized in a particular sequence
that is unique to an individual.
Genes are long segments of DNA and are primarily
responsible for inheritance. Genes are passed
down from parents to their offspring, and they
contain codes for proteins, which the body reads
like a recipe. The specific proteins and sequences
are what make people unique and create physical
variations from person to person. They determine
a person’s eye and hair color, face shape, height,
and other traits and structures based on the genetic
information inherited from the parents. However,
genetic information can change or mutate, and these
mutations can be passed to offspring.
14
Connection
Have you ever seen siblings that look similar
but have different hair or eye colors? The
siblings came from the same set of parents,
but because everyone’s genes are coded
differently, there are variations in their traits
despite being so closely related.
Imagine having a tolerance for pain so
high that it’s almost superhuman.
A woman named Jo Cameron
can describe such a life. She
experiences minimal or no
pain from injuries like burns
and broken limbs—and
even surgeries! After
studying Cameron’s
DNA, pain specialists in
London found specific
genetic mutations
that affect how pain
is signaled and
interpreted within her
body. This “recipe”
for minimizing or
eliminating pain is
being researched
and tested by
bioengineers and
geneticists who study
gene therapy. Gene
therapy is a technique in
which the genes within a
person’s body are altered to
treat certain types of diseases and
disorders. A pain-reducing gene therapy
protocol would be life-changing for
millions of people around the
world who experience chronic
or acute pain and depend on
medications for relief.
A mutation is a type of
variation or alteration that
deviates from the norm,
so for scientists to identify
a genetic mutation, they
must first have a deep
knowledge of “normal”
genes. And to understand
genes, scientists also
need to study and
understand DNA and
chromosomes—the
set of instructions
that work together
to make you who you
are. Genes, DNA, and
chromosomes are passed
down from parents to children
to determine the traits and
structures of offspring.
15
summary: Cells are life's building blocks, containing a nucleus with chromosomes made of DNA and proteins. DNA, a double helix with four bases (adenine, cytosine, guanine, thymine) in unique sequences, carries genetic information. Genes are DNA segments responsible for inheritance, coding for proteins that determine individual traits like eye color and height. Genetic mutations, or changes in DNA, can occur and be passed to offspring, potentially causing disorders or, as seen in Jo Cameron's high pain tolerance, offering avenues for gene therapy to treat diseases by altering genes.

topic: Genetic Mutation Discovery and Gene Therapy Research
lesson_text:
Hi Professor Patel,
Thank you again for recommending me for this internship in London. Working in a biology lab
has turned out better than I expected. Who knew that hunting for genetic mutations could be such
an emotional roller coaster for the people involved?!
The scientists here have been looking for years for genes that control how people feel pain and
have had some success. A few years ago, they heard about an Italian family that feels pain at first,
but after a few seconds, the pain disappears—even the severe pain from a broken leg. The fact
that three generations in the family shared this trait meant that it was likely caused by a genetic
mutation that they inherited.
Blood samples from the family members were sent to England, and it took a couple of weeks
for their DNA to be sequenced, determining the order of the chemical components that make up
the DNA molecule. Then the lab compared the family’s DNA to that of people who sense pain
in the normal way. Computer software does most of the work—without computers and database
software, this kind of search would be nearly impossible.
Next, our lab team looked at the family’s genes that differed from the “normal” group. They found
a mutation of a gene that helps control the nervous system. That seemed promising. But after
months of trying, no differences were found in the proteins produced by the mutated and normal
genes. Discouraging!
Meanwhile, the software improved, and the lab tried again to find a mutation. Sure enough, one
turned up in a gene known to be involved in sending pain signals along neurons to the brain. Even
better, all the Italian family members with the condition had this mutated gene!
Hunting for Mutations

and Change

The next step was to have another lab breed mice that have the exact same mutation as the human
family. When the mice arrived at our lab and were tested, the team found out that the mice were
also less sensitive to heat and pressure than mice with the normal gene. It was exciting to be able
to tell the Italian family that the cause of their condition is a mutation to the gene named ZFHX2!
The best part of it all is the possibility that research into this gene may help people who suffer
from long-term pain. For my next internship, I hope to be able to join a lab where scientists are
working on a gene therapy to help these patients. Stay tuned!
Best,
Kara Nguyen
Undergraduate Biological Sciences, Class of ’25
Word to Know
Gene therapy is a technology
that uses genes to treat,
prevent, or cure a disease or
medical condition.
The mutation to the “no-pain” gene
is a point mutation. This means that
just one spot in the DNA molecule
has permanently changed. The
change can occur accidentally
when the DNA replicates itself
or as the result of the cell being
exposed to X-rays or UV radiation
or substances that cause a chemical
change.
17
summary: Scientists successfully identified a genetic mutation in the ZFHX2 gene responsible for a rare condition in an Italian family where pain disappears after a few seconds. This discovery involved sequencing family DNA, comparing it to 'normal' DNA using advanced software, and validating the mutation's effect in specially bred mice that exhibited reduced pain sensitivity. This research holds promise for developing gene therapies to alleviate chronic pain, with the mutation being a point mutation, a change in a single DNA spot, that can arise from replication errors or environmental factors.

lesson_text:
Variation Within Species
Even within a species, there can be incredible variation in traits. Some
of that variation is the result of how the parents’ genes are doled out
to the offspring. Some of it is due to environmental factors, including
temperature and substances that turn genes on or off. And some of it is
due to how genes can become common across different populations.
Collection 2
Genes, Species,
and Change
1
It’s All in
the Genes
2
Hunting for
Mutations
3
Variation Within
Species
4
Convergence
5
Evo-Devo
These nudibranchs belong to the same species,
Goniobrachus geometricus, but they display
very different colors. Their coloration can help
them blend in among corals, or it can serve as
a warning to would-be predators that eating
them would be a bad idea.
These Himalayan rabbits have different colors and sizes because of
environmental temperature on the expression of genes. The smaller, darker
rabbit was exposed to cold at birth, resulting in darker fur and smaller size.
18
These eastern tiger swallowtail butterflies are of the same species, but they
have very different coloration. Males are yellow, while some females are
dark, as shown here. The darker “morph” seems to have evolved to mimic
another butterfly that is toxic to predators. Males are more attracted to
yellow females, but the advantage of being preyed upon less often has
resulted in the dark morph becoming relatively common.
On the south side of the Grand Canyon lives Abert’s squirrel, Sciurus aberti.
On the north side lives the Kaibab squirrel, Sciurus aberti kaibabensis.
The third part of the Kaibab squirrel’s scientific name indicates that it
is considered a subspecies, or a very closely related type of the same
species. Climate change and the separating effect of the canyon led to
populations of the ancestral Abert’s squirrel becoming isolated from
each other. Over time, differences evolved. The two subspecies can still
interbreed, which means they are not classified as separate species.
19
summary: Significant trait variation exists within a species, stemming from gene distribution from parents, environmental factors like temperature influencing gene expression (e.g., Himalayan rabbits' fur color), and how genes spread across populations. Examples include nudibranchs with diverse colorations for camouflage or warning, eastern tiger swallowtail butterflies with dark female morphs mimicking toxic species for protection, and Abert's and Kaibab squirrels, which diverged into subspecies due to geographic isolation but can still interbreed.

lesson_text:
Convergence
When two things that aren’t
related are similar, this is called
convergence. In evolution,
very similar traits can appear
in species that are not closely
related. This can be observed
between species that exist in
the present day and between
today’s species and long-
extinct species.
Collection 2
Genes, Species,
and Change
1
It’s All in
the Genes
2
Hunting for
Mutations
3
Variation Within
Species
4
Convergence
5
Evo-Devo
Ichthyosaurs were reptiles that lived hundreds of millions of years ago.
They had skeletons made of bone and had caudal (tail) fins and dorsal fins
like those of many modern sharks. But they were air breathers, not fish.
The long tom is a kind of needlefish.
Its long, toothed jaws are very
similar to those of ichthyosaurs, but
the long tom is a fish, and it did not
exist at the time of the ichthyosaurs
and other giant reptiles.
Though it’s known as a fish, the great
white shark and other sharks are not
bony fishes like the long tom. The
dorsal and caudal fins of the great
white are very similar to those of the
ichthyosaurs. The tail is very narrow
and stiff in front of the caudal fin to
give the shark a lot of thrust. Even
though the shark and the ichthyosaur
are not closely related, they have
similar structures because they lived
in and needed to move through the
same environment.
Vocabulary
convergence, n. independent
evolution of similar traits across
unrelated species
20
Bats are mammals whose finger
bones evolved to form the frame
for wings. The wing itself consists
mostly of thin, stretched skin.
Thousands of different insect species
have wings.
Flying fish used their pectoral fins,
which have evolved to function as
wings, to briefly glide through the
air after leaping from the ocean’s
surface to escape predators.
Bird wings are supported by long
arm bones, but they consist mostly of
feathers.
21
summary: Convergence, or convergent evolution, describes the independent development of similar traits in unrelated species, often due to adaptation to similar environments. Examples include ichthyosaurs (reptiles) and sharks (fish) both evolving similar dorsal and caudal fins for aquatic locomotion, and bats (mammals), insects, flying fish, and birds all developing wings for flight, despite fundamental differences in their underlying skeletal or anatomical structures.

lesson_text:
The Most Famous Writer Seldom Read
Charles Darwin’s name is
inseparably tied to the terms
evolution and natural selection.
Though Darwin’s association with
the idea of evolution by natural
selection is common knowledge,
it’s safe to say that most people
in the present day haven’t directly
read his most famous publication.
Darwin’s book, known in short as
On the Origin of Species, was first
printed by the publisher John
Murray in London in 1859. The
full title is On the Origin of Species
by Means of Natural Selection, or
Preservation of Favoured Races in
the Struggle for Life. The saying
“survival of the fittest” is our
modern shorthand for the title
phrase “Preservation of Favoured
Races in the Struggle for Life.” Take
a look at some of the writing
straight from Darwin’s pen. On
the left are a few passages from
Chapter 3 of Darwin’s famous
work. The notes to the right
expand on what Darwin meant.
Collection 3
Selection and
Survival
1

Writer Seldom Read
2
Darwinian
Dictionary
3

Selection
4

Podcast

Pigotie
Survival
24
The only difference between organisms
which annually produce eggs or seeds by
the thousand, and those which produce
extremely few, is, that the slow-breeders would
require a few more years to people, under
favourable conditions, a whole district, let it
be ever so large. The condor lays a couple of
eggs and the ostrich a score, and yet in the
same country the condor may be the more
numerous of the two: the Fulmar petrel lays
but one egg, yet it is believed to be the most
numerous bird in the world… A large number
of eggs is of some importance to those species,
which depend on a rapidly fluctuating amount
of food, for it allows them rapidly to increase
in number. But the real importance of a large
number of eggs or seeds is to make up for
much destruction at some period of life; and
this period in the great majority of cases is an
early one. If an animal can in any way protect
its own eggs or young, a small number may
be produced, and yet the average stock be
fully kept up; but if many eggs or young are
destroyed, many must be produced, or the
species will become extinct. It would suffice to
keep up the full number of a tree, which lived
on an average for a thousand years, if a single
seed were produced once in a thousand years,
supposing that this seed were never destroyed,
and could be ensured to germinate in a fitting
place. So that in all cases, the average number
of any animal or plant depends only indirectly
on the number of its eggs or seeds.
One of Darwin’s key observations was that
different species produce very different
numbers of offspring but that both approaches
to reproduction work in the sense of keeping
a population going and passing on traits of
the parents. Some organisms produce huge
numbers of offspring, while others produce very
few. Those that produce many also tend to lose
many of those offspring. Darwin cites two birds.
The condor lays few eggs, yet it is more abundant
than the ostrich, which lays more eggs. Why?
The condor’s eggs receive more care, so the
young condors are more likely to develop and
reach adulthood. The ostrich takes a “strength
in numbers” approach that also works because
there are so many offspring that losing some to
predators does not stop the parents from adding
some surviving offspring to the population.
The amount of death that occurs in any given
generation of offspring sets the stage for traits
that increase an individual’s chance of survival
to be passed on to the next generation more
than the traits of the offspring that don’t
reach adulthood. If all organisms survived the
different stages of life and died of old age,
Darwin’s theory would
not work because
traits would have
no effect on
chances of
survival.
25
If during the long course of ages and under
varying conditions of life, organic beings vary
at all in the several parts of their organisation,
and . . . variations useful to any organic being do
occur, assuredly individuals thus characterised
will have the best chance of being preserved
in the struggle for life; and from the strong
principle of inheritance they will tend to produce
offspring similarly characterised. This principle
of preservation, I have called, for the sake of
brevity, Natural Selection. Natural selection,
on the principle of qualities being inherited
at corresponding ages, can modify the egg,
seed, or young, as easily as the adult. Amongst
many animals, sexual selection will give its aid
to ordinary selection, by assuring to the most
vigorous and best adapted males the greatest
number of offspring.
Sexual selection will also
give characters useful to the males alone, in their
struggles with other males.
Natural selection, also, leads to divergence
of character; for more living beings can be
supported on the same area the more they
diverge in structure, habits, and constitution, of
which we see proof by looking at the inhabitants
of any small spot or at naturalised productions.
Therefore during the modification of the
descendants of any one species, and during the
incessant struggle of all species to increase in
numbers, the more diversified these descendants
become, the better will be
their chance of succeeding
in the battle of life.
Darwin’s groundbreaking insight was how
variation leads to advantaged individuals
who then produce advantaged offspring.
Even though he did not know how “qualities
being inherited” actually worked, he knew
that something allows traits to be passed on
and that traits that improved an organism’s
ability to survive the “struggle for life” would
be more likely to be passed on than the traits
of organisms that did not survive.
Darwin also recognized that natural selection
accounts for the diversity of life, including
the diversity within a species. Diversity
also leads to an improved chance that the
species—some of its members, even if just a
few—will survive even in dire circumstances.
26
summary: Charles Darwin's 'On the Origin of Species' introduced the concept of natural selection, often summarized as 'survival of the fittest.' Darwin observed that species employ diverse reproductive strategies (many offspring vs. few, well-cared for) to ensure population continuity. His key insight was that variations leading to an advantage in the 'struggle for life' are more likely to be inherited, allowing advantaged individuals to produce advantaged offspring. Natural selection drives the diversity of life, both between and within species, with diversity itself increasing a species' chance of survival.

Survival
adaptation, n. an inherited trait that improves
an organism’s fitness for survival
Clarification: Individuals don’t really adapt;
species do. Individuals only survive or do not
survive. The concept of adaptation doesn’t
mean that an individual plant or animal
changes its traits to perform better in (to adapt
to) its environment. It means that individuals
that are genetically lucky enough to have the
better traits in an environment are better off.
And thus, they’re the ones that can reproduce
and pass their traits on to the next generation.
Over time, the better traits of fortunate
ancestors are common in the population,
so a species overall is better adapted to the
environment.
natural selection, n. the survival and
reproductive success of organisms with
qualities best suited to their environment
Clarification: A more apt name for natural
selection could be “genetic good luck
within the environmental conditions in a
place and time.” Nothing actively gets rid
of disadvantageous traits. The unfortunate
individuals with such traits just don’t
reproduce and pass them on as much.
evolution, n. changes in
the genetic structure of
populations over time
Clarification: The concept
of evolution doesn’t imply
that living things transform
into different species. Instead,
each population passes on
tiny differences that, over
many generations, make the
descendants notably different
from the long-ago ancestors.
And the concept of evolution
doesn’t imply that humans
descended from apes. It
theorizes, from evidence,
that humans and apes are
descendants of the same
common ancestors.
27
summary: Key evolutionary terms are clarified: Adaptation is an inherited trait improving a species' fitness for survival, not an individual's conscious change. Natural selection is the differential survival and reproduction of individuals with advantageous traits, often described as 'genetic good luck,' where disadvantageous traits simply aren't passed on as frequently. Evolution refers to changes in populations' genetic structure over time through accumulated small differences across generations, not sudden species transformations or humans descending directly from apes, but rather sharing common ancestors with them.

Natural selection has shaped life for millions of years. It’s a
result of a population of a species affected by changes in the
environment, in which particular individuals either thrive or
do not. Humans have also acted as agents of selection. They
have shaped certain species (and varieties within species)
through selective breeding, for example. In these cases, species
evolve, not by natural selection, but by artificial selection.
Here’s an example . . .
The cats that people have as pets initially came into human
lives in a kind of symbiotic relationship and did not involve
selective breeding at all. Five thousand years ago, humans
were forming settlements and getting serious about
farming. Farming and then storing grain represented a
source of free food for rodents, which, in turn, attracted
cats. Archaeological and biological evidence from China
shows that compounds in farmed grain eaten by rodents
were ending up in cats. This is fairly direct evidence of
cats being allowed to live among humans to act as rodent
hunters if not pets. Presumably, one thing led to another,
and bonds of trust and eventually affection formed
between humans and cats.
DNA studies suggest that most of the 600 million domestic
cats now kept as pets throughout the world can be traced
to a wild cat species that lived in parts of Asia and Africa.
The wide variety of domestic cat breeds today is the result
of selective breeding that occurred only in the last 150
years. More than forty breeds are now recognized by cat
breeding associations.
28
Artificial selection now goes beyond choosing parent animals to breed and involves inserting
genes directly into the unfertilized eggs of organisms. If the eggs are fertilized, the resulting
offspring can have a new gene that was taken from, say, a fluorescent jellyfish. This has been done
in a number of species to make them fluoresce under ultraviolet light, or “glow in the dark.”
The point of making glowing animals isn’t amusement. It’s done as a kind of tagging. The jellyfish
gene for the green fluorescent protein (GFP) is added to a different organism’s genome along
with other genes intended to make more important changes for study. If the offspring fluoresces
under a UV light, researchers know that the gene transfer worked. If the offspring doesn’t glow,
researchers know the gene transfer didn’t work. This is much less expensive than running genetic
tests on all of the treated animals.
A few animals have been modified to
fluoresce just for the sake of appearance,
though. Genetically engineered
aquarium fish, for example, now
glow in their tanks.
29
summary: While natural selection drives evolution through environmental pressures, artificial selection involves humans deliberately shaping species through selective breeding or direct genetic engineering. Early domestication, like cats attracted to human settlements for rodent control, eventually led to symbiotic relationships. Modern cat breeds, however, are a result of selective breeding over the last 150 years. Advanced artificial selection now includes inserting genes, such as the green fluorescent protein (GFP) gene from jellyfish, into an organism's eggs to create glowing offspring. This 'tagging' method helps researchers confirm successful gene transfer for study, though some glowing animals are also created purely for aesthetic purposes.

Carmen: Hey, listeners. I’m Carmen. It’s good to be back, and thanks for listening to the
Young Scientists podcast. Today we have a very exciting guest here with us, Angelo
Harmon, who is going to talk to us about something close to many of our hearts:
dogs! Welcome to the pod, Angelo!
Angelo: Thanks so much, Carmen. I’m glad to be here.
Carmen: So, Angelo, you have a career as a dog show judge.
Angelo: That’s right. I’ve been a dog show judge for over 20 years.
Carmen: You must know a lot about dogs! I thought it would be fun if you could talk about
the different types of dogs you see in your shows and give us some interesting
facts about them.
Angelo: Of course. You gave us a good starting point when you used the phrase “types of
dogs.” When people refer to types of dogs, what they’re talking about are dogs’
breeds. But keep in mind that all dogs are the same species.
Carmen: Can you tell us more about those two terms, species and breed?
Angelo: Sure. A species is a group of animals that have similar characteristics and are
capable of mating to reproduce. For instance, frogs and horses can’t mate because
they are different species. However, all wolves belong to the same species, Canis
lupus of the genus Canis. That’s where the word canine comes from, by the way.
Anyhow, different varieties of wolves can mate. So what does that have to do
with dogs? Well, dogs are a domesticated subspecies of the wolf. And within this
subspecies of dog, there are over 300 different breeds.
As a dog show judge, my
job is to spot the most exemplary individuals of a breed.
Carmen: I see. Sow how do breeds come about?
Angelo: Golden retrievers, standard poodles, Labradors, dachshunds . . . these are breeds.
A breed is a group of animals within the same species that were selectively
bred. When a dog is selectively bred, it means a breeder chose two parent dogs
and mated them to produce offspring with the characteristics that the breeder

to the teacup Chihuahua. Mastiffs and Chihuahuas are of the same species, believe
it or not; but they are dramatically different breeds.
Carmen: We’ve definitely gotten an amazing variety of dogs through selective breeding,
each with their own wonderful traits. What are some of the advantages and
disadvantages to selective breeding?
Angelo: In the dog show world, we classify dogs into different groups, like the Working
Group, Sporting Group, Herding Group, and so forth. And within each group, we
see different breeds of dogs that can specialize in different things. Some breeds
make great guard dogs, others are fast runners, and some are great hunters. It’s
really incredible. Selective breeding has made it so that we can work with these
animals, but they’ve also become lovable members of our families as pets.
Carmen: Variety is a good thing, right? Is there a downside to it, though?
Angelo: Well, there is, unfortunately. With selective breeding to emphasize certain
characteristics comes certain health disadvantages.
Carmen: Can you give us some examples?
Angelo: Sure. Breeds like pugs and French bulldogs are more prone to breathing problems
because of their flat muzzles. Great Danes, Irish wolfhounds, and other large dogs
can have issues with their bones because their big size puts stress on their bodies.
Dachshunds and toy dogs can have orthopedic problems because of their short
legs. Show dogs obviously represent the finest of their breeds, but every now and
then, with a very trained eye, we can spot a dog with some physical deformities.
Carmen: And the question we’ve all been waiting for: Do you have a favorite dog breed?
Angelo: [pauses] I really love them all. But I would have to say the greyhound. Their
musculature, vision, and speed are super impressive and a very interesting contrast
to their elegance and laid-back personalities. They also occur in dozens of fur
colors and patterns. It makes me want to collect them! [laughter]
Carmen: Well, Angelo, it’s been so interesting having you on the pod today! Thank you so
much for coming on and talking to us about our best friends.
Angelo: Thanks so much for having me, Carmen. It’s been a pleasure. Maybe this episode of
your podcast will be voted “Best in Show”!

(End transcript)

Breeds are developed through selective breeding, where humans intentionally mate animals to produce offspring with desired traits, creating vast diversity like Mastiffs and Chihuahuas. While selective breeding offers benefits such as specialized working dogs and beloved pets, it also carries disadvantages, leading to health problems in certain breeds, like breathing issues in pugs, bone problems in large dogs, and orthopedic issues in dachshunds, due to the emphasis on specific physical characteristics.

Dear Dr. Shiloh,
Thank you for taking time to read my email. I go to Foster Junior High School here in
Homeville, and a friend and I are having a debate. We hope you can settle our friendly argument.
First of all, I’m not even sure whether you are the right person to ask. Our question is about
evolution, so as a biologist, you seemed like a logical person to contact. On the other hand,
maybe I should be writing to a paleontologist? Anyway, we did some internet searches and came
up dry. Then we took our question to our science teacher. Ms. Roman encouraged us to follow
through and reach out directly to an expert, so I’m hoping that’s you!
So here’s the debate. My friend Rene lives out on the edge of town where there are lots of
wooded areas to explore. We hike the trails sometimes. Last week we spotted several lizards that
seem larger than the ones we’ve seen in previous years. Rene is sure the lizards are evolving to
be larger. Rene’s theory is that the birds in the woods eat the lizards, so the lizards are adapting
by growing larger so they’ll become too big for the birds to threaten.
I said that evolution doesn’t work like that. First, a group of lizards can’t just decide they want
to be bigger to fight off birds and then grow that way. Secondly, changes to species don’t happen
quickly enough that we could see, say, a size difference in a whole species of lizard from
one summer to the next. I think maybe we are seeing the larger lizards that have survived to
maturity, but that’s not an adaptation.
Can you settle our debate? Are we witnessing the evolution of a species of lizard into a larger
species? Does evolution of species ever happen quickly enough to be directly witnessed?
With thanks and sincerely yours,
Taylor Drake
36
Dear Taylor,
To start, kudos to you and Rene for two things—first for noticing nature, and second for
asking questions about things you’ve observed. The best way to settle an argument is to
learn about a topic with an open mind and then dig into the evidence. So, I’m happy to
share some information with you about changes in presently living populations. Evolution
by natural selection (and thereby, speciation) is generally a loooong process of genetic
change. In a few rare cases, though, elements of it happen on a timescale that we’re
able to observe.
Taylor, you are correct in noting that organisms do not decide that they need to adapt
and then physically transform. Through mutations and other processes, species are
undergoing minuscule changes all the time, but individuals don’t have a say in the
matter. In fact, most species spontaneously change steadily enough across generations
that the species as a whole rarely lasts more than a few million years before it goes
extinct or changes so much that it is considered a new species. It’s a random process in
which characteristics that happen to be beneficial in the environment get passed on.
It would take systematic research into your specific population of lizards to know
what’s going on with their sizes; still, it’s not fair to automatically say that Rene is 100%
wrong about increments of evolution being observable. Rapid changes, over just a
few generations, are observable in small populations over short periods (from tens to
hundreds of years). However, those don’t tend to “stick” and spread through an entire
species. Here’s an example. When brown anole lizards invaded the Florida habitats
of green anoles, the green lizards adapted over about 20 generations, in just 15 years
after the brown lizard invasion. Green lizards with larger, stickier toe pads could climb
to higher branches to avoid the competition. The high-climbing green lizards with larger
toe pads survived to breed more than their smaller-toed kin, which meant increasingly
more offspring with those bigger, stickier toes. (I’ve included a picture of the green Anolis
carolinensis for you here.)
Generally speaking, though, research across a broad range of species suggests that it
takes about a million years for an entirely new species to branch away from an ancestor
species.
We could make a summer project out of
systematically collecting data on the lizards
you and Rene observed. If you are interested
in doing that, get back in touch with me, and
I’ll help you design an investigation.
Best regards,
Morgan Shiloh, PhD
Department of Biology
37
summary: Evolution by natural selection is generally a long, random process of genetic change spanning millions of years for speciation. Individuals cannot consciously adapt or transform, but beneficial random mutations are passed on. While observing widespread species-level evolution over a single summer is unlikely, rapid evolutionary changes can be observed in small populations over tens to hundreds of years, as seen with green anole lizards evolving larger toe pads over 15 years to climb higher and avoid competition from brown anoles.

Extra Bones? Nope!
In the early 1800s, a French naturalist named
Jean-Baptiste Lamarck suggested that changes
to an organism during its lifetime could be
inherited by future generations. For example,
when giraffes stretched to reach the uppermost
leaves on trees, their necks would lengthen
a bit. Then, when the giraffes had young, the
offspring would inherit the lengthened necks.
By the 1930s, most scientists acknowledged
that patterns of inheritance are based on
interactions among dominant and recessive
genes—not on interactions of individual
organisms with their environment.
So, how did the tallest land mammal get its
height? You might think that giraffes’ ancestors,
through mutations, acquired more neck bones.
But a giraffe has seven cervical vertebrae in its
neck, as do most other mammals, including you.
In 2015, a team of scientists compared the
neck bones of living giraffes with those of their
fossilized ancestors. How many neck vertebrae
did the giraffes’ ancestors have? Yep, seven.
Then the team took a close look at the structure
of those bones. They took measurements and
compared the ratio of the length to the width of
the third bone, and it became clear how giraffes
got their long necks.
The scientists concluded that, over millions of
years, the bones that support the neck changed
in shape. The fossil record doesn’t show a
simple linear progression, but it does show that
older giraffe-like species had shorter vertebrae
while more recent species had vertebrae that
were elongated. For about 5 million years, the
vertebrae nearest the head had elongated but
not the bones closer to the animals’ backs. More
recently, about 2 million years ago, fossils show
giraffe ancestors whose vertebrae nearest the
back were also elongated. Eventually, giraffe-
like animals had elongated vertebrae along
their entire necks.

So, what’s the competitive advantage of a
long neck? The answer is still up in the air.
Was Lamarck correct in saying that a long
neck allowed a giraffe to reach tasty leaves
at the tops of trees where other giraffes
couldn’t? Scientists are still not sure. Some have
suggested that longer necks make the males
better able to attract—and battle for—potential
mates. Others hypothesize that longer necks
make it easier to stay cool in very hot climates.
Or maybe the advantage is being able to better
see predators off in the distance.
The fossil record makes it clear that a long
neck is not the only way for grazing species
to survive. Approximately 16 million years
ago, Canthumeryx was a smallish animal with
a slightly elongated neck. This animal is the
ancestor of two groups of living species, giraffes
and okapis. One branch of the family tree
evolved to have much longer necks, and the
other shorter necks. Giraffes live on the savanna
of Africa, a relatively open habitat of trees,
shrubs, and grasses. Okapis live in a rain forest
in central Africa, where their shorter
necks are adapted for moving
among densely growing tree
trunks, low-hanging
branches, and
tangled vines.
Words to Know
A dominant version of a gene
shows its effect even when
the offspring inherits only one
copy of the gene. A recessive
version of a gene only shows
its effect when two copies of
it are inherited.
39
summary: Contrary to Lamarck's discredited theory that acquired traits are inherited, giraffes evolved their long necks not by gaining more vertebrae, but by the elongation of their existing seven cervical vertebrae over millions of years, as evidenced by the fossil record. Early giraffe-like species had shorter vertebrae, with elongation progressing from head-proximal to back-proximal vertebrae. The precise evolutionary advantage of a long neck (e.g., reaching high leaves, mate attraction, cooling, predator vigilance) remains debated, as evidenced by the divergence of their ancestor, Canthumeryx, into long-necked giraffes in savannas and short-necked okapis in dense rainforests, both successfully adapted to their environments.

lesson_text:
A Sheep Named Dolly
On a tropical island in Jurassic Park, cloned
dinosaurs roam freely, and the tourists are
confined for their own protection. In the film
Multiplicity, a construction worker gets himself
cloned so he can manage his life better. In Star
Wars: The Clone Wars an army of clones battles
for domination of a galaxy far, far away. Clearly,
many movie and TV viewers are fascinated by
the idea of cloning.
When an organism is cloned, an exact copy of
its DNA is made. It can happen in nature, such
as when identical twins develop. Scientists can
also make clones. The first mammal cloned by
a team of scientists, a sheep named Dolly, was
born in 1997. The team proved that the DNA
in the nucleus of adult animals’ body cells, say
a skin cell or a gland cell, can be copied in a
laboratory to produce an offspring that will
develop into an adult. Dolly’s arrival surprised
many other scientists, who did not think body
cells could behave like a fertilized egg cell,
dividing and forming all the different kinds of
cells needed for a new individual.
The news about Dolly raced around the
world, and within a few years other kinds of
mammals were cloned, including pigs, cats,
dogs, and horses. Immediately, people started
asking if humans could be cloned. And more
importantly they asked whether they should be
cloned. The answers ranged from “never” to “I
don’t see why not.”
“Could they?” is a question that biologists can
answer. “Should they?” is a question for ethicists.
Consider whether there should be an exact
genetic replica of yourself. Not a twin who is
the same age, but a baby. Should animals that
people eat be cloned? Should a favorite dog
who is old and sick be cloned so that the owner
has company when the older dog dies? And
what about cloning a world-renowned scientist,
artist, or musician at the end of their life?

From Ancient to
Modern Species
1

2

Humanity
Dolly lived for many years near the lab in Scotland where she was cloned.
40
In 2005, UNESCO (United Nations Educational,
Scientific and Cultural Organization) called for a
worldwide ban on human cloning. Several other
organizations agree, including the WHO (World
Health Organization). Most object to human
cloning on the grounds that the practice will
reduce human dignity. They said that a person
should not be used as a means to an end. Other
experts disagree and say that people have
babies using all sorts of methods and for all sorts
of reasons. They argue that the most important
influence on the lives of children come from how
they are brought up, rather than their genetics.
So, should scientists keep working on cloning
technology with the aim to eventually clone
humans? This is where ethical concerns collide
with science. Ethics is an area of study that
identifies humans values and right and wrong
behavior and explores the purpose of living as
a human. Following ethical principles makes an
individual person feel good, but they also guide
human communities to work well for their
members and other communities.
Ethicists might ask, “What is the purpose of
cloning?” Or, “Is it okay to make clones in a lab
to better understand how living cells work?” Or,
“Is cloning ethical if it helps people who have
diabetes or heart disease?”
But what about using cloning to produce human
babies? What if the process turns out to be
unsafe and causes harm to the child? Will cloned
people feel less an individual than other people?
If thinking about these questions is interesting
to you, you might consider a career in bioethics,
or ethics related to the life sciences. Bioethicists
work in many settings. Most hospitals employ
bioethicists, as do pharmaceutical companies,
biotechnology companies, and government
health agencies. Depending on where you
work, you may give advice about how to make
ethical decisions, represent patients when
decisions are being made about their care, or
help educate the public about controversies
over medical procedures.
Some people have careers that combine
bioethics with another field. Often medical
doctors, social workers, nurses, lawyers, and
college professors get additional education
and training to be able to address bioethics in
their work.
Bioethicists working in hospitals may work with patients to
discuss their medical testing and treatment options.
41
summary: Cloning creates an exact genetic copy of an organism, occurring naturally (e.g., identical twins) or scientifically. The 1997 cloning of Dolly the sheep proved adult body cell DNA could create a new adult organism, leading to cloning in other mammals. This sparked ethical debates about human cloning: whether it's possible and, more importantly, whether it's morally permissible, considering human dignity, potential harm, individuality, and societal values. Bioethics is the field that addresses these complex moral questions at the intersection of life sciences, guiding decisions in healthcare, research, and policy.

topic: What Makes Humans Unique in Evolution
lesson_text:
Unique Humanity
Human beings and other animals are similar
in many ways. Other animals do many of the
things that humans do. For example, several
other species care for their young for lengthy
periods of time. Elephant young remain
with their mothers for 16 years on average.
Many other species use simple tools to solve
problems and teach survival skills to the young
in their communities. Other animals play for fun,
just like humans do. If you have a pet, you’ve
probably witnessed an animal at play.
So what is it that sets humans apart from all
the other species? One way to answer that
question has to do with the way we accumulate
knowledge and pass it on to future generations.
Humans are unique in our engagement in
the purposeful practice of collecting and
passing on knowledge. A mother chimpanzee
will show her offspring how to use a stick to
retrieve termites from a mound. But she doesn’t
record her instructions in a written language
to teach other chimpanzees at a later time. She
might figure out the best length stick to get
the job done, but she doesn’t pass on data to
save other chimpanzees the time of their own
termite-probing trial and error.
In contrast, human language and the ability
to record it in writing have allowed humans to
pass on what they know to future generations
for thousands of years. The result is an
astonishing accumulation of knowledge. And
even though one person could never learn
everything that humanity has now recorded,
the knowledge is preserved. It is there for the
taking for those who would seek it. You don’t
need to have witnessed the first flight of an
airplane to know what happened at that event.
You don’t have to get sick eating toxic plants

Because of humans’ preservation of knowledge,

Human brains are unique in terms of the scale
