topic: Exothermic Reactions in Ice Melting Products
lesson_text: Thawing Out Ice Melt Myths Another Michigan winter is approaching us. We all know the drill. A few weeks into November, we stock up on canned goods, buy jugs of water, test our generators, and purchase products for melting snow and ice in our driveways. Time and time again, we have power outages and snow days. Then there are the days we wish we were off from work or school because there’s so much snow in our driveways that it’s impossible for us to get out. I’ve been a home real estate agent in Michigan for 23 years, and every year homebuyers ask me how to tell if a driveway is in good condition due to the use of ice-melting products. The shared concern among my homebuyers is that ice melting products damage the surfaces they come into contact with. It’s a reasonable concern, especially for homebuyers who are coming from out of state and are unfamiliar with how these products work. So I decided to dedicate this month’s newsletter to thawing out the ice melt myths once and for all. Michigan Homes and Land Newsletter Thawing Out Ice Melt Myths Let’s start by discussing ice-melting products. They consist of different blends of salts, with calcium chloride as the star ingredient. They help melt the ice quicker than the time it would take for the ice to melt naturally. This is important because we usually need to get rid of the ice “now” and not “several days from now.” Some products are fast-acting. Others are long-lasting. Some can be sprayed instead of sprinkled, and others turn colors when they hit the ice for easy visibility. In the end, all of these products use an exothermic reaction to melt ice quickly (or prevent ice from forming in the first place). An exothermic reaction gives off heat. When calcium chloride contacts water, it undergoes a chemical reaction that releases heat. This heat then melts the ice. It makes sense for homebuyers to be concerned with the integrity of the driveway, especially as it relates to ice-melt salts. It is not, however, realistic to think that the chemicals from ice-melting products seep into the porous driveway, lurking and waiting to cause damage over time. That’s not how these products work. Let’s thaw the icy myths once and for all: Ice-melting products do not damage driveways. In fact, these products hardly even come into contact with the surface of the driveway. A brine forms on the surface of the ice (and the ice is on top of the driveway). Sure, some of the salt product could touch the driveway when you are scattering it around. But overall, these salts will not have a negative effect on the cement itself. The exothermic reaction involved in melting ice with salt takes place between the salt and the ice, not between the salt and the cement. Here’s hoping all of you out there have a warm and safe winter season! Calcium chloride is the main ingredient used for thawing icy roads and driveways. It creates an exothermic reaction when mixed with water. Snow can be plowed or shoveled away from roads, but it is difficult to crack ice to break it free from a surface. Salts are used to dissolve ice more quickly. Consider the Source This article was written by a real estate agent who sells houses. What about the author makes them a credible source for information about ice-melting products and the condition of driveways?
summary: Ice-melting products, commonly using calcium chloride, melt ice faster than natural thawing by employing an exothermic chemical reaction. When calcium chloride mixes with water, it releases heat, which directly melts the ice. The article debunks the myth that these products damage driveways, explaining that the exothermic reaction occurs between the salt and the ice, forming a brine layer, rather than directly interacting with and harming the cement surface itself.

topic: Dangers of Mixing Common Household Cleaning Chemicals
lesson_text: Never Mix These Chemicals We all want to clean and disinfect our homes regularly to kill unwanted viruses and bacteria. It can be tempting to try out different cleaning chemical combos to make your own super-strength solutions, but . . . It can be dangerous—even fatal!—to mix certain chemicals together due to the exothermic reactions that can occur as a result. While commercial cleaning chemicals are safe to use on their own, when combined with the wrong solutions, things can go sour very quickly. Bleach and vinegar are two common household cleaners. Used separately, they can be very effective at ridding your house of germs. But when mixed, these chemicals produce chlorine gas. If you come into contact with chlorine gas, it can make you cough, make breathing difficult, and burn your eyes. When you mix bleach and ammonia, you get a toxic gas called chloramine. Chloramines on their own may not pose as much of a health threat. In fact, chloramines are used as disinfectants to treat the water that you drink. However, chloramine gas is very dangerous. It can cause shortness of breath, chest pain, burning in the eyes and lungs, and even death if inhaled at high doses. When you combine bleach with rubbing alcohol, you get chloroform. This product can cause severe problems if you inhale it, get it on your skin, or accidentally ingest some of it. In other words, you do not want to come into contact with this chemical. It can lead to heart problems, nervous system dysfunction, and other impairments. If you’ve ever gotten a scrape, you may have poured hydrogen peroxide on it to clean out any germs. Vinegar is often used for cleaning and cooking. Separately, both chemicals are safe to use, but a mixture of them can be very corrosive. Unlike the other dangerous chemicals mentioned before, this mixture is more harmful when it is touched rather than inhaled. Combining hydrogen peroxide with vinegar makes an acid that is often used to sanitize medical or food processing equipment. In all of its applications, the acid is only handled by professionals trained to use it safely.
summary: Mixing common household cleaning chemicals can be extremely dangerous, even fatal, due to exothermic reactions producing toxic gases. Combining bleach and vinegar creates chlorine gas; bleach and ammonia form chloramine gas; and bleach with rubbing alcohol produces chloroform, all posing severe health risks like respiratory issues, chemical burns, or organ damage. Hydrogen peroxide mixed with vinegar creates a highly corrosive acid, dangerous upon contact, and should only be handled by trained professionals.

lesson_text: The Exo Expo The Modern Gallery of Art and Science welcomes you to experience the work of some up-and-coming artists in our latest exhibition: The Exo Expo! This brochure is your guide to the art pieces in this dynamic gallery of works inspired by exothermic reactions. We are proud to bring this amazing collection to you and hope that you will join us in experiencing the exhibit in person. The Colors of an Exothermic Reaction This vibrant piece depicts the temperature changes involved in an exothermic reaction, with red, orange, and yellow representing increased heat and light. The artist incorporates a small amount of blue in the space to the left, symbolic of the coolness that exists prior to the reaction. Technique: Acrylic on Canvas Artist: René Thompson The Life and Death of Iron Chlorine In this beautiful painting, the iron-chlorine exothermic reaction is dancing inside a glass cylinder. Our eyes are immediately drawn to the focal point, the bright flame inside the glass, which tells a story about a fiery reaction, while the smoke at the top serves to remind us of the significance of released energy during a chemical reaction. Technique: Metal Print Artist: J. J. Graham Element of Life Water is the “element of life.” In this symbolic painting, water gives off a violent reaction when added to potassium. The exothermic reaction produces the gases hydrogen and potassium hydroxide. Allow yourself to be mesmerized by the depth of the texture and movement in this painting. Technique: Acrylic on Canvas Artist: Andy Green Flight Balloons are symbols of joy and delight. The irony behind this beautiful painting is that the balloon is filled with hydrogen, which, when exposed to heat, is highly reactive in the air in which it floats. The thin, colorful walls of the balloon are the only thing standing between the hydrogen gas and the oxygen in the air. Then the balloon is lit with a flame, and it combusts in an exothermic reaction. Technique: Acrylic on Canvas Artist: Xia Teng Chain Reaction Firecrackers are traditionally used around the world in celebration of holidays. This artist is depicting their innocence, as they lie flat and unused. Our eyes are drawn to the lively colors, then we remember the excitement of the flashes and bangs coming from the reaction that will chase the lit fuse from one end of the strand to the other. Technique: Metal Print Artist: Al Mlynowski Old and New Perhaps our exhibit’s most renowned piece, “Old and New,” depicts the oxidation process of iron containing metal (the old) and the formation of rust (the new). Here, the artist takes a simple reaction that we encounter in our daily lives and turns it into art to show the beauty in everyday exothermic reactions. Technique: Mixed Medium Artist: Di’angelo M.
summary: “The Exo Expo” is an art exhibition showcasing works inspired by exothermic reactions, illustrating the artistic interpretation of energy release. Pieces depict various exothermic processes: temperature changes (colors of heat), the fiery reaction of iron and chlorine, the violent reaction of water with potassium, the combustion of hydrogen-filled balloons, the flashes and bangs of firecrackers, and the everyday oxidation process of iron forming rust. The exhibit aims to highlight the beauty and dynamism of these chemical phenomena.

topic: Introduction to the Engineering Design Process
lesson_text: The Engineering Design Process Have you ever tried to build a model airplane, bake a cake, or make a fort in your living room, only to have things go horribly wrong? You may have experienced some type of design failure. There is much to learn from the engineering design process. This process encourages people to use problem-solving skills, and it embraces the idea of learning from failure. Engineers follow a systematic series of steps to design, test, improve, and retest their ideas to make solutions to problems. Sometimes designs work, and sometimes they don’t. While there are core characteristics of the engineering design process, the process also has flexibility. You can repeat certain steps before a design is finalized, and you can conduct some of the steps out of sequence. Vocabulary engineering design process, n. the steps that engineers go through when designing something new or improving a design criteria, n. the goals that a design needs to meet constraints, n. the limitations of a design Word to Know Simulate means to imitate the function or appearance of something else.
summary: The engineering design process is a systematic approach for problem-solving that encourages learning from failure. Engineers iteratively design, test, improve, and retest solutions, with flexibility in repeating or reordering steps. Key terms include 'criteria' (design goals) and 'constraints' (design limitations), and the process emphasizes simulation to imitate real-world functions.

topic: The Engineering Design Process Illustrated by Fictional and Real-Life Movie Engineers
lesson_text: Famous Hollywood Engineers There is nothing Hollywood loves more than producing action-packed movies that contain innovative and sophisticated technology designed to leave the audience in awe. But even in the movies, designs do not always go according to plan. It’s possible you’ve seen the engineering design process play out on the big screen without even realizing it! Some of the most well-known movie engineers and their designs are described here. Tony Stark in Iron Man One of the most popular movie engineers is Tony Stark from Iron Man and The Avengers. According to Marvel Comics, Stark is an electrical and mechanical engineer. He’s a genius and has a double major in physics and engineering. Soon after we first meet Stark in Iron Man, he is kidnapped. He needs to escape, but he has limited tools, resources, and time. He manages to escape by using an “arc reactor” that is implanted in his chest. Once back home, Stark works tirelessly to improve his Iron Man suit design. The audience gets to watch as several of his designs fail comically. Eventually, Stark improves the design enough to share the solution with the world as a comic book hero. The Engineers from Apollo 13 The blockbuster hit Apollo 13 is based on true events. In 1970, the astronauts aboard Apollo 13 launched for the moon, but an oxygen tank exploded, and they had to abort the mission. The movie shows how they fought to stay alive in space as carbon dioxide (CO2) levels crept higher and higher. Meanwhile, NASA engineers on Earth carried out the engineering design process to make a square CO2 filter fit inside a round connector using only tools available on the spacecraft. Throughout the movie, we see the dramatic steps involved in the engineering process, from brainstorming to building and testing prototypes. Time is a major constraint for the engineering team. They must act fast, as the astronauts’ lives are in their hands. In Apollo 13, the engineers can develop a workable design in just three days to save the astronauts! Wayne Szalinski in Honey, I Shrunk the Kids Wayne Szalinski from Honey, I Shrunk the Kids is a home-based inventor of interesting gadgets. One day he designs a machine, stored in his attic lab, that accidentally shrinks his and the neighbor’s kids. Before realizing what happens, Szalinski breaks his machine after feeling defeated at his career. Talk about a problem! But once Szalinski learns that his machine works, it’s up to him to save the kids. Szalinski must rebuild the machine to bring the kids back to normal size. Throughout the movie, we see Szalinksi engaging in parts of the engineering design process by identifying the problem, brainstorming solutions, and building the machine that will restore the kids to their normal sizes. In the end, his solution works, and his shrinking machine is a success! “Doc” Brown in Back to the Future Emmett Lathrop “Doc” Brown, PhD, from the Back to the Future trilogy is another one of our favorite Hollywood scientists. Doc Brown is a physicist who uses the engineering design process to build the fan-favorite DeLorean time machine. He wants to travel through time, but he needs to power his ”flux capacitor” to do so. In Back to the Future, the flux capacitor is originally powered by nuclear material. However, when Marty McFly is sent back in time, the nuclear material is not available to him there. For him to return to the current timeline, Doc Brown has to redesign the time machine so that it works without nuclear material. In the engineering design process, this is both a problem and a new constraint. Doc Brown has the challenge of brainstorming and testing ideas. Eventually, he works out how to make a lightning bolt power the flux capacitor. Dig into Data The DeLorean in Back to the Future takes 1.21 gigawatts (GW) to power the flux capacitor and travel through time. There are 1 billion watts in 1 GW. That’s a lot of watts! By comparison, it takes about 350–780 watts to power a home refrigerator.
summary: Fictional and real-life movie engineers demonstrate the engineering design process, including problem identification, brainstorming, building prototypes, and testing, often under significant constraints. Examples include Tony Stark iteratively improving his Iron Man suit; NASA engineers adapting a CO2 filter in Apollo 13 under time pressure; Wayne Szalinski rebuilding his shrinking machine; and Doc Brown redesigning the DeLorean to use lightning as an alternative power source, highlighting learning from failures and iterative problem-solving.

topic: Successful Products Born from Design Failures
lesson_text: Funky Failed Prototypes Designs do not always go according to plan, even when the engineering design process is carefully followed. Designs may start out one way but turn into something else. Here is a list of some famous design failures that turned into useful products. WD-40 If you’ve ever had a creaky door in your home, you may have seen someone put WD-40 on it. WD-40 is a commercial product, a lubricant that helps take away grease and protects against rust. But let’s break down the name: WD stands for “water displacement”; 40 represents the number of attempts it took to get the formula right! This means the developers of WD-40 failed at their formula 39 times before they could package it and put it out for commercial use. That’s 39 times of going around and around in the engineering design process’s build-test-improve cycle! Bubble Wrap It’s easy to think that bubble wrap was designed as a common packaging material. However, bubble wrap was originally designed to be a trendy new wallpaper in the 1960s. The trend did not take off, and the wallpaper was a flop. Later, the engineers of bubble wrap—Marc Chavannes and Al Fielding—tried to market it as housing insulation. But that failed, too. Eventually, IBM discovered that the material could be used to package and protect a computer when it was being transported. From there, bubble wrap became an overnight packaging success. Synthetic Dye Malaria is a serious disease that makes people very sick with high fever, headache, muscle aches, and exhaustion. In the mid-1800s, chemist William Perkin was trying to create an artificial version of quinine, a drug then used to treat malaria. His experiments failed again and again. They also left behind a sludgy, dark residue. Eventually, Perkin realized that the residue could turn materials a pretty shade of purple. He had accidentally created the first synthetic dye, mauvine. Synthetic dyes are commonly used in the interior design and fashion industries. In fact, you may be wearing a synthetically dyed piece of clothing right now! Wheaties Wheaties, the “breakfast of champions,” was the result of a fortunate misstep at the Washburn Crosby Company. While making bran gruel (a type of hot cereal that resembles oatmeal), a worker at the food production factory spilled some gruel onto a nearby stovetop. The gruel crackled and turned into crispy flakes. Curious, the worker tasted it, and everyone agreed that the flakes were better than the gruel. The Washburn Crosby Company decided to scrap their gruel recipe and focus on this tasty flake that could be eaten cold instead of warm. It took the company 36 tries (that’s 35 failures!) to develop the perfect flake that tasted great, would hold up in milk, and wouldn’t crumble when stored and shipped in cereal boxes. Workers on the product development team must have tasted a lot of wheat flakes during that design process! Slinky A Slinky doesn’t look like a traditional toy, and that’s because it was originally intended to work as an industrial equipment stabilizer. In 1943, Richard James—a naval engineer—developed springs that kept fragile equipment stable on boats. One day, James accidentally bumped into a spring that was on a shelf. The spring did its famous Slinky walk down the shelf, rather than just falling and hitting the floor. It was James’s wife who saw the potential for a toy. Together, they demonstrated the Slinky in front of the famous Gimbels department store in 1945, and it was an instant hit. Post-it Notes The Post-it Note was another prototype flop. In 1968, Spencer Silver, who worked for 3M laboratories, was trying to develop a mega-strength adhesive, but it was never sticky enough to fulfill the criteria. The adhesive worked well enough to stick to objects, but it could be easily lifted off. Silver tried to pitch the design to his company, 3M, but nobody was interested, that is, until a colleague used the sticky note as a bookmark for a hymnbook. It was then that they realized the Post-it Note had potential! In 1980, 3M began selling Post-it Notes to the public, and they have been a success ever since.
summary: Many successful products, from WD-40 to Post-it Notes, originated from failed prototypes or unexpected discoveries, illustrating that design processes often involve numerous iterations and learning from what doesn't work. WD-40 required 39 attempts; Bubble Wrap, initially wallpaper then insulation, found success as packaging; William Perkin accidentally created the first synthetic dye (mauvine) while seeking quinine; Wheaties resulted from a spilled bran gruel; the Slinky was initially an equipment stabilizer; and Post-it Notes arose from a 'not sticky enough' adhesive repurposed as a bookmark.

topic: Methods for Gathering Feedback in the Engineering Design Process
lesson_text: Gathering Feedback It’s very common to buy something and then afterward receive a phone call or an email from the company wanting to know how you like the product or service. Feedback is important to the engineering design process. Feedback can make improvements, solve problems, or address other concerns. Engineers rely on feedback to know how well their product works. There are different ways to gather feedback, depending on the industry. Some methods focus on the customer or user. Other methods are based on internal testing and peer reviews. Satisfaction Surveys A customer satisfaction survey is among the most popular forms of feedback. A survey is a list of questions that customers answer so an engineer may gather feedback on their product. From there, improvements to products can be made for quality control and to better meet the needs of consumers. Customer Ratings A rating is equivalent to a score. The question “How would you rate this product?” offers quantifiable options that can be measured. Ratings are usually quick and simple means of collecting feedback, requiring the customer to only click a button or a star on a digital device. Engineers use ratings to give themselves an idea of how well their product is working. Customer Reviews Customer reviews are short editorials about how a customer liked, disliked, or experienced a product or service. Some reviews are kept between the customer and the engineers. In these cases, engineers use the feedback to make improvements where necessary. Other reviews are made public for anyone to read. As with a rating, a review can influence whether or not other consumers purchase a product. Beta Testing A more technical and specific process for gathering user feedback is beta testing. Engineers test their nearly finished prototypes on customers before the products have been developed for general use. Participants use a product, such as a home security camera or a toaster, in the real world and describe their experience with it. Their feedback is sent to the engineers and developers to help them adjust their prototypes. Internal Testing Engineering companies have internal labs where designs are tested and evaluated against rigorous criteria. According to the engineering design process, once a prototype is built, it needs to be tested. The people who perform these tests are trained in setting up testing environments and simulations in a lab that will adequately assess a design to see how well it works. Whether an engineer is designing a software code or the seat belt for a vehicle, all designs go through a testing and feedback process. The results of a test are evaluated and presented to the engineers. A design that passes the tests and receives positive feedback can move forward. If the feedback is poor, engineers move a step back in the design process. Once improvements are made, the design is retested. This process can repeat as many times as needed for the product to work as intended and satisfy all design criteria. Peer Reviews Engineers also gather feedback through a process in which a peer, such as a coworker or other engineer of equal expertise, reviews a design and provides feedback. It is common for engineers to review each other’s work, checking to see that a design makes sense, is effective, is resourceful, meets the criteria, and works as intended. Word to Know When something is quantifiable, it means it can be counted or measured. Connection We live in a feedback-centric world. Feedback creeps into our daily lives in many ways. For example, the number of followers and likes on a social media account are all forms of feedback. Even comments as simple as “Love it!” or “Same!” are feedback. Where else do you notice feedback in your day-to-day life?
summary: Feedback is critical in the engineering design process for product improvement and problem-solving. Methods for gathering feedback include customer-focused approaches like satisfaction surveys, quantifiable ratings, and detailed customer reviews, which can be private or public. More technical methods involve beta testing, where users test near-final prototypes, and internal testing within company labs against rigorous criteria. Peer reviews by fellow engineers also ensure designs are effective, resourceful, and meet intended criteria, with poor feedback necessitating re-evaluation and retesting.

topic: Poetic Expression of Engineering and Design Concepts
lesson_text: Engineering in Poetry Poets have long expressed desire to understand the design of beautiful things and creatures, the architecture of physical spaces, and the meaning of life and love. Here are a few poems that embrace concepts of engineering and design, directly or through symbolism. Word to Know Symbolism is a literary method of using words or other means to represent something else, such as an idea or an object. Design Robert Frost 1874–1963 I found a dimpled spider, fat and white, On a white heal-all, holding up a moth Like a white piece of rigid satin cloth— Assorted characters of death and blight Mixed ready to begin the morning right, Like the ingredients of a witches’ broth— A snow-drop spider, a flower like a froth, And dead wings carried like a paper kite. What had that flower to do with being white, The wayside blue and innocent heal-all? What brought the kindred spider to that height, Then steered the white moth thither in the night? What but design of darkness to appall?— If design govern in a thing so small. The Props Assist the House Emily Dickinson 1830–1886 The Props assist the House Until the House is built And then the Props withdraw And adequate, erect, The House support itself And cease to recollect The Augur and the Carpenter – Just such a retrospect Hath the perfected Life – A Past of Plank and Nail And slowness – then the scaffolds drop Affirming it a Soul – Passage to India Walt Whitman 1819–1892 1 Singing my days, Singing the great achievements of the present, Singing the strong light works of engineers, Our modern wonders, (the antique ponderous Seven outvied,) In the Old World the east the Suez canal, The New by its mighty railroad spann’d, The seas inlaid with eloquent gentle wires; Yet first to sound, and ever sound, the cry with thee O soul, The Past! the Past! The Past— the dark unfathom’d retrospect! The teeming gulf—the sleepers and the shadows! The past—the infinite greatness of the past! For what is the present after all but a growth out of the past? (As a projectile, form’d, impell’d, passing a certain line, still keeps on, So the present, utterly form’d, impell’d by the past.)
summary: Poetry often explores concepts of engineering and design through direct mention or symbolism, reflecting on the intricate structures of nature, human creations, and life itself. Robert Frost's 'Design' questions a darker, underlying design in nature; Emily Dickinson's 'The Props Assist the House' uses architectural metaphors for life's development; and Walt Whitman's 'Passage to India' celebrates modern engineering achievements while acknowledging the past as the foundation for the present.

topic: Role of Stakeholders in the Engineering Design Process
lesson_text: Who Are Stakeholders? Designers, developers, and engineers must consider the opinions of stakeholders of a product when brainstorming the possible solutions to a problem. Some types of stakeholders are more engaged in the engineering design process than others. They help establish the criteria and constraints early in the steps. Other types of stakeholders are far removed from the process but still have an interest in the product later. Vocabulary stakeholder, n. an individual who has an interest in something
summary: Stakeholders are individuals with an interest in a product, whose opinions designers, developers, and engineers must consider during the engineering design process. Some stakeholders are deeply involved, helping to define initial criteria and constraints, while others have a more distant interest in the final product.

topic: Using a Design Test Matrix in Engineering
lesson_text: Design Test Matrix Whether you are building a portable air conditioner or a computer program, everything has its own set of standards. These standards often link back to the original criteria of the product. In other words, does the product do what it is supposed to do? As part of the engineering design process, products are tested once the prototypes are built. People who test the designs keep track of the test results. The information helps developers know if their designs work or need improvements. In engineering, it is common for testers to use a design testing matrix. This visual tool tracks important information, such as design criteria, the status of tests, and other notes. On the previous page is an example of a design test matrix that pertains to the development of a website. Design test matrices can vary, but they usually have certain basic features in common. Feature names are the parts of the design being tested. Design criteria are described in the requirements column. The criteria/requirements are what the product is being tested for. Features may have one or more lines of criteria. Below, you can see the feature for User Security Preferences taken from the table. Some design test matrices may include more columns for retesting features that previously failed their tests. When features are retested, the design test matrix must make it clear that the newer version is being tested. This means a new test case ID number may be assigned, the feature name may be changed, and/or the revised feature may get a new row on the design test matrix. Connection A design test matrix can be created for almost anything you make. If you wanted to perfect the recipe for the ultimate chocolate chip cookie, you could create a design test matrix that lists the different batches of cookies, what was different about each batch, and whether they pass or fail the taste test. You can keep testing and testing your recipes until you arrive at the perfect cookie.
summary: The design test matrix is a crucial visual tool in the engineering design process, used to track product testing results against original design criteria. It typically includes feature names, detailed requirements/criteria for testing, and notes on test status. This matrix helps developers determine if a design meets standards and identifies areas for improvement, often incorporating additional columns for retesting failed features and clearly marking revised versions.

topic: Application of Criteria and Constraints in Culinary Competitions
lesson_text: (Begin transcript) (Intro theme music) Jordan: Welcome back, friends; I’m Jordan, your science correspondent, and I want to thank you, as always, for listening to my Science Interviews Podcast. I’ve got a very special guest in the studio for today’s episode. I’m pleased to bring you a conversation with one of the world’s most famous pastry chefs . . . Patricia Collins, or as she’s known in the industry and on TV . . . Chef “Pastry Patricia” Collins. Chef Collins, thanks for joining us on the pod! Chef Patricia: Happy to be here, Jordan! Jordan: I must apologize right off the bat because I’m sure this interview won’t be as satisfying as your normal job, where you get to eat delicious pies all day long. Chef Patricia: [laughing] That’s true. I rarely work a day when there isn’t food for me to taste. Jordan: But trust me, it’s a good thing you aren’t tasting my cooking, so I’m doing you a favor by not having any food around. [laughing] So let’s just jump right into some background about you. I understand that you’re a pastry chef who graduated from the French Culinary School and went on to work as an apprentice for some high-level chefs in Europe. You opened your own pastry shop and then wound up as a judge on one of the most popular pastry competition shows on TV. Chef Patricia: You got it! After I opened my pastry shop, there was a series of events that put me in contact with the TV network. They asked if I would do a show with them because they currently did not have any available chefs with my pie specialty. Jordan: So, Chef Collins, as you know, this is a science podcast. And I always try to trace different topics to the science in them. So today I wanted to talk about how you go about selecting the best pie among the competing bakers on your show. I assume you use a strict set of criteria. Chef Patricia: For our baking competition show, all the contestants get a set of criteria. The criteria are the things that the pies need to have. All pies need to have a buttery crust that is flaky but doesn’t fall apart when you slice it with a knife. The filling of the pie needs to stay intact and not be too watery. There also needs to be a good proportion between the crust and the filling. Sometimes we add to the criteria to say that all the contestants need to include figs in their pie filling and things like that. Jordan: And you judge the pies according to whether they meet the criteria. Chef Patricia: That’s right. The pies not only have to meet the criteria, but they have to also taste delicious! And taste is a little harder to nail down as a criterion because it’s so subjective. Jordan: Do you use a checklist to keep track of all these criteria? Chef Patricia: Oh yes. We keep a matrix that lists all the contestants and their pies, as well as all the criteria. And we go through each one, line by line, to see whether the pie satisfies the requirements. Jordan: This sounds like it’s a lot more technical than how it appears on the show. Chef Patricia: It’s very technical. And contestants also must work within a variety of constraints. Jordan: Such as? Chef Patricia: Well, for one, time is their biggest constraint. They are racing against the clock. They also have limited resources and can only use the tools, equipment, and ingredients that we give them. So they have to get really creative. Jordan: And how do you select the best pie out of all the competition? Chef Patricia: The best pie is the one that meets and exceeds all the criteria and the one in which the quality of the pie is not sacrificed because of the constraints. The best pie also has something that makes it stand out from the rest. This boils down to ingredients and technique. Contestants may be working with the same ingredients, but one contestant may add more of one ingredient or less of another and come up with a brilliant flavor profile or consistency that no one else achieves. This is the sort of thing that sets the winners apart from the rest. Jordan: What happens when things go horribly wrong in a competition? Chef Patricia: Well, if something fails, it can lead to a series of cascading consequences. For example, if someone adds too much liquid into the filling of a pie, the flavor balance will be off, it will make the crust soggy, then the crust will fall apart, and then the filling will spill out of the crust, and you will be left with a messy soup. Trust me: the judges are not pleased when we are presented with pies like this. Jordan: Yikes. Well, here’s hoping there are no soggy pies in your near future! Thank you so much for joining us today, Chef Patricia. Chef Patricia: It’s my pleasure, Jordan. Thanks for having me! (Closing theme music) (End transcript)
summary: Chef Patricia explains the technical judging process for a pastry competition, which mirrors the engineering design process. Contestants must adhere to specific 'criteria' for their pies, such as a flaky, stable crust, intact filling, and proper proportion, sometimes with added ingredient requirements. They also operate under 'constraints' like time and limited resources. Judges use a matrix to evaluate adherence, and the winning pie not only meets but exceeds standards without sacrificing quality due to constraints, often excelling through unique ingredient ratios or techniques. Failures, like a watery filling, lead to cascading issues.

topic: Evaluating Scientific Claims and Advertising in Toothpaste Marketing
lesson_text: Toothpaste to Smile About! Denta-Pro Advanced Brush Your Way into Freshness Our customers are smiling and so will you when try Denta-Pro Advanced! Our all-new toothpaste is designed to instantly make your teeth healthier, shinier, and whiter so you can feel confident all day long. Denta-Pro Advanced toothpaste is better than other so-called leading brands. Denta-Pro Advanced offers dentist-tested and -approved cavity-fighting protection. Thousands of consumers have tested our product, and it is the number-one toothpaste used by celebrities. Our whitening formula is guaranteed to remove unsightly stains to make your teeth up to 50 times brighter! Now THAT’S something you can smile about! Spot the BS Heads up! There’s some bad science on this page. Can you detect which ad is making questionable claims? Which brand of toothpaste seems to have done a more robust job at testing their product? Nine out of ten dentists choose Denta-Pro Advanced as their number-one toothpaste and recommend it to their patients. Consider the Source Both ads feature toothpastes designed to do the same thing. Which ad contains more scientific claims to appear to have more robust testing? What can you infer about the quality of the design process based on the way the ads are written? A Smile So Bright, It Shines DentaDyne Advanced Toothpaste Try DentaDyne Advanced! And give your teeth the whitening protection they need. DentaDyne Advanced is designed to make your teeth healthier, stronger, and noticeably whiter after 14 days so you can feel confident in your smile. Our new and improved toothpaste is clinically proven to provide 8 hours of fluoride protection against cavity-causing bacteria. Unlike other leading brands, DentaDyne Advanced’s formula contains vitamin D, which helps prevent dental decay while mineralizing and strengthening teeth. Activated charcoal whitens your teeth while being safe and gentle on sensitive gums. Patients with periodontal disease reported feeling no sensitivity in clinical trials of DentaDyne Advanced. DentaDyne Advanced is endorsed by the American Dental Association.
summary: This lesson contrasts two toothpaste advertisements to highlight the importance of critically evaluating scientific claims in marketing. The 'Denta-Pro Advanced' ad makes vague, exaggerated claims (e.g., 'instantly make your teeth healthier,' 'up to 50 times brighter') and uses an unsubstantiated 'nine out of ten dentists' statistic, indicating questionable scientific robustness. Conversely, 'DentaDyne Advanced' presents more specific, measurable claims ('noticeably whiter after 14 days,' 'clinically proven to provide 8 hours of fluoride protection'), mentions specific ingredients with claimed benefits, and carries an endorsement from the American Dental Association, suggesting a more rigorous scientific design and testing process.

topic: Critically Analyzing Survey Design, Data, and Conclusions
lesson_text: A Survey of Food Poisoning Victims from MREs by Angela Yakowsky, MD Medical Director, FresherFoodsForYou Introduction Foodborne illness, also called food poisoning, is a serious and preventable condition that results from eating food that was contaminated by not being prepared or handled properly. Dozens of people recently became sick with foodborne illness after their Meal, Ready-to-Eat (MRE) warming mechanisms failed to heat their food to the appropriate temperature. In response, we conducted a survey of 230 households, all of which purchased MREs within the past 6 months. The survey consisted of 7 questions, and respondents could select from 5 answer choices. Of the households that were sent the survey, 125 responded. The results are shown in the table below. Question Extremely Very Somewhat or N/A Barely Not at all 1. How satisfied are you with the MRE you purchased? 17 36 5 13 54 2. Does the activated food-warming mechanism in the MRE work to your expectations? 9 13 10 20 73 3. How much has your digestive health been adversely affected by consuming MRE foods? 23 86 7 5 4 4. How disturbed are you by false claims that guarantee air-activated food-warming devices are safe to use? 91 10 8 2 14 5. How bothered are you that the MRE did not come with safe-handling instructions, which could have helped avoid foodborne illness? 88 27 1 7 2 6. How much has the severity of preexisting digestive ailments such as celiac disease, Crohn’s disease, or IBS been increased by the use of MREs? 38 32 50 2 3 7. Prior to the use of air-activated warming mechanisms, how concerned were you about getting a foodborne illness? 11 9 19 64 22 Spot the BS Heads up! There’s some bad science on this page. Can you detect the problems with this study’s design and the author’s conclusions? Consider the Source The author of this article is a single person holding a medical degree. While she appears to be the medical director of an organization, the organization’s name suggests that she is already invested in an outcome—getting more fresh foods to people—that could be more likely if the findings of her survey cast MREs in a negative light. Dig into Data What is one problem with how the author acquired responses to her survey? How could the data outcomes have been different if the questions were worded differently? 87% of respondents reported having serious digestive problems after consuming MREs. Conclusions The results are clear: the food-warming mechanisms for MREs are faulty and cause consumers to have digestive issues and food poisoning. MREs are unsafe to use, and the vast majority of those surveyed responded that their preexisting health issues worsened after eating MREs. There are too many false claims being made about MREs being safe, which misleads consumers, since most of them were not worried about getting foodborne illness prior to using MREs. Most consumers are bothered by the misguided advertisements that push MRE products on to people without properly informing consumers of how the warming system should work. It’s time to keep our consumers safe! Please help in our endeavor to pull MREs from the shelves and replace them with safer and healthier alternatives. - Angela Yakowsky, MD
summary: This lesson presents a survey report on MREs, designed to highlight flaws in scientific study design and biased conclusions. The author, Angela Yakowsky, MD, affiliated with 'FresherFoodsForYou,' likely has a conflict of interest predisposing her to negative findings. The survey design is problematic due to selection bias (targeting 'food poisoning victims') and leading, emotionally charged questions. The conclusions, such as 'MREs are unsafe to use,' are overstated and generalize findings from a biased sample, advocating for MRE removal based on flawed data.

lesson_text: Everyone needs to eat. Many people love to eat. A lot of people also want to look a certain way. These demands and interests create huge markets for food as well as diets. Don’t eat fat! No, fat is fine, but don’t eat meat! No, actually, meat is fine as long as you don’t eat carbs! One day a food seems great for you, and the next day it’s not. It seems like food and diet advertisements are everywhere! How can you know what’s true and what’s false? How can you apply the information to your own life? Keto Diet! Enjoy the fat, but cut the carbs! Go Paleo: Why eating like your Neanderthal ancestor might save your life! Carb-Loading: A Marathoner’s Menu The Mediterranean Diet Fish Oil Fraud? That’s what this book is about—scientific literacy, which means knowing how to think about science topics that you read or hear about. Our world has 24–7 news, social media, and too many websites to count. The amount of information we have to sort through is overwhelming, and all the information is not reliable. In the internet age, sources of information are often obscure or not trustworthy. It is good to process information with a healthy degree of skepticism. We will make our way back to various topics around food and diets by the end of the book. Along the way, the series of reading selections and the writing exercises that go with them will help you flex your mental muscles and sharpen your science literacy skills. The ability to read about science, understand the information, and tell truth from fallacy or misrepresentation is really important. Science literacy helps you as an individual and as a consumer, and it shapes the ways you affect the community in which you live.
summary: The widespread, often contradictory information about food and diets, driven by market demands and changing trends, highlights the need for science literacy. Scientific literacy involves critically evaluating science topics from various sources like news and social media, discerning reliable information from untrustworthy content, and approaching it with skepticism. Developing these skills is crucial for individuals, consumers, and community engagement.

lesson_text: Determining if someone’s weight is healthy or unhealthy isn’t as simple as labeling anything over X pounds as “overweight” or under Y pounds as “underweight.” The primary reason for the difficulty is the wide range in height and body types among humans. Some healthy adults are under five feet tall. Others are over seven feet tall. There is weight in simply being taller. Longer bones, wider muscles, and larger organs all add to a person’s weight. A seven-foot professional basketball player weighing 250 pounds is likely to be considered neither overweight nor underweight, while a six-foot person who weighs the same could be considered overweight or obese. To adjust to the differences in body types, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) uses body mass index (BMI) to estimate whether someone’s weight is potentially unhealthy. You can use the table below to see how height and weight yield a BMI measurement. For example, look for the height in inches of a 5’8” person in the first column: 68. Then find the weight, 177, to the right in that row. Move up from that 177 to the top of that column. That number, 27, is the BMI for a 5’8”, 177-pound adult. What does a BMI of 27 mean? The CDC translates the raw numbers into useful information like this: <18.5 = underweight 18.5–24.9 = normal, healthy weight range 25.0–29.9 = overweight range 30.0+ = obese range Okay, so an adult BMI of 27 means overweight, right? Well, not exactly. Because BMI calculations are based on average builds, they can be misleading. Muscle is denser than fat, so having a lot of muscle mass might skew a person’s BMI upward. Even people with normal BMIs might develop health problems if they have excess fat near major organs in their abdomen. Because of this and other factors, physicians and nutritionists take other measurements of a person’s physique to better assess their body mass. Body fat percentage can be estimated using calipers or by comparing a person’s weight in water and out of water. It can also be estimated by passing a small current of electricity through the body. None of these measurements are foolproof. That is why it’s important for a person’s perception of their health to be based on a variety of observations, not just one or two numbers.
summary: Determining a healthy body weight is complex due to diverse human heights and body types. The Body Mass Index (BMI) is used by the CDC to estimate healthy weight ranges, but it can be misleading for individuals with high muscle mass (as muscle is denser than fat) or excess abdominal fat. Physicians and nutritionists use additional measurements like body fat percentage (estimated by calipers, water displacement, or electrical currents) for a more comprehensive health assessment, emphasizing that health perception should stem from various observations, not just a few numbers.

lesson_text: Debate: Can a wrestler regain ten pounds by drinking a glass of water? College soccer teammates Scott, Stephen, and Andy are having dinner after a tough practice. Stephen has gone back to the beverage dispenser multiple times to refill his juice glass. He and his twin brother Andy reminisce about their days as high school wrestlers. Andy: Stephen, remember when we wrestled how we would lose so much weight at practice? Way more than we do in soccer. Seriously, I dropped ten pounds at some practices. Stephen: Same here. But then we’d go home for dinner. Mom would give us a meal, and we’d drink a glass of water and—bang—all the weight would be back on. Scott is a science major, and this story is not making sense. The Law of Conservation of Matter seems to have been broken, if Stephen and Andy are to be believed. Scott: Guys, are you saying your mom made you nine-pound dinners? And you drank one glass of water, and this somehow added up to ten pounds? That’s not possible. Andy and Stephen (in identical-twin unison): It’s true! Scott: No! You can’t lose ten pounds and then put that weight back on a few hours later without taking in ten pounds’ worth of stuff. You probably had a big meal and drank a gallon of water. A gallon of water is eight pounds by itself! Stephen: Scott, we know you’re a chem major and all, but we wrestled for four years and we know what we’re talking about! It was one glass of water, plus dinner! Scott: Okay, go to Professor Zimmer in your Intro to Chemistry class tomorrow, and ask him if what you’re saying is physically possible. If I’m right and you’re wrong, you both owe me a tuna melt from the snack bar on Friday after the game. If I’m wrong, I’ll eat a pound of raw onions. Stephen and Andy: You’re on! Your breath is going to be so bad! What do you think? Is it possible that the twins gained back all of their weight loss from just one meal and the water? The next day, in the chemistry building . . . Stephen: Hi, Professor Zimmer. Please settle a bet. When we wrestled in high school, we would lose ten pounds at practice and then put all that weight back on with dinner and one glass of water. Our friend Scott says we’re wrong. What do you think? Professor Zimmer: I’m sorry, but that’s impossible. You would need to ingest some combination of food and drink that adds up to the weight that you had lost. Your body cannot create matter from nothing. That Friday, the twins each buy Scott a tuna melt on rye. He ate it all in one sitting, adding one pound and three ounces to his body weight! The quickest but not always the safest way to lose weight is to lose water. The human body is, by mass, about 60% water. That percentage is even higher in infants. Where is all this water? Two-thirds is in cells. The other third is in extracellular fluids, including urine, lymph, and blood plasma, the liquid that carries red and white blood cells throughout the body. Some tissues and organs have more water than others. The brain is about 73% water. For muscles and kidneys, it’s 79%. As you might expect, bones are less watery but are still 31% water. You release water all the time. It’s exhaled when you breathe. It seeps out of sweat glands when you’re hot or exercising. Your excretory system sends it out of your body when you use the bathroom. A person’s weight can fluctuate by pounds within a single day just by increasing the amount of water that leaves the body. A wrestler, for example, might need to “make” or “cut” weight to be eligible for a match. That means the wrestler needs to gain or lose weight in a short period of time to qualify for a certain weight class. A wrestler who needs to lose weight might go for a long run while wearing hot, heavy clothing. Miles later, the wrestler might have sweated and breathed out anywhere from two to ten pounds of water. Some wrestlers take things too far and put their own health at risk to cut weight. Wearing rubber suits during heavy exercise and taking dehydrating drugs are concerns in the sport. The second way to lose weight is to lose muscle mass, although this takes much more time than losing water weight. Any person can see a decline in the size of their muscles if they are physically inactive for a long period of time. Muscles that are not used will shrink and atrophy. This occurs when the proteins that make up muscle break down faster than the body can make them. Some illnesses can lead to muscle atrophy. A diet that is very low in protein can also make it difficult for a person to maintain their muscle mass, even if they are getting enough food overall. Some people deliberately gain or lose muscle mass to alter their appearance. In 2005, the actor Christian Bale appeared in two feature films looking very different. To play the lead in the The Machinist, Bale lost sixty pounds in just four months by living on a diet of canned tuna and apples. He lost whatever fat he had but also muscle. To bulk up for the role of Batman, Bale gained a hundred pounds, much of it muscle. To do this, he ate protein-rich foods and lifted weights. This kind of rapid loss and gain of weight is not advisable, nor do most people attempt this sort of thing. A doctor carefully monitored these kinds of weight changes. The process of aging can also lead to a loss of muscle mass. After age 30, a person can expect to lose about 5% of their muscle mass per decade. Part of the reason may be a decline in activity, but it’s also a function of an older body not being as good at breaking down proteins in foods. To combat the general trend of losing muscle as one ages, it is recommended that people use resistance training (lift weights, use resistance bands, or do body-weight exercises) and consume more protein. Another way of losing weight is to slowly and safely shed fat. This method is between water weight loss and muscle wasting in terms of speed. Unlike water and muscle, fat is used as an energy source. The key is reducing food intake while maintaining a healthy diet so that your metabolism taps into body fat to get the energy it needs. Diet and exercise, especially resistance training, can lead to a loss of fat and a gain of muscle mass, for a net weight loss that is less than the amount of fat lost.
summary: Weight loss occurs through three main mechanisms: water loss, muscle mass loss, and fat loss. Water loss is the quickest and can cause significant daily fluctuations due to bodily processes like breathing, sweating, and excretion; however, extreme methods for rapid water loss (e.g., by wrestlers) are risky. Muscle mass loss is slower, resulting from inactivity, illness, aging, or low-protein diets, but can be countered by resistance training and sufficient protein. Fat loss is the slowest and safest method, involving reducing food intake to prompt the body to use stored fat for energy, with diet and resistance exercise promoting fat reduction and muscle gain.

lesson_text: Spot the BS Heads up! There’s some bad science on these pages. The idea that exercising a certain part of your body might lead to fat loss in that same part is a myth. Stored fat must be broken down into glycerol and fatty acids before it can become energy. The bloodstream distributes these by-products far and wide in the body. When the body needs to “burn” fat, any of the body’s fat cells can be called into action. How muscular a person appears does depend, to some extent, on muscle mass and tone, but it’s largely a function of having very little body fat. Someone can spend hours on abdominal muscle exercises, but if they don’t burn off belly fat, those strong abs will not be visible.
summary: "Spot reduction," the belief that exercising a specific body part burns fat in that area, is a myth. Stored fat is broken down into glycerol and fatty acids, distributed throughout the bloodstream, and can be used for energy from any fat cell in the body. Visible muscle definition, such as abdominal abs, depends less on specific muscle exercises and more on reducing overall body fat.

lesson_text: Unexplained weight changes are sometimes a sign that a person’s digestive system is not working as it should. Physicians need to see inside the body to diagnose the problem. Endoscopy is the use of various technologies to see inside a person’s body using cameras or “scopes” of some type. Endoscopies are often prescribed to figure out what might be causing weight loss or to identify the source of bleeding or discomfort in the intestines. As technology advances, more techniques and devices are added to the endoscopic toolkit. Upper Endoscopy An upper endoscopy investigates the upper digestive tract. A camera is mounted on a flexible, snakelike tube with a camera and light mounted on the end. Various tools, such as a tiny grasping device, may also be attached to the endoscope. The tube is inserted into the patient’s mouth and throat, down into the esophagus, stomach, and first part of the small intestine. Air is pumped into the stomach to make it easier for the endoscope to illuminate and view the inside of the stomach and intestines. Depending on what the physician sees, tissue samples can be taken or minor surgical procedures can be completed, with the endoscope serving as the window into the patient’s digestive tract. Colonoscopy A lower endoscopy is known as a colonoscopy. The endoscope that is used is similar to the one used in an upper endoscopy. It is inserted through the anus and rectum and then maneuvered through the U-shaped colon after air is pumped in to give the colonoscope’s camera a broader view of the interior of the colon. If an unusual growth is found, a sample can be taken, and in some cases the growth is fully removed. Such growths can develop into colon cancer. For this reason, colonoscopies are now prescribed to most middle-aged adults as a preventive screening. Capsule Endoscopy Endoscopic surgery probably sounds quite unpleasant to you. Fortunately, a less invasive procedure is now possible thanks to the invention of the capsule endoscope. This is a wireless, pill-shaped camera that can be swallowed by the patient. It takes hundreds or thousands of photographs inside the digestive tract. The capsule does not need to be retrieved. Instead, the image files are sent wirelessly to a recorder worn by the patient for about eight hours as the capsule works its way through the patient. The recorder is returned to the physician for analysis of the images, and the capsule is eventually excreted. Connection The capsule endoscope is one of many modern digital cameras made possible by advances in small-scale lenses, microchips, and high-capacity memory cards. Each of these are vital components. Wireless technology allows the capsule endoscope to be disposable.
summary: Unexplained weight changes or digestive issues often require endoscopy, a procedure using cameras and scopes to visualize the body's interior. Upper endoscopies examine the esophagus, stomach, and small intestine, allowing for diagnosis, tissue sampling, and minor procedures. Colonoscopies, or lower endoscopies, explore the colon, enabling the detection and removal of growths that could lead to colon cancer. Capsule endoscopy offers a less invasive alternative, using a swallowable pill-camera to wirelessly capture images of the digestive tract, which are then analyzed by a physician.

topic: The Science of Animal and Human Feces
lesson_text: It’s natural to think poop is icky and funny, but it’s something that pretty much all animals do. Scientists can learn a lot about an animal by taking a close look at its poop! North Atlantic right whales are endangered. In a race to save this species, scientists collect their poop, which is orange and greasy and easy to spot on the ocean surface. Small samples are then analyzed for hormones that indicate whether the whale was stressed, hungry, or well-fed. Another large ocean animal, the whale shark, releases plumes of poop that are twenty feet long. Shark researchers think that analyzing samples of shark poop can help them know exactly what these animals are eating, which in turn can reveal where they have been. Mammal poop is often called scat. Scientists can tell from the scat in an area which animals live there. From this sample of bear scat, a researcher can extract DNA to study the local population. The scat can also tell what the bear’s been eating. Hard seeds in the scat mean the bear has been eating berries. Fish bones might indicate the bear gorged on salmon. Paleontologists can learn about the diets of ancient animals, including dinosaurs, by studying fossilized feces called coprolites. Sometimes the study of animal poop mixes with the study of rock and Earth’s history. The island nation of Nauru in the center of the Pacific Ocean is made of limestone, the remains of an ancient coral reef. The island also has large amounts of phosphate. The phosphate accumulated on the island over thousands of years because of bird poop that became fossilized. Because phosphate is a very effective fertilizer, Nauru was strip-mined of this resource—80 million tons of it—leaving the landscape scarred and degraded. Insects poop, too. Their poop is called frass. Some insects use frass to signal to others of their kind that it’s time to mate. Others use their own poop to help their young. When a female stink bug lays her eggs, she excretes a layer of frass on them. When the young hatch from the eggs, they eat the poop and get helpful gut bacteria from the mother. Civets are small, catlike mammals native to Asia and Africa. Most are omnivores, meaning they eat both plants and animals. A plant product consumed by one type of civet is the fruit of coffee plants. The seeds, or beans, inside coffee fruits are slightly altered by the chemicals in the digestive system of the civet and then pooped out. Beans are plucked from the scat of wild civets and sold for very high prices. The coffee made from these beans is less acidic than normal coffee. Unfortunately, in some cases civets are being captured and held in cages, with coffee fruit as their only food, to produce this special coffee. Earthworms are important for developing and maintaining soil all over the world. In one acre of land, earthworms produce tons of worm poop, called castings. The castings recycle nutrients back into the soil. Some people keep a worm composting box in their yard. Adding worms turns decomposing banana peels and coffee grounds into rich compost for gardening. Human poop can be analyzed to determine whether someone carries parasites. Sewage from a city can be analyzed for signs of communicable diseases. The COVID-19 virus, for example, can be detected and measured in sewage. At the Deer Island Treatment Plant near Boston, Massachusetts, sewage from Boston and nearby towns is processed so the water can be recycled. Samples of this water were tested for the presence of the virus. The graph shows sample data. Peaks on the graph correlate with when the numbers of known COVID-19 cases were highest in the Boston area.
summary: Feces provide valuable scientific insights into animals and humans. Scientists analyze whale poop for hormones, shark poop for diet, and mammal scat for DNA and dietary information. Fossilized feces (coprolites) reveal ancient diets, and bird guano contributed to phosphate deposits on Nauru. Insect frass is used for mating signals and nutrient transfer to young. Civet poop, containing partially digested coffee beans, produces expensive coffee. Earthworm castings enrich soil with recycled nutrients. Human sewage is analyzed for parasites and disease surveillance, like COVID-19, demonstrating the diagnostic utility of waste.

topic: Feed Conversion Ratios in Animal Farming
lesson_text: Raising animals to produce meat, milk, or other products can be a good way to make a living, but it requires an investment in land, food, and other costs. You need to have some idea of how much you’ll need to put into each animal to get the desired amount of product out of it. Feed is a big component of that calculation. One way that farmers think about this is to use a feed conversion ratio, or FCR. A low ratio means the animal’s digestive system is very good at converting its food into growth or production of the desired human food product, whether that’s the flesh of the animal or it’s something else, such as milk. The table provides FCRs for some animals that are raised for human consumption. FCRs are based on dry feed weights. For example, dry hay rather than wet grass is measured to calculate the FCR of cattle. Animal Feed type Product FCR Cattle grasses, grain meat 6:1 milk 8:1 Pig fruits, vegetables, grains meat 1:1 as piglet; 3.5:1 when in 200-pound range or above Lamb grain, soybeans, grasses meat 4.5:1 Chicken grain, fruit, vegetables, insects meat 2:1 eggs 2:1 Rabbit grasses meat 3:1 Atlantic salmon fishmeal (fish oil and other fish parts) meat 1.5:1 Catfish soybean pellets meat 2:1 Crickets fruit, vegetables, grain whole cricket 1:1 A piglet’s metabolism is so efficient that it adds almost as much mass to its body as it takes in. The piglet’s mother, on the other hand, has a higher FCR. A lamb fed concentrated, manufactured feed has a low FCR. If the lamb were to graze on grass, the FCR would be many times higher. The FCR for farmed Atlantic salmon is very low. However, this is based on a concentrated fish feed made of fishmeal and fish oil processed from other fish. For wild salmon, the FCR is closer to 4:1. Crickets can be farmed by providing them with a habitat and grain or other plant matter to eat. An FCR of 1:1 makes the cricket one of the most efficient animals to raise. There is great interest in adding more insects to the human diet because of the low FCRs and the high protein content of insects. Connection There are other costs in farming. Cattle eat a lot of food and need space, but they also emit a lot of methane—a powerful greenhouse gas—and consume a lot of water. Salmon farming requires pens to contain them if the farm is in the ocean or large, constructed pools if the farm is on land.
summary: Feed Conversion Ratio (FCR) measures an animal's efficiency in converting feed into growth or product (meat, milk, etc.), with lower ratios indicating greater efficiency. FCR is a critical economic factor in animal farming. Examples include crickets and piglets with very low FCRs (around 1:1), making them highly efficient, while cattle have higher FCRs (6:1 for meat, 8:1 for milk). FCRs can vary based on feed type (e.g., concentrated vs. grazing). Beyond feed, farming also involves other costs and environmental impacts like methane emissions from cattle and space requirements for aquaculture.

lesson_text: Ruminants are large, hooved mammals, including cows, sheep, and goats. They eat grasses, hay, and straw. Humans and other many other mammals cannot efficiently ingest and digest these fibrous materials. Ruminants get their name from their rumen, the first of four chambers of their stomachs. Follow the illustration to track food as it is eaten by the cow. 1. Large teeth chop and grind plant matter into smaller pieces. Very large amounts of saliva begin the chemical digestion of the food. 2. Food moves through the esophagus to the rumen, the largest chamber of the stomach. A large cow can hold about 95 liters of material in its rumen. Microbes in the rumen help break down the thick cell walls of the plant matter in the cow’s food. The muscular rumen contracts, churning the material softer. Gases produced by the microbes’ activity accumulate near the top of the rumen. Older, heavier material sinks to the bottom. Tiny projections called papillae absorb nutrients released by the food. 3. The rumen sends some partially digested material to the next chamber, called the reticulum. The rumen and reticulum are mostly open to each other, like a kitchen and dining room connected by an open doorway. 4. Older, softer material in the rumen goes to the third chamber of the stomach, called the omasum. The omasum is lined with leaflike projections that absorb water from this material. 5. From the reticulum, material can be sent back up the esophagus to the mouth. There it is chewed more and digested further by the saliva. This is called “chewing cud.” If you see a ruminant chewing when it hasn’t eaten in a while, it is probably chewing cud. The saliva in the mouth helps neutralize the acid in the cud. 6. Next is the abomasum, or the “true stomach.” It introduces acidic juices and enzymes to break down the food even further. This is similar to what the human stomach does. 7. The food is passed through the small intestine, where most of the nutrients are absorbed. The rest moves into the large intestine. Here, microbes draw out more nutrients to be absorbed. The large intestine also absorbs water. The indigestible material is sent on to the rectum, where it becomes feces that are expelled through the anus. 8. The large volumes of food eaten by ruminants result in large volumes of feces, called manure. Connection Some words from ruminant digestion are used to describe similar actions in different situations. For example, someone who “chews the cud” is pondering an idea over and over. Likewise, to “ruminate” means to reflect on thoughts over and over.
summary: Ruminants like cows, sheep, and goats efficiently digest fibrous plant matter through a specialized four-chambered stomach. Digestion begins with teeth and saliva, followed by the rumen, where microbes break down plant cell walls and nutrients are absorbed. Partially digested food moves to the reticulum, from where it can be regurgitated and re-chewed as "cud" for further breakdown. The omasum absorbs water, and the abomasum, the "true stomach," uses acidic juices and enzymes for further digestion. Finally, nutrients are absorbed in the small intestine, and water and remaining nutrients in the large intestine before indigestible material is expelled as manure.

It's crucial to approach these claims with skepticism, as digestive aids and dietary supplements are not regulated by the FDA, meaning their claims are not necessarily proven or tested, nor are they investigated for potential harm.

topic: Products Derived from Animal Digestive Systems
lesson_text: Cheese is made by adding rennet to heated milk. Rennet is a set of enzymes made in the four-chambered stomachs of ruminants, such as goats and cows. Rennet causes a protein in milk, casein, to form clumps called curds. The curds can be removed and treated by aging, salting, and flavoring to make cheese. Many people love to eat sausage. Not as many people like to know how sausage is made. The natural “casing” for sausage is the long flexible, cleaned-out small intestines of pigs and other animals. Insulin is a hormone that regulates how much glucose, or sugar, is in the blood. The pancreas produces insulin, but in diabetics the production of insulin is ineffective. Insulin can be extracted from other animals such as cattle and pigs for use in humans. It is also manufactured using genetically modified bacteria. Insulin can be injected when needed, or it can be pumped in automatically from a belt-mounted insulin pump. Intestines are made of smooth muscle, which is a very elastic type of muscle. When the intestines are dried, the elasticity is preserved and turned into a very tough, long-lasting, wirelike material. Natural gut, made of cow intestines, is sometimes used to make strings for tennis racquets, guitars, and other products. Most modern racquet strings are made from synthetic materials. Connection The phrase “how the sausage gets made” is used in the context of something that might be unpleasant, often as a way of avoiding hearing how something is actually made or taken care of. This phrase comes from the production of sausage, which involves not only ground-up animal flesh but squeezing that meat and fat into casings made of animal intestines. The liver of the basking shark can weigh several thousand pounds. Because liver is rich in useful oils, this species has been heavily fished. A liver from the shark could be squeezed to yield hundreds of gallons of oil. This oil could be burned to light lamps or refined into different lubricants. Liver oil from fish is, in general, considered a healthy food due to a high concentration of vitamins D and A. However, overfishing can reduce the numbers of certain species to dangerously low numbers.
summary: Various products are derived from animal digestive systems. Rennet, an enzyme from ruminant stomachs, is used to curdle milk for cheese production. Natural sausage casings are made from the cleaned small intestines of pigs and other animals. Historically, insulin for diabetics was extracted from cattle and pigs, though now it's often bio-engineered. Dried animal intestines ("natural gut") are used for durable strings in sports equipment and musical instruments. Liver, particularly from fish like basking sharks, is valued for its oils (rich in vitamins D and A) used for fuel, lubricants, and health supplements, though overfishing poses a threat to species.

topic: Lactose Intolerance and its Genetic Basis
lesson_text: Out and About with Seojun A Food and Travel Blog I love pizza. Nothing is quite as satisfying as a slice with fresh mozzarella from Leo’s on Houston Street. It’s my favorite thing about living in New York. The problem is, if I have more than one slice, my digestive system rebels. This happens with ice cream, too, or any dairy products. My gastroenterologist friend Adam says I’m probably lactose intolerant. In medical speak, I suffer from lactose malabsorption. What does that mean? Here’s the text Adam sent me about it: Consider the Source This blog doesn’t appear to be written by a scientist, but the writer does include information from a friend who is a doctor specializing in the digestive system, and the blog cites a specific study from a well-known journal on medical topics. Take a look at the percentage for South Korea on the map. Just one word: eek! So, I’m guessing some of my lactose intolerance might come from my mom’s genes. I also looked on the map at Ireland and Germany, where my dad’s genes come from. The numbers are way lower there, meaning the Irish and Germans might be able to eat more cheese and drink plenty of milk than people from other parts of the world. Scientists think the gene associated with lactase production probably became more common over time in Europe as people became reliant on milk for survival. It makes sense. Someone migrating from Pacific Islands wouldn’t have had access to dairy cows. There would be no benefit to having a tolerance for lactose. In Europe, if your family had a cow and there wasn’t much to eat, you could at least have milk and other dairy products. If ingesting those gave your family a better chance of survival, then the tolerance for lactose in that area might become more common over time. Natural selection at work! Adam says I should just take a lactase tablet before I go down to Leo’s for a slice. I’ll give that a try. Right about now sounds good.
summary: Lactose intolerance, or lactose malabsorption, results in digestive discomfort after consuming dairy. This condition often has a genetic basis, with its prevalence varying significantly across populations globally. Scientists theorize that the gene for lactase production (the enzyme that digests lactose) became more common through natural selection in European populations as they developed a reliance on dairy for survival, contrasting with regions like the Pacific Islands where such a genetic advantage was absent. Individuals can manage lactose intolerance by taking lactase enzyme supplements.

lesson_text: Gastroliths Gastroliths (Latin for “stomach rocks”) are small pieces of rock that some animals ingest on purpose, despite the fact that these stones cannot be digested. Birds use gastroliths, which in the case of birds are called gizzard stones, to help them break food into smaller pieces. Because birds have beaks and lack teeth, they swallow large pieces of food. Ahead of their stomach is a muscular organ called the gizzard, which squeezes the stones against swallowed pieces of food. This functions almost like a toothed mammalian mouth, grinding the food into smaller pieces that are then more easily digested. Some marine animals, such as the whale and sea lion, have gastroliths but lack gizzards. One theory is that the dense stones help these animals remain neutrally buoyant in the water—that is, they won’t float too much or sink too much, allowing them to better control their bodies as they swim and dive. Another theory is that they simply ingest the stones by accident when feeding on prey on the sea floor. Eat Dirt Some animals eat dirt. And we’re not just talking earthworms. Mountain gorillas consume soil to absorb vital iron, which promotes the development of red blood cells. Elephants eat clay when they don’t get enough salt from their food. Even some humans eat clay based on the theory that the positively charged particles of clay attract particles of toxins, which tend to be negatively charged, in the stomach. The clay then carries the toxins out of the digestive system. This “detox” effect is seen in parrots, which ingest clay along with seeds and fruit that are slightly toxic on their own. Chimpanzees and baboons appear to do the same thing for the same reason. Eating clay lets these animals expand their diets. Plastic Pollution Plastic is so abundant on Earth’s surface, and often mismanaged, that it now ends up in the stomachs of many organisms that ingest it because it resembles food. Whales, sea turtles, and sea birds are especially vulnerable to this problem. Plastic bags can resemble the jellyfish that turtles hunt. Plastic cigarette lighters have been found in the nests of albatrosses. Presumably they were carried there by the parents to feed the young as though they are food. Many albatross chicks die as a result of all the plastic they consume.
summary: Animals ingest non-food items for various reasons, with significant consequences. Gastroliths (stomach rocks) are deliberately swallowed by birds (gizzard stones) to grind food, and by some marine animals potentially for buoyancy control. Geophagy, the eating of earth, is seen in gorillas for iron, elephants for salt, and parrots, chimpanzees, baboons, and some humans who consume clay for its purported "detox" effect by absorbing toxins. However, pervasive plastic pollution is accidentally ingested by many marine organisms, mistaking it for food, leading to severe health issues and mortality, particularly in whales, sea turtles, and seabirds.

lesson_text: August 4, 2021 I’m so sick of being sick! It seems like every other day I’m either vomiting or having diarrhea—or both. I’ve lost so much weight that my clothes feel like they’re hanging on my body. I’m a coatrack.
