Most recent comments Consider the Sources Of the four people who commented on this post, who constructs theories primarily from observations of personal experience? And who provides science-backed documentation for their reasoning and explanation?
summary: This lesson uses a social media post and comments to explore the reasons for marine animal beaching, specifically a great white shark. Initial reactions often attribute such events solely to human activities like fishing or pollution. However, the ensuing discussion highlights that natural factors are also significant contributors, including illness, injury, disorientation from tidal patterns, or seeking refuge from predators. The text emphasizes the importance of critically evaluating information sources and avoiding immediate conclusions based solely on personal observations, acknowledging that while human activities contribute to environmental issues, they are not the only cause of marine animal beaching.

lesson_text: Collection 4 Population Dynamics 2 Harmony in Nature In the boreal forests of Canada, the lynx and the snowshoe hare exhibit a classic predator- prey population cycle. The lynx is dependent on the hare for food. The hare eats a variety of plants but is vulnerable to predation, and it can have trouble finding enough food, too. When hare numbers decline, the lynx population takes a few years to start declining. During Dig into Data What do you notice in the graph about the numbers of hares and lynx in relation to each other? periods of hare scarcity, female lynx have more trouble reproducing, and many lynx kittens die soon after birth. However, the decline in the lynx population allows the hare population to rebound. This occurs quickly because hares mature at a young age and breed well. The lynx population takes longer to rebound because the lynx does not mature quite as quickly and they do not produce as many young. Instead of having populations that remain balanced, the lynx and hare show what ecologists call dynamic equilibria—populations that fluctuate up and down as they affect each other. Isle Royale Wolves and Moose Isle Royale is a 207-square-mile island in northern Michigan. Wolves and moose migrated to the island long ago. The wolves probably got there by walking over the frozen lake in winter, while the moose are thought to have arrived on the island by swimming. Resident populations have lived there for over a century, engaging in predator-prey population cycles. The moose population can be replenished by moose swimming to the island, but ice bridges and human intervention are the only ways to bring more wolves to Isle Royale. Recently, the wolf population got so low that scientists began the process of applying for permission to bring in several dozen wolves from elsewhere. Without a healthy population of wolves, the moose population could soar to the point that they could overgraze on plants of the island’s forests. Animal populations rise and fall due to four factors. If the sum of the death and emigration rates is higher than the sum of the immigration and birth rates, the population is probably in decline. In some cases, such as islands that become cut off from sources of immigration, population change is entirely about the birth and death rates.
summary: Predator-prey relationships, exemplified by the lynx and snowshoe hare, demonstrate dynamic equilibria where populations fluctuate in cyclical patterns. Lynx populations are directly tied to hare abundance, declining after prey scarcity and recovering slower due to reproductive differences. Similarly, on Isle Royale, wolves and moose exhibit such cycles, with wolves crucial for preventing moose overgrazing. Animal population dynamics are influenced by birth, death, immigration, and emigration rates, with isolated populations (like Isle Royale wolves) being particularly sensitive to these factors, sometimes requiring human intervention to maintain balance.

lesson_text: Collection 4 Population Dynamics 3 The Bottleneck Effect October 12, 2020 It’s close to dusk on Southeast Farallon Island near San Francisco, California. We’re wrapping up another day watching for white shark predation on northern elephant seals. The seals are mainly juveniles that spend much of the year in other colonies of the California coast. The Farallon Islands offer food in the water as well as haul-out spots tucked into their rocky shorelines. The downside is, obviously, the presence of great white sharks, which also spend much of the year elsewhere but come here to feast on seals. A century ago, this predator-prey dynamic was probably absent from these islands, at least for this species of seal. In the 18th century, northern elephant seals and northern fur seals were all but wiped out by humans. There was a big trade in seal furs at the time. The Marine Mammal Protection Act has protected seals and sea lions since 1972. The large-scale hunting of elephant seals served as a bottleneck. The population was greatly reduced in a short span of time, leaving a very small population that had less genetic diversity than the original population. This is known as the bottleneck effect. Picture a bottle full of 100 marbles, with lots of different genes. Now imagine that 98 of the marbles vanish and only two remain. Those two marbles might be able to be the founders of a new colony of marbles, but the genetic diversity of the population is much lower. In some small founding populations of other species, bottleneck effects have let certain genetic disorders become more common in the new population. To use the marbles analogy, if the two marbles that survive and keep the population going happen to have genes that are associated with some type of cancer, those genes are going to be more likely in the new population as it grows. Even if the population rebounds, many individuals within the population might suffer from cancer and die at younger ages than did their ancestors. At one point, the entire northern elephant seal population was down to just 10 to 20 individuals. From that founding population more than a century ago, the population soared to about 150,000, most of which live in California’s waters. It’s unclear if the seals suffered from the bottleneck effect. That’s something we’re trying to figure out and part of why I’m out here watching for shark- seal interactions. When sharks prey upon seals, we race out by boat to collect seal tissue samples that might be floating in the water. This lets us run genetic tests on today’s elephant seal population to determine how that bottleneck that a small number of seals passed through in the 18th century affects the gene pool of today’s population.
summary: The bottleneck effect describes a sharp reduction in population size, leading to a significant loss of genetic diversity, which can subsequently increase the prevalence of certain genetic disorders in the rebound population. Northern elephant seals experienced a severe bottleneck in the 18th century due to human hunting, reducing their numbers to a critical 10-20 individuals. Despite a rebound to 150,000, ongoing research using genetic tests on tissue samples aims to determine if this historical bottleneck continues to impact the genetic health and susceptibility to diseases of the current elephant seal population, particularly in the context of predator interactions with great white sharks.

lesson_text: Collection 4 Population Dynamics 4 Strategies for Survival and Reproduction r-Selection Some organisms live in environments that are unstable, or experience a lot of change. In an unstable environment, it can make more sense for a species to mature early and produce lots of small offspring that require little care. By producing lots of offspring, the odds are pretty good that at least some of those offspring will have characteristics—or just good luck—that allows them to survive in the environment. This means the parents’ genes will be passed on to a new generation. By not spending a lot of energy and time caring for the offspring, the parents do not have to invest as much in the act of reproducing. This often allows them to reproduce earlier or more often. In general, this is a “quantity over quality” approach. Evolution has moved many species toward this reproductive strategy, which is known as r-selection. The chum salmon, Oncorhynchus keta, is an example of an r-selected species. Number of eggs laid: 900–8,000 Time from egg fertilization to hatching: 3–4 months Length at hatching: 30 mm Time spent with mother: none Maturity age: 3–5 years Lifespan: 5 years Adult mass: 5 kilograms Spawning chum salmon spend time building and guarding a nest in a stream bed, but for the most part the offspring are entirely on their own after birth. Many of the offspring will not survive their first weeks. K-Selection If organisms live in stable environments, a different reproductive strategy might make more sense. K-selected species tend to have long lives, mature late, and produce relatively few offspring that need more care. The offspring tend to be larger when they are born, and in some cases they receive a great deal of care from their parents for weeks or years after birth. This is a “quality over quantity” approach. The African elephant, Loxodonta africana, is a K-selected species. Time from egg fertilization to birth: 22 months Number of offspring at one time: 1 Mass at birth: 110 kilograms Time spent with mother: 4–6 years Maturity age: 10–12 years Lifespan: 60–70 years Adult mass: 2,700 kilograms A mature female African elephant gives birth to one calf at a time and will need to nurse that calf for four to six years. This is a tremendous investment of time and energy, but the payoff is a higher chance of survival for the offspring. Humans are another K-selected species. Vocabulary strategy, n. in biology, a behavior that occurs naturally in a population through evolutionary processes and reproduction (It does not require thought or deliberate actions of the species in the way that a strategy used by humans might. It is more like a pattern in how organisms exist over time.)
summary: Organisms employ distinct reproductive strategies—r-selection and K-selection—adapted to environmental stability. r-selected species, like chum salmon, thrive in unstable environments by maturing early, producing numerous small offspring with minimal parental care (a 'quantity over quality' approach), increasing the likelihood of some surviving. K-selected species, such as African elephants and humans, inhabit stable environments, characterized by long lives, late maturity, and few large offspring that receive extensive parental investment ('quality over quantity'), thereby maximizing individual offspring survival through dedicated care.

lesson_text: Collection 4 Population Dynamics 5 Extinction Events Every million years or so, about five families—groups of related species—have gone extinct. This is called background extinction. It occurs without a large-scale natural disaster or major event serving as a cause. However, some major extinction events have wiped out half of all families and over 90% of all species within relatively short periods of time. Dig into Data Which of the five mass extinctions in history caused the highest extinction rate? Analysis of some trends in biodiversity loss today suggests that humans are setting up Earth’s biosphere for a sixth mass extinction event. There are five major causes of species loss, as shown in the figure below. Scientists with the Zoological Society of London established a living planet index based on wildlife numbers in 1970 and declines in populations since then. That index has dropped by 70%. Connection What could a 70% drop in the living planet index indicate, and how would this affect Earth as a whole?
summary: Extinction occurs naturally at a background rate of about five families every million years. However, history records several mass extinction events that obliterated half of all families and over 90% of species in short periods. Current analyses of biodiversity loss, including a 70% drop in the Zoological Society of London's living planet index since 1970, indicate that human activities are contributing to what could become Earth's sixth major mass extinction event. This signifies a severe, human-driven decline in global wildlife populations and overall biodiversity.

lesson_text: Collection 5 Valuing Ecosystems 1 Bans, Boycotts, and Bargains People’s environmental concerns can lead to change. For example, when the United States passed the Marine Mammal Protection Act in 1972, it meant immediate protections for marine mammals from practices that harmed those animals in U.S. waters, including the trade of products made from marine mammals. However, that act, which was a federal law, did not protect marine mammals that were being harmed in international waters or in the waters controlled by other countries. People who wanted to stop whaling in non-U.S. waters launched the “Save the Whales” campaign in 1977. This was aimed at compelling other countries to stop hunting whales by boycotting goods made in those countries. For example, the campaign called for broad boycotts of goods made in Japan and Russia. The goal was to exert market pressure on the nations that were whaling. If, for example, a Japanese television manufacturer saw its sales to the United States decline due to the boycott, it might exert its own pressure on the Japanese government to ban whaling. In fact, Japan did ban commercial whaling by 1986. However, it allowed “scientific” whale harvests to continue, and the meat from those “sampled” whales ended up in food markets. This popular T-shirt in the 1970s called for people to boycott products made in Japan and Russia, two nations that were still hunting whales for commercial purposes. In California, a relatively small fleet of boats that uses drift gill nets to catch swordfish has been under fire for decades because the gill nets also tend to snag dolphins, sea lions, and other marine mammals that are supposed to be protected. This kind of “incidental take” of marine mammals in fisheries was not banned by the Marine Mammal Protection Act. So as long as the catch of these mammals in the gill nets is not deliberate, it is not illegal. Pressure from people who felt the fishery was getting away with killing or injuring innocent marine mammals led to the National Marine Fisheries Service’s new requirement that gill net vessels carry observers on board to monitor the catch and record incidents of marine mammal interactions with the fishing gear. The nets also needed to have pingers attached to them. The pingers emit a sound that warns some marine mammals away from the nets. Pingers and other rules have reduced the incidental take of marine mammals in the drift gill net fishery. The rules worked to protect the mammals, while the fishers were allowed to keep fishing. Word to Know A boycott is a deliberate, organized refusal to purchase certain goods or services. Dig into Data How do you think the graph of the incidental take of beaked whales would look if the National Marine Fisheries Service did not have rules that protected marine mammals?
summary: Environmental concerns can drive significant change through both legislative action and public pressure tactics like boycotts. The U.S. Marine Mammal Protection Act of 1972 protected marine mammals in U.S. waters, but international protection required further effort, exemplified by the 1977 'Save the Whales' campaign which used boycotts of Japanese and Russian goods to pressure those nations to end commercial whaling. Similarly, public outcry over incidental marine mammal bycatch in California's gillnet swordfish fishery led to new regulations, including onboard observers and acoustic pingers, which successfully reduced the incidental take of protected species while allowing the fishery to continue.

lesson_text: Collection 5 Valuing Ecosystems 2 Stability through Diversity A Lesson from the Irish Potato Famine and the U.S. Rust Belt When an ecosystem relies a lot on just one thing—one type of tree or one crop—it’s vulnerable to catastrophe. Diversity is a source of stability in ecosystems, economies, and agriculture. In the early 1800s, the human population in Ireland was growing quickly, but there wasn’t enough food. To solve this problem, potatoes were planted, and the potato became the staple of the Irish diet. This worked out well for a while, because potatoes can be planted by cutting them into pieces instead of waiting for seeds. Virtually all of the potatoes growing in Ireland by the 1840s were clones of the original type of potato that was planted decades before. This monoculture of potatoes was not genetically diverse, and it made the potatoes especially vulnerable when a fungus, called the potato blight fungus, came along and infected the plants. Potato blight destroyed the primary source of food for Ireland for many years, leading to the starvation and death of a million people and mass emigration of Irish people to other nations. If a greater variety of potatoes had been planted, some of them would have been resistant to the blight, and those varieties could have been planted in greater numbers in the following seasons. The lack of genetic diversity in the potatoes growing in 1800s Ireland made the crop more vulnerable to blight and led to famine and starvation after the potatoes were infected. We see a similar vulnerability in economies, especially those of small towns. If a small town has more than half of its workers employed by a factory or employed by businesses that depend on the factory, the closing of the factory can leave thousands without work. The person who installed car seats for 20 years may not have another good job to turn to, and the people who cut that person’s hair, sold them gasoline, bagged their groceries, taught their children at school, and provided other services could also be out of work. An economy that has more going on is less likely to be devastated. Why I Plant Monocrops I’m a farmer in southern Illinois. I have 800 acres that are not irrigated. That means my crops need rain and weather that isn’t too extreme. While I would love to grow a variety of vegetables such as tomatoes, eggplant, and lettuce greens, it simply isn’t an option for me. What can I grow and make a living on? Corn and soybean. The rainfall we get here is adequate for either, and by planting one crop for two years and then switching to the other for one year, the soil doesn’t get too sapped of its nutrients. Sometimes I have a mix of soy and corn, but a rotation usually makes more economic sense for my farm. In the winter, I plant clover so the soil doesn’t erode too much, and some nitrogen gets back into the soil before I plant the next season’s corn or soy. But that’s about all I can do, despite the call for diversifying America’s farms and moving away from monocropping. If I were to switch to the kind of diverse farming that the average American might hold in their imagination as a picturesque, harmonious ideal, I would need a major influx of money (lottery?), or my industry would need to stop getting subsidies from the government for soy and corn. For example, a few years ago, corn farmers received $2 billion in subsidies from Uncle Sam, which meant it was better for me to plant corn than anything else. The economics of this business and the physical realities of the climate in this area do not give me many options. Until things change, I am basically stuck planting soybean or corn on all 800 acres. Word to Know A subsidy is a payment from the government to an industry so the product of the industry has a relatively low price and remains abundant and the industry stays in business.
summary: Diversity is a fundamental source of stability in ecosystems, economies, and agriculture, preventing catastrophic vulnerability associated with over-reliance on a single resource. The Irish Potato Famine exemplifies this, where a lack of genetic diversity in monoculture potato crops led to widespread blight, famine, and mass emigration. Similarly, local economies dependent on a single industry face devastation if that industry fails. A farmer's perspective illustrates how economic realities, such as government subsidies for monocrops like corn and soybeans, and environmental constraints, can limit diversification despite its recognized benefits, trapping farmers in less resilient practices.

lesson_text: Collection 5 Valuing Ecosystems 3 Selectivity in Logging and Fishing Forest ecosystems are often affected by the extraction of timber, which is a term for the tree trunks that are cut down and then cut into lumber. There are several ways to harvest timber. Selectivity in Fishing Fishing is different from logging because in most cases the target species in a fishery are moving around, sometimes several thousand miles each year. Marine organisms are also harder to see than trees. But there are some similarities to the approaches that fishers and loggers take to resource extraction. Some fishing gear is not very selective. Other gear types are very selective and result in less bycatch and less degradation of marine habitats. Spearfishing is not very efficient, but it avoids harm to nontarget species. Hook-and-line fishing is more selective than trawling, but depending on the gear used, it can also catch nontarget species. Vocabulary bycatch, n. the incidental capture of organisms that are not targeted by a fishery or fishing gear Trawling involves pulling a large net through the water, often along the bottom. Some fish may be small enough to slip through the mesh of the net, but many are not, and not all the fish caught are target species. The seafloor can be heavily damaged by trawling.
summary: Resource extraction, whether logging or fishing, significantly impacts ecosystems, with varying degrees of selectivity determining the environmental consequences. Logging practices range from clear-cutting, which causes extensive ecosystem damage, to more selective methods that promote regeneration and habitat preservation. In fishing, where target species are mobile and harder to observe, the selectivity of gear is crucial. Non-selective methods like trawling result in high bycatch (incidental capture of non-target species) and severe degradation of marine habitats. Conversely, highly selective gear, such as spearfishing or certain hook-and-line techniques, minimizes bycatch and reduces damage to marine environments, despite potentially being less efficient.

lesson_text: Collection 5 Valuing Ecosystems 4 Tillman Marsh Town Hall Mayor: Fellow citizens, thank you for attending our town hall, where the topic of discussion tonight is Tillman Marsh. You may have read the letters that our own neighbors Dorothy Tillman and Stu Moore wrote in The Stillwater Tribune regarding their positions on what to do about Tillman Marsh. Tonight they are here to speak more directly on the various issues and seek your understanding and support so that we, as a community, can make an informed decision. Welcome Ms. Tillman and Mr. Moore. Dorothy: I’m Dorothy Tillman, and I’m here to speak on behalf of a group I’m proud to have founded, Friends of Tillman Marsh. I’m biased in favor of preserving this marsh because I’m a Tillman, but first and foremost I’m a human being who understands that I’m just one tiny piece of this town and the ecosystems that compose it. It’s easy for us to overlook each other and the contributions we make to our town, just as it’s easy to overlook what the fish, birds, crabs, clams, marsh grasses, algae, and even the mud and peat do where the land meets the sea, in Tillman Marsh. Those ecosystem services are so valuable, both to our town and to the larger system—Earth—that we all rely on. We should not sell out our town, our ecosystems, our fellow organisms, and the planet for a short-term influx of money in the form of shops, restaurants, and condos. Thank you. Stuart: Good evening, everyone. I’m Stuart Moore, but you know me as Stu. I appreciate the select board hosting this debate. I’d like to thank Ms. Tillman for her advocacy on behalf of the Friends of Tillman Marsh. I consider myself a friend of the marsh, too, but as a man whose made his living off the sea for a long time, I’m here to bring some reality to this discussion. Our town needs some diversity of economic activity to complement the biodiversity of Tillman Marsh. We need to find a balance between conserving and valuing that special habitat and conserving and valuing the people and economy of this town, which has fallen on hard times. We should not assume that developing a piece of the marsh into an engine of economic growth is an all-or-nothing, black-and-white thing. Much of the marsh will remain intact, including the creek and just about every inch of the marsh that is in direct contact with the sea. Fish will continue to come and go, and I’ll continue to clam. The shops and restaurants and condos will bring much-needed income and tax revenue to the town. Thanks. Consider the Sources Of the two speakers presenting positions in this forum, who constructs arguments from personal experience, and who provides science-backed information for their reasoning and explanation? Dorothy: Stu, I admit that you are correct that habitats and ecosystems can be reduced in size without necessarily destroying them. You’re right about that. But what concerns me is not just the footprint of the development that’s proposed, but the amount of damage that could be done during construction and how the development will affect everything around it once it’s done. The proposal caps the affected area at 50% of the marsh’s current area, but there’s no telling what percentage will be receiving sand, mud, concrete dust, and other stuff that could spill out from the construction site. Marshes are sensitive. You can’t just put up an orange plastic fence and some hay and assume everything’s fine. The same is true when this thing is done. Where will rainwater go? Does it all get diverted into the marsh or the creek? Does it become a heat island that heats the air above the marsh? Too many questions and unknowns. We know what the marsh does, and it’s taken hundreds or maybe thousands of years to reach its current state. Let’s respect that by leaving it be! Stuart: Dorothy, nothing is permanent. Some of the marsh is probably going to erode into the sea as climate change raises the sea level in the coming decades. If the marsh is strong enough to withstand hurricanes and other periodic threats, I think it’ll be okay with some construction dust and storm runoff. State regulations on coastal development will keep a tight leash on the construction company so pollution is controlled. I don’t like the idea of losing any of the marsh, but the fact of the matter is we really need more revenue in this town, and the proposed development is the best option we have. I really think that by giving up a piece of this marsh we will save the town and, by extension, help save the rest of the marsh and other green spaces.
summary: A town hall meeting debates the future of Tillman Marsh, featuring two main perspectives. Dorothy Tillman argues for complete preservation, emphasizing the marsh's invaluable ecosystem services, such as supporting biodiversity, buffering coastal areas from storms, and providing long-term ecological and economic benefits. She expresses concern about construction damage and unpredictable long-term environmental impacts. Stuart Moore, a local fisherman, advocates for partial development to diversify the town's struggling economy, believing a balance can be achieved between conservation and economic growth. He suggests state regulations can mitigate construction pollution and that the marsh's resilience will handle some changes, arguing that sacrificing a portion could ultimately benefit the town and indirectly protect remaining natural spaces.

topic: Science Literacy and the Climate Change Debate Introduction
lesson_text:
Elijah is spending a week at his grandparents’ house on the coast of Virginia. They bought a seaside house in Virginia in 1975 and have lived there ever since, working on the water.
Bill and Edie are telling Elijah that the beach has gotten smaller and that the sea has been rising for decades. “We probably don’t have many more years left in this house, Elijah. We hope it’s still in the family when you are our age, but that might depend on understanding the causes behind the rising sea levels and what, if anything, we can do about it.”
Elijah asks, “Has the sea really risen that much?”
“Sure,” Edie replies. “The high-water marks on the piers and where the tide reaches on this beach have all crept higher over the years. The beach used to be much wider, too.”
“Grandma’s right,” Bill says. “I’d say the sea is about a foot higher than it was when we were your age.”
“Now, don’t go and alarm Elijah,” says a familiar voice. It’s the next-door neighbor, Mike. Mike and Elijah’s grandparents are friends, but they disagree on a lot of things, including sea level rise and its causes.
“Elijah, one of the interesting things about the geological history of Virginia is a thing called subsidence,” Mike says. “It’s when a coastal area slowly sinks, which can make it seem like the sea is rising. But really, it’s the land that’s dropping. It’s been happening here for a long time. I know this because I’m an engineer, and I’ve worked on a lot of projects that the state has undertaken to deal with the effects of subsidence. Whatever sea level rise you see here is due to subsidence, not climate change.”
Elijah glances at his grandparents while Mike keeps talking.
Bill interrupts. “You say that climate change isn’t real, and we disagree. We also disagree on the reason the sea seems to be rising and also about the carbon we’ve put into the atmosphere, which you say isn’t doing anything at all. Now, go get to your fishing, and don’t forget to save us a couple of tuna steaks!”
Mike laughs and says, “Elijah, don’t worry. If your grandparents run away from the coast, you can come stay with us!”
While Mike keeps chatting away, Grandma Edie quietly says to Elijah, “Don’t mind the disagreements, kiddo. Mike’s smart and an old friend, but he’s held a different position about climate change for decades.”
Who’s right? Elijah wonders. This question of climate change seems pretty complicated. How can I find out more about it?
This book is about scientific literacy, which means knowing how to think about science topics that you read or hear about. Our world has 24–7 news, social media, and too many websites to count. The amount of information we have to sort through is overwhelming, and all the information is not reliable. In the internet age, sources of information are often obscure or not trustworthy. It is good to process information with a healthy degree of skepticism.
We will make our way back to the topic of climate change by the end of the book. Along the way, the series of reading selections and the writing exercises that go with them will help you flex your mental muscles and sharpen your science literacy skills. The ability to read about science, understand the information, and tell truth from fallacy or misrepresentation is really important. Science literacy helps you as an individual and as a consumer, and it shapes the ways you affect the community in which you live.
summary: The narrative introduces Elijah, whose grandparents observe rising sea levels over decades, attributing it to climate change, while their neighbor argues it's due to natural land subsidence. This disagreement highlights the complexity of climate issues and sets the stage for the book's focus on science literacy: the ability to critically evaluate diverse and often conflicting information about scientific topics.

Historical Evidence of Climate Events
In the winter of 1861, California experienced 43 straight days of heavy rain. This was caused by what’s called an atmospheric river— a climate event in which a vast amount of water vapor in the atmosphere, fueled by evaporation from the ocean and a steady breeze carrying the vapor over a continent. There the warm, wet air collides with a cold front and condenses into precipitation. The Central Valley, now home to some of the best farmland in the United States, was turned into an inland sea 300 miles long and 20 miles wide. Rivers that normally trickled from the Sierra Nevada mountains were turned into raging torrents that flooded their banks and swept away mining communities and 800,000 cows. It was an enormous disaster for the state.
Atmospheric rivers (ARs) are very similar to liquid rivers in terms of how much water they can move. California can be flooded when an atmospheric river that stretches all the way to Hawaii brings warm, moist air from the Central Pacific to the West Coast. Certain conditions in the ocean and atmosphere can produce long-lasting ARs, such as the one that flooded California in 1861.
Vocabulary
climate event, n. an occasion of extreme values of climate indicators such as temperature, precipitation, or wind
Historical records of droughts have been pieced together from written documents, stone tablets, archaeological evidence, and soil samples. In the Middle East, evidence suggests that many cities in the region were abandoned around 4,200 years ago, when the Akkadian Empire ruled the region. There is a thick layer of dusty soil that corresponds to that time. Above and below that layer is better soil. Archaeologists think the Akkadian people abandoned their homes to farm the irrigated land around the Tigris and Euphrates Rivers. People moved back to their cities when rainfall returned and the soil was farmable again.
Evidence of droughts can also be gleaned from dendrochronology, the study of growth rings of trees. In years with lots of precipitation, rings are thicker. During a drought, rings are narrow. If tree rings corresponding to a certain year are narrow across a large region, paleoclimatologists have evidence of a major drought event.
Ruins of ancient cities can provide clues about climates in ancient times.
This ancient tree trunk’s growth rings are tagged with historical events.
summary: Historical climate events, such as the 1861 California flood caused by an atmospheric river, illustrate extreme weather's impact. Evidence for past climate patterns, like droughts, is gathered from archaeological records (e.g., Akkadian Empire abandonment due to dusty soil layers) and dendrochronology (tree ring analysis), where thick rings indicate high precipitation and narrow rings signify drought.

Climate History
Left: freshwater paddlefish; middle: marine ammonite; right: depiction of asteroid strike
In 1991, a scientific paper announced the discovery of a massive crater in Mexico that represented the impact zone of an asteroid that struck Earth 65 million years ago. The asteroid exploded, filling the atmosphere with dust and debris, including iridium from the asteroid itself, and raining fire down upon the continents. Photosynthesis ground to a halt, and much of Earth was cold after the fires burned out. In 2013, in what is now North Dakota, a paleontologist discovered a snapshot of that terrible day: layer upon layer of stirred-up sediment and fossilized fish, mammals, trees, and marine organisms, all mixed up with tiny fragments of molten material that had exploded out from the asteroid impact. The inland sea that covered part of North America had been hit by massive earthquakes caused by the impact, and the sloshing action of the water acted like a tsunami, killing organisms from the ocean, rivers, and dry land and burying them in a mass grave of mud and sand. A fossilized mammal’s burrow dug into the site showed how the few survivors of the disaster tried to survive the cold and darkness.
It’s not possible to go back in time and record temperatures, rainfall, or other climate data in a direct way. Instead, paleoclimatologists look at fossils, layers of sediment, ice cores, and other types of evidence to infer what climates were like thousands or millions of years ago.
The thick ice of Antarctica has tiny bubbles of trapped air. By analyzing the bubbles and measuring how deep they are, paleoclimatologists know how much carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases were in the air hundreds of thousands—or even millions—of years ago. This has helped them make connections between other evidence of climate change—such as the absence or presence of fossilized plants and animals, the surface-shaping work of glaciers, and what greenhouse gases meant for climates in the past—and what they might mean for the future. The graph below indicates a rise in CO2 recently. Is this a result of human activity? What research data could help answer this question?
Ice core being packed for storage
summary: Paleoclimatologists reconstruct Earth's ancient climate history using indirect evidence such as fossils, sediment layers, and ice cores. A prime example is the asteroid impact 65 million years ago, evidenced by a crater and a mass grave of fossils and debris, which dramatically altered Earth's climate. Ice cores, containing trapped air bubbles, reveal atmospheric greenhouse gas concentrations over millions of years, linking past climate changes to greenhouse gas levels and aiding in future climate predictions.

Heads up! There are some questionable statements being made on these pages. Can you spot the bad science?
Words to Know
A logical fallacy is an argument or line of reasoning that can be disproven or taken apart by further reasoning. For example, if a person claims that something has occurred without human involvement, that does not mean it cannot happen as a result of human activity.
A straw man is an argument or point that one side of debate claims is being made by the other side, when in reality it is not. Usually, the straw man consists of exaggerated or distorted claims that the actual opponent has not made. In political arguments, this often involves unnamed people on the other side, because without naming an actual person, the straw man (or woman) can be as bad as its builder wants them to be, and their beliefs can be as scary as the builder needs them to be in order to convince people of something.
summary: Understanding logical fallacies and straw man arguments is crucial for evaluating scientific claims. A logical fallacy is flawed reasoning easily disproven. A straw man argument misrepresents or exaggerates an opponent's actual position, making it easier to attack, often used in debates to distort beliefs without naming specific individuals.

Climate Maps
Maps of climate data can help us see patterns. Unlike a weather map, which is a snapshot of a short period of time, a climate map shows data from a longer period. For example, on this page are maps of the United States (minus Alaska and Hawaii) showing the average temperatures for two months, January and July, over a 30-year period. Making these maps required thousands of temperature readings from thousands of weather stations from 30 different Januarys and 30 different Julys, across 48 states. That’s a lot of data and a lot of number crunching.
The data in these climate maps show a pretty clear pattern from a 30-year period: temperatures are cold in January and hot in July.
Historical temperatures from a long period of time can be compared to data from a short, more-recent period to assess if climate is changing. The map below shows which parts of the “lower 48” were warmer or cooler than usual in June 2021. In this case, “usual” was defined by the 30-year average for June from 1981 to 2011. The far right end of the scale represents an 11-degree increase in average temperature for the month of June, on the Fahrenheit scale. The far left end represents an 11-degree decrease.
Now also consider this. By definition, climate is “weather averaged over 30 years.” Is it good science to compare one year’s values to the 30-year average and make a valid conclusion? What if 2021 were an El Niño or La Niña year? Was there any other cyclical climate event that peaked that year?
summary: Climate maps visualize long-term weather patterns, unlike short-term weather maps, by averaging data over extended periods (e.g., 30 years). Comparing current data to these long-term averages can indicate climate change, but it requires careful analysis; a single year's data might be influenced by cyclical events like El Niño/La Niña and should not be used in isolation to draw conclusions about long-term climate shifts.

Water, Water, Everywhere
Eva, September 3, 2005
Looks like we’ll be seeing you a lot sooner than Thanksgiving! Katrina hit New Orleans directly on the 29th, and we’ve been staying in motels on I-59 since then, slowly heading toward Charlottesville. I’m emailing from the laptop of a former marine who’s heading down there to help with search-and-rescue operations.
We knew it was going to be a bad hurricane, maybe the worst of my lifetime, so we had the car packed and the house boarded up a few days earlier, and we hit the road on the 27th. New Orleans is vulnerable to a rising sea, and when a Category-5 hurricane is bearing down on it, it seems like water is coming in from every which way. The storm surge brings in ocean water, and the rain floods the city directly but also indirectly, as the river swells and punches holes through the levees. The canals within the levees flooded all at once, and the levees simply collapsed in some spots. Last we heard, they think at least 75% of the city is flooded, including 95% of St. Bernard Parish—our family’s home for as long as anyone can remember.
Like you, we’ve been watching footage of the damage and chaos on the news. People with nowhere to go but their rooftops, waving helplessly at helicopters. Motorboats in the street instead of cars. People crowded into the Superdome, with nothing but the shirts on their backs. A hundred thousand people just stuck in a flooded city. It’s early, but it’s hard to imagine how there won’t be a lot of fatalities from this thing.
We have no idea what’s left of our house and probably won’t know for weeks. Our assumption, just based on the footage on TV, is that our house is probably sitting in six to ten feet of water that’s going nowhere anytime soon. My dad says the mold that settles in the walls will probably make the home unlivable even if it survived the flood structurally.
Anyhow, it sounds like your parents have offered to take us in, and my mom has already been in touch with your school about enrolling me for the fall. Maybe we’ll be classmates? In English we were reading this long poem by Samuel Coleridge called “The Rime of the Ancient Mariner.” There’s a line in there that’s famous: Water, water, every where, nor any drop to drink. I keep thinking about that one line as my city drowns. :(
Love,
Jeanette
Hurricanes and cyclones are damaging (and often deadly) natural disasters that happen every year globally. Our best defense is to improve our landfall predictions and local response. In some parts of New Orleans, the floodwater filled homes, forcing people onto rooftops.
Hurricanes are fueled by warm ocean water and conditions in the atmosphere. Climate scientists predict that severe hurricanes will be more frequent and more destructive as Earth gets warmer. What scientific sources would you consult to determine if hurricane frequency is increasing or related to changing climate or not?
summary: A personal account of Hurricane Katrina highlights the immense devastation and human suffering, detailing how New Orleans' vulnerability to rising seas and catastrophic storm surge led to widespread flooding and homelessness. Hurricanes, fueled by warm ocean water, are predicted by climate scientists to become more frequent and destructive with global warming, emphasizing the critical need for improved landfall predictions and local disaster response.

In 2021, the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) reported that global warming was likely to reach or exceed a number by the year 2040 that the IPCC had been concerned about for years: 1.5ºC. The IPCC defines global warming as “an increase in combined surface air and sea surface temperatures averaged over the globe and over a 30-year period.” Some climate scientists have stated that the temperature increase is the result of emissions of carbon from coal-burning power plants, engines that power vehicles, and other industrial practices.
While the 1.5ºC increase is almost guaranteed, the IPCC warns that an increase of 2ºC would be much worse for ecosystems and human societies. Whether we hit 1.5ºC of warming (bad) or 2ºC (worse) depends on how much and how quickly we reduce carbon emissions into the atmosphere. The green “pathway” part of the graph below is based on emissions being reduced to zero by 2055. If emissions are not reduced, warming will likely reach 2ºC.
Did you know there are ways that any person can help slow the rate of global warming? Easy lifestyle modifications can make a big difference when people around the world make these simple adjustments:
✓ Reduce, reuse, and recycle the products that you use.
✓ Use public transportation, ride-share, walk, or bike when you need to go somewhere.
✓ Turn off lights, computers, and other electronics when you are not using them.
✓ Conserve water by taking fewer or shorter showers, using low-flow shower systems, and maintaining landscapes that are drought-resistant and do not require constant watering.
✓ Purchase products that have biodegradable or less plastic packaging.
There are also more permanent types of modifications people can make to help address global warming concerns:
✓ Make sure homes are well insulated.
✓ Install solar panels on rooftops.
✓ Seal windows so cool or warm air does not escape your home.
✓ Eat fewer meat and dairy products and consume more vegetables, fruits, and grains in your diet.
Dig into Data
The IPCC is concerned about global temperature changes reaching 2°C. The green area is a projection of what might happen, but many events could alter this prediction.
summary: The IPCC projects global warming will likely reach 1.5ºC by 2040, primarily due to carbon emissions from industrial activities and fossil fuels. A 2ºC increase, however, poses significantly worse risks to ecosystems and societies, with the outcome dependent on the speed and extent of carbon emission reductions. Individual actions like reducing consumption, using public transport, conserving energy and water, choosing sustainable packaging, improving home insulation, installing solar panels, and adopting a plant-rich diet can contribute to slowing global warming.

Tough Times in Tuvalu
This is my tenth trip to Tuvalu in the last two decades, and each time I’m here the sea seems to have swallowed up a bit more of this peaceful, lovely place. Tuvalu is one of the smallest nations in the world, both in total land area and population (around 10,000). It is one of the poster children of the climate crisis because the average height of its nine inhabited islands is 1.83 meters above sea level and the islands are just a few hundred meters wide.
I’m part of a seven-year project whose aim is to protect these islands and their people from the rising sea and some of the specific threats it poses. On this trip we are using lidar technology to produce highly detailed images and measurements of the islands, right down to distances from homes to the water. This will help us determine the best locations for concrete sea walls, which will protect the islands from erosion from typical wave action as well as cyclones.
Word to Know
Mitigation means reducing damage or severity of something.
Low-lying islands in the Pacific usually have groundwater that can be tapped for use by people, but when saltwater intrudes, the water can get too salty to be consumed. This has been happening on Tuvalu for years. Cement rainwater catchment tanks are one solution to the lack of potable groundwater, but climate change is making the dry season drier, which means it’s tougher to keep those tanks full. What’s more, the soil is getting saltier from the tainted groundwater and wash-over from storms. It’s a double whammy that’s making it harder to grow crops.
Meanwhile, the reefs are suffering from coral bleaching—another effect of global warming—and there are fewer fish and other sources of protein from the marine ecosystem.
I love Tuvalu and its people. My fear is they are running out of time. And as much as I believe in the climate mitigation work we’re doing here and elsewhere in the Pacific, I sometimes wonder if we’re just putting bandages on wounds that are too big to heal. Many of these people will need to leave Tuvalu and hope for refuge in other nations.
summary: Tuvalu, a low-lying island nation, faces severe threats from rising sea levels, including coastal erosion and saltwater intrusion into groundwater, rendering it non-potable and making soil infertile for crops. Coral bleaching, another effect of global warming, further depletes marine food sources. Mitigation efforts, such as sea walls and rainwater tanks, are underway, but the ongoing crisis suggests that many residents may eventually become climate refugees due to the overwhelming scale of the environmental challenges.

Causes of Sea Level Rise
Subsidence
Earth’s crust is solid, but it can behave more like the membrane that contains water in a waterbed. For thousands of years, North America was largely covered by thick, heavy ice. This weight caused the edges of the continent, including the East Coast, to pop up. As ice melted away, much of the continent rebounded, causing the edges to sink back down. This is called subsidence, and the process can continue even long after the ice is gone because the crust flexes slowly. Much of the East Coast is still subsiding for this reason. Subsidence can make it seem like the sea is rising when in reality the land is sinking relative to the sea level.
Vocabulary
sea level, n. the height of the ocean’s surface, measured via satellite and observable at shorelines
Plate Movement
This island also was lifted about two meters by an earthquake. Dead corals show where the sea level used to be.
This island was lifted about two meters by an earthquake. Dead corals show where the sea level used to be.
Earth’s crust is broken up into tectonic plates. When the edge of a plate is undercut by the edge of another, it can pop up. Sometimes this occurs very abruptly, as in an earthquake. This can change the relative heights of landmasses and the ocean in an instant. In other cases, the edge of a continent or a set of volcanic islands can rise or fall slowly over time.
More Liquid Water Means Less Ice
With very minor exceptions, the amount of water on Earth is fixed. What can change is the amount of water that is in solid, liquid, or gaseous states. When there is more ice, there is less liquid water. This means the ocean is shallower and landmasses seem taller relative to sea level. When ice is scarcer, as is the case today, the volume of the ocean gets larger, and sea level rises. The melting of the ice caps of Greenland and Antarctica and the glaciers of the Americas and Europe could cause the ocean to rise many meters over the next century.
These photos, taken from the same location in Glacier Bay, Alaska, one century apart, speak to how much of the world’s ice has melted and run into the sea. Consider this: The photos were taken from the same spot one hundred years apart, but were they taken in the same season? Would a seasonal difference in this location account for a substantial difference in this type of glacial ice?
Thermal Expansion
Satellite data show a steady increase in sea level in recent years. Melting ice has been the main contributor so far, but thermal expansion has also played a role. The above graph indicates that the global sea level is rising. Local conditions may vary. Sea level is falling along the Pacific coast of North America due to tectonic uplift and is falling along parts of the Scandinavian coast because of rebound upward due to removal of glacial ice formed during the last ice age.
Most substances expand when warmed. While water is somewhat unique in how it is less dense as a solid than as a liquid near the freezing temperature, liquid water does expand as it is warmed. As the ocean gets warmer, the molecules of water get farther apart. This means the volume of the ocean is growing even without the addition of meltwater from landmasses. It also means sea level will continue to rise even after the glaciers and ice caps have melted away.
summary: Sea level rise is influenced by several factors. Subsidence, the slow sinking of landmasses, such as the East Coast of North America post-glaciation, can make the sea appear to rise. Tectonic plate movements, whether sudden (earthquakes) or gradual, can alter relative land and sea heights. Critically, the melting of glaciers and ice caps increases the ocean's volume, contributing significantly to rising sea levels. Additionally, thermal expansion, where warmer ocean water molecules spread apart, also increases ocean volume and sea level, a process that will continue even after all ice has melted.

Effects of Warming Water
Mass Migration
Many aquatic organisms are cold-blooded. They can’t regulate their own body temperatures. This means they need to find and be in water that is neither too cold nor too warm. As bodies of water get warmer, some populations are migrating to higher latitudes to find cooler water. The American lobster is an example. Over the last 50 years, lobster have shifted from southern New England, whose waters have warmed, to the Gulf of Maine. This was great for lobster fishers in Maine but bad for those in New York, Connecticut, and Rhode Island. Since 2014, signs have pointed to the lobsters shifting even farther north, to Canadian waters.
Warmer Water, Less O2
Fish can die in water for many reasons, including toxic chemicals, disease, overcrowding, or prolonged cloudy weather. They can also die from lack of oxygen. Aquatic organisms need oxygen, just like air-breathing organisms. When water is cold, it can hold more dissolved oxygen. When it is warm, it can hold less. When a body of water gets warmer, levels of dissolved oxygen get too low to support fish and other organisms. Low dissolved oxygen can result in sudden die-offs of fish, known as fish kills. This occurs faster in lakes and ponds than in the ocean. Why? Smaller bodies of water heat up faster. In a lake, high air temperatures can cause the surface water to get much warmer than the deep water. The denser, colder water toward the bottom is less likely to mix with the less-dense, warm surface water when their temperatures are very different. Meanwhile, the amount of oxygen dissolving in the surface water is declining because it’s too warm.
A study of hundreds of European lakes showed that warming is connected to lower levels of dissolved oxygen. Most lakes with increasing surface temperatures had decreasing dissolved oxygen (DO). This could spell trouble for fish and other aquatic organisms.
Coral Bleaching
The white parts of these hard corals on a reef in Indonesia are bleached.
Coral reefs are important marine habitats, particularly in the tropics. Warming ocean waters are causing a phenomenon known as coral bleaching. Corals typically have color due to photosynthetic algae that live inside the corals. The algae provide food for the coral in exchange for a relatively safe place to live. This mutualistic relationship ends when the water is too warm and the corals expel the algae. The corals become noticeably whiter and are less capable of surviving. Vast swaths of reefs such as Australia’s Great Barrier Reef have died as a result of bleaching. Data seem to indicate the main cause is an increase in water temperature. Other factors, such as increased UV light, sedimentation, pollution, freshwater dilution, and disease, may also contribute to coral bleaching.
summary: Warming water significantly impacts aquatic ecosystems. Cold-blooded organisms, like American lobsters, undergo mass migration to cooler, higher latitudes as their habitats warm. Warmer water also holds less dissolved oxygen, leading to dangerously low levels that cause fish kills, particularly in smaller, faster-heating bodies of water like lakes. Furthermore, rising ocean temperatures induce coral bleaching, where corals expel vital photosynthetic algae, losing their color and ability to survive, threatening major marine habitats like the Great Barrier Reef.

Cows and Methane
What exactly do cattle have to do with global warming? It turns out the link between cows and the climate has to do with one type of natural gas: methane.
Each time a cow belches or passes gas, methane is released into the atmosphere. Scientists estimate that one cow can belch about 220 pounds of methane in a single year. But what’s the problem? Methane is about 25 times more potent than carbon dioxide (CO2) in being a greenhouse gas (GHG).
There are several different gases that account for the greenhouse effect, which is the trapping of heat by Earth’s atmosphere. Carbon dioxide is the GHG that is emitted the most by human activities, especially the combustion of fossil fuels such as coal and oil. When a CO2 molecule is struck by infrared radiation, it vibrates and redirects the energy in all directions. Infrared radiation ends up staying in the atmosphere longer than it would have if CO2 and other GHGs were not there to absorb it.
But let’s get back to the cows. When methane is burned, it produces water and CO2. If it does not burn and is released into the air, methane is better than CO2 at absorbing and redirecting infrared radiation. Methane emissions are believed to be much smaller than CO2 emissions, but because methane is such a powerful GHG, it is a contributor to climate change.
Methane is a natural product of the breakdown of organic material, such as the remains of plants and animals. This breakdown can occur relatively quickly, as in the digestive system of a cow. It can also occur over the course of centuries in Earth’s crust and in peat bogs.
Scientists and agriculture experts around the world are exploring creative strategies for reducing methane emission from cattle. New formulations of cattle feed may reduce methane, and certain chemical additives to food can also help.
Vocabulary
greenhouse gas, n. a gas in Earth’s atmosphere that traps heat
summary: Methane, a potent greenhouse gas (GHG) 25 times more powerful than CO2, is significantly released into the atmosphere by cattle through belching and passing gas. While human activities emit more CO2, methane's high heat-trapping ability makes it a substantial contributor to climate change. Methane naturally forms from organic material breakdown, including in animal digestion. Scientists are actively researching new feed formulations and chemical additives to reduce methane emissions from livestock.

Consider the following:
Ÿ The annual emissions of carbon dioxide from vehicles and industrial activity is 24 billion tons. According to the United States Geological Survey (USGS), the world’s volcanoes emit 200 million tons of carbon dioxide in a year. That’s all of the volcanoes combined, including the ones that are underwater.
Ÿ If volcanic eruptions were major sources of carbon dioxide in modern times, they would cause blips in the graphs of CO2 concentration in the atmosphere. Instead, such graphs are relatively smooth and with a clear upward trend.
In reality, major volcanic eruptions tend to have cooling effects on the climate. In addition to emitting carbon dioxide, volcanoes emit sulfur dioxide as well as ash that rises into the stratosphere and provides a shading effect by blocking some of the sun’s energy from reaching Earth’s surface. After Mt. Pinatubo erupted in the Philippines in 1991, Earth’s surface was about 0.5ºC cooler on average, despite the overall warming trend.

Melissa Perron
Hey, @Melissa. This is an old meme that’s been bouncing around for years. Volcanoes emit carbon dioxide, but it’s not even in the same ballpark as the amount emitted by automobiles in a year, let alone all human industry. And that’s just one year, certainly not all of human history. Take it from me, the only volcanologist in the family!

Annually, human industrial and vehicle activity releases 24 billion tons of CO2, while all global volcanoes combined emit only 200 million tons. Atmospheric CO2 graphs show smooth upward trends, not volcanic 'blips.' Major volcanic eruptions primarily cause short-term cooling due to sulfur dioxide and ash blocking sunlight, exemplified by Mount Pinatubo's 1991 eruption.

Climate and the Water Cycle
Of the greenhouse gases, water is the only one that condenses in the atmosphere at certain temperatures. Several major processes involving water are amplified by the warming trend.
Feedback Loops
A warming planet means the atmosphere and bodies of water are warmer. Warmer seas and lakes mean more evaporation. This puts more water into the atmosphere, which is also warming. A warmer atmosphere holds more water, which in turn absorbs more heat. This is a positive feedback loop that is changing the water cycle. There is also a negative feedback loop involved here. As temperature increases, so does the amount of cloud cover formed by increased evaporation. The increased cloud cover reduces incoming solar radiation and limits warming. Scientific data can give an indication of how these two loops work together.

warmer air holding
more water vapor
Saltier Tropics, Wetter Poles
Evaporation rates in warmer areas are increasing as Earth gets hotter, and the warmer atmosphere means that water vapor is slightly less likely to condense into rain clouds in the tropics. As a result, the water cycle is amplified but is also shifting more of Earth’s water away from the tropics and toward the poles. Ocean water is getting saltier near the equator due to the higher rate of evaporation and the decline in precipitation there, while more precipitation is falling at higher latitudes. There, the precipitation dilutes the salinity of seawater. In the North Atlantic, for example, the ocean receives fresh meltwater from Greenland’s ice cap and precipitation from the atmosphere, causing a decline in salinity. Scientists are keeping track of these issues. And science informs decision-making. If these changes in ocean salinity and a shift in the distribution of water are real, they would present a disadvantage to some regions and an advantage to other regions. What should the response of governments be to such possible changes?
summary: Global warming significantly amplifies the water cycle, creating positive feedback loops where warmer air and water increase evaporation, leading to more atmospheric water vapor that traps further heat. Conversely, a negative feedback loop involves increased cloud cover reflecting solar radiation, potentially limiting warming. This amplified water cycle is also redistributing Earth's water, making tropical oceans saltier due to increased evaporation and reduced precipitation, while higher latitudes become wetter and less saline from increased precipitation and meltwater.

In working with the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC), we can now safely say that the world should expect hurricanes to be more intense and wetter in the coming centuries as Earth warms.
Specifically:
Ÿ Hurricanes will cause more coastal flooding thanks to sea level rise, a product of global warming.
Ÿ Hurricane rainfall rates are projected to increase due to more moisture in the atmosphere.
Ÿ More hurricanes will reach Category 4 or 5 status, which is a measure of sustained wind speed.
Ÿ The overall number of hurricanes per year is expected to decrease or change very little.
IPCC observations show that since 1980, the intensity of hurricanes has increased, with a larger proportion of powerful hurricanes and an increase in how fast they intensify. It’s a matter of looking at the numbers. The 2021 hurricane season in the North Atlantic, for example, had both a high number of named storms and a high number of intense hurricanes, with six storms in Category 3 to 5.
I wish I had better news to report from the Dominican. I’m not sure where I will be off to next. Maybe we’ll see where the hurricane winds take me.
According to NOAA, in 2021 the North Atlantic had a high number of named storms, meaning tropical storms or hurricanes that were given names by the World Meteorological Organization. Only 2005 and 2020 had larger numbers of named storms in the North Atlantic basin.

Specific projections include increased coastal flooding due to sea level rise, higher rainfall rates from more atmospheric moisture, and a greater proportion of storms reaching Category 4 or 5 strength. Ocean Acidification
Not all of the carbon dioxide that’s been emitted into the atmosphere has stayed there. The ocean absorbs gas molecules from the air. Marine photosynthetic organisms need carbon dioxide, but the excess is causing problems as the seawater, which is naturally alkaline, becomes more acidic.
In water, carbon dioxide forms carbonic acid, which quickly dissociates into hydrogen ions and bicarbonate ions. This is what’s lowering the pH of the ocean.

Corals and many other marine organisms form their hard exoskeletons by absorbing carbonate ions from seawater and putting them together with calcium ions to form calcium carbonate. But with many carbonate ions instead meeting hydrogen ions and forming bicarbonate, there’s less free carbonate for these “calcifiers” to use. This pteropod is a small marine snail. Its shell is being dissolved because the seawater it lives in has become more acidic. Corals, oysters, clams, and other calcifiers are also projected to have a much harder time forming and maintaining their exoskeletons in the future.
summary: The ocean absorbs significant amounts of atmospheric carbon dioxide, which then reacts with water to form carbonic acid, increasing the ocean's acidity and lowering its pH. This process reduces the availability of carbonate ions, crucial for marine calcifiers like corals, oysters, and clams to form and maintain their calcium carbonate exoskeletons and shells, threatening their survival and broader marine ecosystems.

A Climate Refugee
I was born in The Bahamas on September 1, 2005. My parents were from Haiti, a very poor island nation not far from The Bahamas, and they settled in a Haitian neighborhood on the island of Abaco called The Mudd. It got its name from the fact that it was basically built on mud that was dredged out of the harbors and from the muddy roads—if you can even call them that—between the homes. Everyone lived in little shanties made of spare materials from construction projects in the nicer parts of Great Abaco Island. We were poor, but my parents said Haiti was worse, and they managed to make a living along with a lot of other Haitians. My mom was a housekeeper for the wealthy. My dad worked construction.
Close to my fourteenth birthday, September 1, 2019, Hurricane Dorian hit Abaco. It was the fifth Category 5 hurricane in the Atlantic in a four-year Hurricane Dorian flattened The Mudd, a settlement in Marsh Harbour, Bahamas, on September 1, 2019.
period, and it was one of the most intense storms on record. People who could leave the island did, but a lot of us didn’t have time or money or anywhere else to go. Some fled to the church, which was made of cinderblocks and could withstand the winds. Others stayed in their shanties. The wind and storm surge flattened The Mudd, killing thousands. We didn’t even try to look for any of our belongings. We knew they were either washed out to sea or buried in mud.
For a few days, we were allowed to stay in the church. Then the Bahamian government told us to head to Nassau, where we were supposed to get “help.” Instead, the government demanded our papers. My dad had a visa, but my mom didn’t. My dad stayed, but my mom and I went to Haiti, a place I’d never been and one that my mom did not want to see again. I guess this is what the prime minister meant when he campaigned with the slogan “Bahamas First.”
My dad is trying to find work so he can send us some money every month. There’s very little work here in Haiti, so my mom is trying to figure out a way for us to get back to Nassau even though we could get deported right back to Haiti. Supposedly the people on Abaco whose homes survived—including some of the wealthy—are struggling to find workers to fix and maintain their homes because the hurricane displaced so many of us from the island. Despite the need for workers for rebuilding, the Bahamian government's strict immigration policies forced the narrator and her mother to Haiti, highlighting the dire challenges faced by climate-displaced populations and the complex issues of refuge and nationalistic policies.

What Does It Cost?
When it comes to the topic of climate change, there are some people who fully support the idea of transitioning away from traditional sources of energy in order to use renewable ones. These people would like to see solutions like solar energy and wind power replace fossil fuels that emit carbon into the atmosphere. They argue that there are costs associated with inaction—specifically, it will be expensive to address the issues that come from climate change, such as increased severe storms, more frequent wildfires, and other problems.
They also argue that the costs of utility-scale solar and onshore wind power are declining. Both are already cheaper than coal, and with natural gas predicted to get more expensive, solar and wind will be cheaper than gas by 2030, according to the National Renewable Energy Laboratory.
There are other people who believe that if we make a choice to modify climate change, it will be expensive because it costs a lot of money to transition from old sources of energy to new ones. Humans have been reliant on coal, natural gas, oil, and other forms of fossil fuels for so long that there’s just a tremendous amount of infrastructure that is set up to use those fuels, not to mention billions of small-scale devices (lawnmowers, leaf blowers), vehicles, and appliances that use them also. Switching from nonrenewable energy sources to renewables, such as solar and wind, will require significant investment by governments and individuals. Turbines, transmission lines, and other machinery necessary to make renewable energy possible will need to be built. Building and establishing this equipment will be costly. Some estimates suggest the cost to combat climate change might be as high as $4 trillion per year.
Ÿ An economic analysis by the U.S. Office of Budget and Management and the Network for Greening the Financial System found that the annual costs of climate inaction in America would be $2 trillion by the end of the century.
Ÿ Federal crop insurance subsidies—what the United States pays farmers when crops fail—will cost between $330 million and $2.1 billion per year.
Ÿ Costs of responding to coastal disasters such as hurricanes will increase by $22 billion to $94 billion.
Ÿ Costs of dealing with wildfires could increase by 78 to 480 percent.
Ÿ More than 12,000 federal buildings and structures could be flooded by a ten-foot increase in sea level, at a replacement cost of $43.7 billion.
Although supporters of renewable energy claim that wind, hydro, and solar power are cheaper than nonrenewable sources (and thus will offset these manufacturing costs), others argue that renewable energy sources are only less expensive in the beginning phases of the transition and that the prices for these energies will surge once they become the more dominant form of power. So will they really be less expensive for the average household in the long run? There are also a lot of risks associated with transitioning to a new primary power source, especially when those sources are dependent on natural elements—elements that humans cannot control. There are questions as to whether or not renewable energy is as reliable and predictable as nonrenewable energy. If it’s not, this can become costly for a country that has made the switch but suddenly faces problems with getting stable and consistent streams of energy to its citizens. When people look at the costs of transitioning away from fossil fuels, are they considering how much money would be spent if things go awry and communities suddenly need financial assistance from their governments?
There are always financial costs in any decision. When it comes to climate change and the use of resources, who is right?
The graph compares the levelized costs of power generation of five sources. “Levelized costs” means the total costs of generating power per source, including power plant construction, their operation and maintenance, and the costs of any fuels. Because sunlight and wind are “free,” the levelized costs of these renewables have declined and will continue to decline through 2050.
Keep in mind that all of these technologies are changing and that some are quite new. Many factors go into total cost, such as transportation and storage.

summary: The debate over climate change costs pits the expense of transitioning to renewable energy ($4 trillion/year estimate) against the higher costs of climate inaction ($2 trillion/year in America by century's end, with escalating costs for disasters, crop failures, and infrastructure damage). While renewables like solar and wind are becoming cheaper than fossil fuels, concerns remain about the upfront investment, long-term price stability, and reliability of weather-dependent energy sources, prompting a critical examination of overall financial implications for individuals and governments.

Letting the Ocean Be
a Better Carbon Sink
The ocean has already absorbed a great deal of the carbon that humans have moved from Earth’s crust to the atmosphere. If it had not, warming of the atmosphere would already be much worse and the concentration of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere would be much higher than 415 parts per million.
When fish and other organisms are removed from the ocean, the impact on the carbon cycle is twofold: 1) Instead of organisms and their waste cycling into the deep ocean where large stores of carbon could be sequestered, millions of metric tons of carbon (MtC) in the form of organisms have been taken ashore and turned into food. That carbon ends up cycling mainly into the atmosphere as people digest the food and their cells respire. 2) Fishing vessels, which run mainly on diesel fuel, emit many tons of carbon dioxide directly into the atmosphere. Shipping seafood products adds to the overall emissions of the extraction of carbon from the ocean. Consuming less seafood could restore the carbon cycle in the ocean and enhance the ocean’s ability to act as a sink for “blue carbon.” The more carbon that’s allowed to sink to the ocean floor in the form of remains or waste, the less will enter the atmosphere.
One way to do this is to not take much carbon out of the ocean in the form of fish and other organisms we call “seafood.” Instead, if we let marine organisms go through their natural life cycles and allow their remains—and their poop—to drift to the ocean floor, more carbon will remain sequestered there instead of ending up in the atmosphere.
summary: The ocean currently serves as a vital carbon sink, absorbing atmospheric carbon. Reducing seafood consumption can enhance this role by allowing marine organisms to complete their life cycles, enabling their remains and waste to sink to the ocean floor, sequestering carbon. This prevents millions of metric tons of carbon from being released into the atmosphere through human digestion and the CO2 emissions from diesel-fueled fishing and shipping vessels, thereby strengthening the ocean's capacity to store 'blue carbon'.
