summary: At the library, Hanna creates a user account for the computer by first entering her library card number. She then creates a unique username, emphasizing that it should not be her real name to protect her private information. Following this, she creates a private password, known only to her and her dad, to prevent unauthorized access to her account. After successfully establishing her library account, Hanna proceeds with her homework, using the search icon (a magnifying glass) to find the required game website. She types "public TV games" into the search window and presses "return," which generates a list of websites. She learns that underlined words indicate links that direct users to other internet pages. Hanna uses the mouse to navigate and clicks the link at the top of the list, which leads her to a familiar TV channel website featuring kids' games. To play, she realizes she needs to create a separate account for this website. Drawing on her recent experience, she creates a new username (again, not her real name) and a strong password combining letters, numbers, and a symbol to ensure it is not easily guessed. With this new account, she successfully logs in to access the games.

3

She customizes her avatar by selecting various features like skin color, hair, eyes, clothes, and shoes from a menu of available options, demonstrating the creative flexibility to design unique, non-human characters if desired. Her dad then points out that colored tabs at the top of the screen categorize the games. She sorts these vegetables into designated baskets or bowls using drag-and-drop actions within a one-minute timer. After the game, her score is displayed and she saves it, aiming to improve it later. lesson_text:
Christopher Columbus was an explorer who sailed across the Atlantic Ocean and arrived in the Americas in 1492.
King Ferdinand and Queen Isabella of Spain had paid for his voyage. The fact that Christopher came upon land mostly unknown to Europeans made the king and queen happy. They hoped to find many riches in the Americas.
The Conquistadors
CHAPTER
1
2
The Spanish, and the Portuguese who followed, soon discovered that some places in Central and South America, as well as in Mexico, were rich in gold and silver. People just had to dig it out of the ground. The Spanish and the Portuguese sent conquerors to take control of the land and the people. Spanish conquerors were called conquistadors.
This is what gold looks like when it is first taken out of the ground. 
3
Hernán Cortés and Francisco Pizarro were Spanish conquistadors. They helped to make Spain rich. Hernán Cortés conquered the Aztec of Mexico and took their land. Francisco Pizarro conquered the Inca of Peru. The Spanish killed many people with their swords and guns. Some also died from diseases the Spanish brought with them, while others were forced to dig for gold and silver.
4
Spanish ships in particular, sailed across the Atlantic with gold and silver taken from Mexico, and Central and South America. This made some European kings and queens jealous. They wanted their countries to become rich too! And Spain and Portugal were not only searching for riches in the Americas, they were setting up colonies there also.
5
summary: Christopher Columbus arrived in the Americas in 1492, funded by King Ferdinand and Queen Isabella of Spain who sought riches. The Spanish and Portuguese later discovered abundant gold and silver in Central and South America and Mexico. They dispatched conquerors, known as conquistadors, to seize control of these lands and their people. Notable conquistadors included Hernán Cortés, who conquered the Aztec of Mexico, and Francisco Pizarro, who conquered the Inca of Peru, significantly enriching Spain. The Spanish conquest resulted in many deaths, caused by their weapons and diseases, and forced many to labor for gold and silver. Spanish ships frequently transported these precious metals across the Atlantic, prompting jealousy among other European monarchs who also desired wealth and sought to establish their own colonies in the Americas.

topic: Queen Elizabeth and the Lost Colony
lesson_text:
Some of the other European countries, including England, sent their traders and fishermen to the “New World” to make money. One ruler, Queen Elizabeth of England, wanted English settlers to go there and also take land, just as the Spanish and Portuguese had done.
To do this, Queen Elizabeth needed someone brave enough to set off on a dangerous voyage to find land that could be settled on. She chose Sir Walter Raleigh.
Queen Elizabeth and the Lost Colony
6
Sir Walter set sail to explore the eastern coast of North America. He needed to find the perfect place to build an English colony. Sir Walter found just the spot! When he returned, he sent a group of men to Roanoke Island, just off the coast of what is today North Carolina.
Sir Walter felt sure that they would be able to set up an English colony on this small island.
7
The first group of English settlers sent to Roanoke Island did not last long. Life there was too difficult, and they returned to England, leaving only fifteen men behind. Sometime later, Sir Walter sent a second group of English men, women, and children to Roanoke Island to try again. For a while, things went well.
A child, named Virginia Dare, was born there. But less than three years after they arrived, these settlers had all disappeared. No one knows for sure what happened to them.
8
summary: Other European nations, including England, sent traders and fishermen to the "New World" to profit. Queen Elizabeth I of England, seeking to establish English land claims similar to Spain and Portugal, commissioned Sir Walter Raleigh to find a suitable location for a colony. Raleigh explored the eastern North American coast and selected Roanoke Island, near present-day North Carolina, as an ideal site for settlement. The initial attempt to colonize Roanoke Island failed due to harsh conditions, with most settlers returning to England, leaving only fifteen men. A second group, including men, women, and children, was sent, and for a time, the colony seemed to thrive, even witnessing the birth of Virginia Dare. However, within three years of their arrival, all the settlers mysteriously vanished, and their fate remains unknown.

lesson_text:
For a while, the English did not send any more settlers to the New World, though they did continue to trade and fish there. These English traders brought back many valuable goods, such as furs, lumber, and pearls. They became rich.
9
Eventually, some of these traders went to the new ruler of England, King James, with a plan. They wanted to try again to set up an English colony in the New World. And they wanted to send settlers to search for gold and silver. King James agreed. The traders hurried off to find ships, supplies, and men.
10
Just before Christmas in 1606, three ships sailed into the Atlantic Ocean. They were named the Susan Constant, the Godspeed, and the Discovery. One hundred and five male passengers and thirty-nine sailors were on board. Also on board was a letter from King James telling the settlers what to do and how to behave when they arrived in the New World.
11
Soon after these English settlers set out, the winds died down and the sailing ships went nowhere. For six weeks, the three ships sat in the Atlantic Ocean, waiting for a wind to fill the sails and take them west.
As they waited, the settlers ate food they had planned to use in their new home. They drank the water they had brought with them. And as the weeks went by, they became sick.
12
Finally, strong winds did arrive. But the winds were so strong that they blew the ships in the wrong direction. Bad storms swept across the ocean, and enormous waves pounded the ships. Eventually, four months after leaving England, the three ships reached what is today Virginia.
13
summary: After the failure at Roanoke, the English paused sending settlers but continued profitable trading and fishing in the New World, bringing back valuable goods like furs, lumber, and pearls. Wealthy traders eventually approached King James with a proposal to establish another English colony, specifically to search for gold and silver, to which the King consented. In late 1606, three ships—the Susan Constant, Godspeed, and Discovery—departed with 105 male passengers and 39 sailors, carrying instructions from King James for their new settlement. The voyage was plagued by initial calm, leaving the ships stranded for six weeks, causing the settlers to consume their supplies and fall ill. Later, severe storms diverted their course, and after a challenging four-month journey, they finally reached the area known today as Virginia.

lesson_text:
Shortly after arriving in Virginia, the king’s letter was read out loud. The king wanted the settlers to find a good place to settle, where they would not be seen by passing Spanish ships. The land should also be near a wide, deep river.
This colony was to be named Jamestown, after King James. The settlers were to search for gold and silver as soon as they could.
John Smith and the Powhatan
14
A number of men had been chosen to run the colony. One of them was a young adventurer named John Smith. John Smith was a natural leader. But the other chosen leaders of the colony didn’t like John Smith. He was not rich and powerful. They refused to treat such an ordinary person as an equal. Instead, they left John Smith tied up on one of the ships.
15
This was a big mistake. The other leaders chose swampland to settle on. The land was also bad for farming. The damp swampland was good for one thing though—mosquitoes that carried a disease called malaria. The settlers were also not near clean drinking water.
To add to their problems, the Powhatan—the Native Americans whose land the settlers had taken—were not happy that they had arrived.
16
Eventually, John Smith became the leader of the colony. Even though half the settlers died in the first few months, John Smith persuaded those who survived to get to work. They chopped down trees, and they built homes. A strong log wall was built around the settlement.
17
That first winter was very difficult for the settlers. They were all cold and very hungry. John Smith knew they would have to make peace with the Powhatan. They needed to trade with the Native Americans for food. John Smith set off to do just that.
18
John Smith became friends with Chief Powhatan, the leader of the Powhatan, and with his daughter Pocahontas. The Powhatan agreed to trade corn and meat for axes and blankets. The food the Powhatan gave to the settlers was enough to last them through the winter. In the spring, those who had survived were able to plant their own crops.
19
Pocahontas helped the settlers a lot. She encouraged her father to give the starving settlers food. And she may even have saved John Smith’s life. After she married a settler by the name of John Rolfe, Pocahontas traveled all the way to England and met King James.
20
summary: Upon reaching Virginia, King James's letter instructed the settlers to establish a colony, named Jamestown after him, in a location hidden from Spanish ships and near a wide, deep river, with the primary goal of finding gold and silver. John Smith, a natural leader, was initially ostracized by the other wealthy and powerful leaders of the colony, who chose an unsuitable swampland for settlement. This site was poor for farming, infested with malaria-carrying mosquitoes, and lacked clean drinking water, further complicated by the Powhatan Native Americans' displeasure at their arrival. Despite half the settlers dying in the first months, Smith eventually assumed leadership, motivating survivors to build homes and a defensive log wall. Facing a harsh, hungry first winter, Smith sought peace and trade with the Powhatan. He befriended Chief Powhatan and his daughter, Pocahontas, securing vital corn and meat in exchange for goods, which sustained the settlers until they could plant their own crops in spring. Pocahontas played a significant role in aiding the starving settlers and potentially saving Smith's life, later traveling to England to meet King James after marrying John Rolfe.

lesson_text:
As the settlers got to know the Powhatan, they saw that they grew tobacco plants and smoked tobacco in pipes. The English settlers had not found gold, but they had found a plant that could make England rich. They realized that if they grew their own tobacco, they could ship it back to England and sell it.
Enslaved People in the Colonies
Many different Native American groups smoked tobacco. They made beautifully carved tobacco pipes. 
21
Before long, people in England were smoking lots of tobacco from Virginia. In fact, Jamestown was making so much money that the colony’s farmers wanted to grow even more tobacco. To grow more tobacco, they needed more people. Some people came from England to do this hard work, but before long, there was a need for many more workers.
22
Over a period of time, people were enslaved and brought from Africa to work on large farms, called plantations. These plantations were mostly in English colonies in the South. Enslaved Africans were not free. They did not choose to plant tobacco. These enslaved people were bought and sold like the tobacco they were growing. This is a sad part of our history.
23
summary: Through their interactions with the Powhatan, English settlers discovered tobacco, a crop already cultivated by Native Americans, which quickly became a source of potential wealth for England. Realizing its commercial value, the settlers began growing their own tobacco for export. Jamestown rapidly became profitable from tobacco sales to England, driving a demand for increased production and, consequently, more labor. While some workers initially arrived from England, the need soon escalated dramatically. This led to the tragic practice of enslaving and forcibly transporting people from Africa to the American colonies, primarily to work on large agricultural estates known as plantations, particularly in the Southern English colonies. These enslaved Africans were denied their freedom, compelled to labor in the tobacco fields, and treated as commodities to be bought and sold, marking a deeply sorrowful chapter in history.

lesson_text:
One group of people, called the Pilgrims, set off for Virginia for different reasons. They did not want to grow tobacco or find gold. Instead, they wanted to pray to God in their own way. This was not possible in England. So the Pilgrims set sail on a ship called the Mayflower.
24
The Mayflower was a small ship, and there was not much room for its 102 passengers and thirty sailors. The passengers slept mostly on the floor and in hammocks below the main deck. For the first month, the voyage went well. Then stormy weather arrived, and some passengers became very ill.
25
The storms at sea were so bad that the Mayflower was blown off course. The Pilgrims never arrived in Virginia. Instead, they arrived in what is today Massachusetts, in New England. The place they chose to settle had once been a Wampanoag village. The Pilgrims named their new home Plymouth.
The Pilgrims had also arrived as the weather was turning cold. It was too late to plant crops, and somehow the settlers needed to get through the cold winter months.
26
The Pilgrims set about building homes. Because it was so cold, the women and children slept on the Mayflower. Many people died due to the cold, sickness, and lack of food. People began to lose hope, but then spring came, and help arrived too!
A Native American by the name of Squanto, who spoke English, showed the Pilgrims how to plant crops on land that was new to them. 
27
Squanto also showed the Pilgrims how to hunt and fish. With more food to eat, the Pilgrims grew strong again. To celebrate, Squanto and members of the Wampanoag joined the Pilgrims for a feast of thanksgiving.
They ate roasted deer and turkey. They ate the fish they had caught and the vegetables they had grown. Once again, Native Americans had helped people from another land to survive.
28
summary: The Pilgrims embarked on their journey aboard the Mayflower seeking religious freedom, aiming to worship as they pleased, a right denied in England, unlike other settlers who sought wealth. The Mayflower, a small ship, carried 102 passengers and thirty sailors, with cramped conditions. After a month of smooth sailing, severe storms caused illness and blew the ship off its intended course for Virginia. Consequently, the Pilgrims landed in present-day Massachusetts, New England, in a former Wampanoag village, which they named Plymouth. Their arrival coincided with the onset of cold weather, making it too late to plant crops, leading to a desperate struggle for survival through the winter. Many perished from cold, disease, and starvation while the women and children remained on the Mayflower. Hope was rekindled with the arrival of spring and the assistance of Squanto, a Native American who spoke English. Squanto taught the Pilgrims how to cultivate crops suitable for the new land, as well as how to hunt and fish. This newfound abundance of food restored their strength. To commemorate their survival and the harvest, Squanto and members of the Wampanoag people joined the Pilgrims in a feast of thanksgiving, sharing deer, turkey, fish, and vegetables, underscoring the critical role Native Americans played in the settlers' survival.

lesson_text:
Just a few years after the Pilgrims’ first feast of thanksgiving in Plymouth, another group of people came to New England. They were called the Puritans. Like the Pilgrims, the Puritans left England because a king would not let them worship as they wanted.
King Charles I was happy to get rid of the Puritans. The king signed a paper called a charter, giving them permission to start a colony in Massachusetts Bay.
29
The Massachusetts Bay Colony was run by the Puritans, and not by the king of England. From the beginning, this colony was bigger than Jamestown or Plymouth. It began with a thousand men, women, and children!
30
Massachusetts Bay Colony was a little more successful from the start. The Puritans had brought lots of food and tools with them. They began building a city called Boston, as well as a number of towns.
31
With things going so well in the Massachusetts Bay Colony, more Puritans arrived. Within ten years, there were over ten thousand people living there.
This colony also did well because the Puritans made sure that everyone worked. Even young people had to work. The Puritans believed that children should be taught job skills they could use when they became adults. This way they would always be useful.
32
The Puritans also wanted their children to learn to read and write. They wanted everyone to read the Bible. Because education was so important to them, Puritan law said that every town must have a school.
All the townspeople had to pay for the school and the teacher. We still pay for public schools this way. The Puritans also started Harvard College. 
33
After a while, the Puritans and others began moving to areas farther away. New settlements began in what would become Rhode Island, Connecticut, and New Hampshire. Before long, there were thirteen colonies. Although they didn’t know it at the time, the colonists were helping to create a new country—the United States of America.
34
summary: Shortly after the Pilgrims, another group, the Puritans, arrived in New England, also seeking religious freedom from King Charles I, who readily granted them a charter for the Massachusetts Bay Colony. This Puritan-governed colony was notably larger and more successful from its inception than Jamestown or Plymouth, starting with a thousand individuals and establishing Boston and other towns with ample provisions and tools. Its prosperity attracted over ten thousand settlers within a decade. The Puritans' success was largely attributed to their strong work ethic, mandating labor for all ages and emphasizing vocational skills for children to ensure lifelong usefulness. Education was paramount, driven by their desire for everyone to read the Bible, leading to a law requiring every town to fund a school and teacher, a practice that continues in public education today. The Puritans also founded Harvard College. Over time, this expansion led to new settlements in areas that would become Rhode Island, Connecticut, and New Hampshire, eventually contributing to the formation of the thirteen colonies, unknowingly laying the foundation for the United States of America.

lesson_text: Long ago, America was called the colonies. Colonies are lands controlled by other countries that are far away. There were thirteen colonies in America. Many of the people in the thirteen colonies came from England, Wales, Scotland, and Ireland—though some came from France, Germany, and other European countries too. Generally, people living in the thirteen colonies had traveled to America for a better life. Many thought of themselves as British, not as American. They liked to buy clothes and books from Great Britain. They liked to drink tea. They obeyed King George III, who ruled over England, Wales, Scotland, Ireland, and the colonies in America. The colonists were proud of their king. Great Britain had just won a war against France. But to pay for that war, King George had borrowed a lot of money. The answer was from the colonists in America. The king and his parliament decided that when the colonists bought such things as sugar, paint, newspapers, writing paper, glass, or tea, they would be charged a payment, or sales tax, making the cost of these items more expensive. The colonists showed their anger by protesting and not buying any of these things. In the end, the tax on everything except tea was dropped. There is another story of life in the thirteen colonies, though. Not everyone had gone there for a better life. Not everyone was free. Many Africans were enslaved and forced to travel to the colonies. Enslaved Africans worked on large plantations, or farms, growing crops. Their hard work helped to make the British colonies rich and strong.
summary: America was once comprised of thirteen colonies, lands governed by distant European nations, predominantly Great Britain. Many colonists migrated seeking improved lives, identifying as British subjects, and importing goods from Britain while obeying King George III. After Great Britain's victory in a war against France, King George and Parliament imposed sales taxes on various goods, including sugar, paint, and tea, to repay war debts. This led to colonist protests and boycotts, resulting in the repeal of all taxes except for tea. However, not all inhabitants were free; numerous Africans were forcibly enslaved and brought to the colonies to toil on plantations, significantly contributing to the British colonies' economic prosperity.

lesson_text: Many people in the thirteen colonies in America drank tea. Though tea was not cheap, people liked it so much they saved up to buy it. That was until the British Parliament and King George placed a tax on it. Then the colonists said they would stop drinking British tea. British ships bringing tea to the colonies were turned away. Then, on a cold winter day, the governor in Boston allowed three British ships carrying tea to sail into Boston Harbor. That night a group of men who were dressed like Native Americans climbed onto the ships. They threw the tea into the water. This became known as the Boston Tea Party. News of what had happened in Boston spread. Soon, many people in the colonies were celebrating the Boston Tea Party. However, when the news reached King George and Parliament, they became very angry. They sent British warships to close Boston Harbor. With the harbor closed, no food or supplies could get in. To show their support for the people of Boston, colonists from across the thirteen colonies sent food and clothes. The British sent more British soldiers to keep order. The colonists called the British soldiers redcoats because of their bright, red uniforms.
summary: Colonists in America widely consumed tea, a habit that shifted dramatically when the British Parliament and King George imposed a tax on it, prompting a boycott of British tea. Despite this, Boston's governor permitted three British tea ships to enter Boston Harbor. In response, a group of men, disguised as Native Americans, boarded the ships one winter night and dumped the tea into the harbor, an event famously named the Boston Tea Party. This act of defiance was celebrated throughout the colonies but angered King George and Parliament, who retaliated by deploying warships to close Boston Harbor, thereby blocking all incoming food and supplies. Other colonies demonstrated solidarity by sending aid to Boston, while the British dispatched more soldiers, known as redcoats, to maintain control.

lesson_text: It was September, and the leaves were beginning to change color in Philadelphia. Samuel Adams put on a new, red suit. He didn’t normally wear such fancy clothes, but he was going to meet with other leaders of the thirteen colonies. These leaders were meeting in Philadelphia to write a letter to King George III explaining why they were so unhappy. When all the leaders were gathered together, they began to write the letter. In it, they asked King George to take away all unfair laws and taxes. They said that if he did not, the colonies would no longer buy anything from Britain. Each leader signed his name on the letter. One of the men who signed the letter was George Washington. After signing the letter, the colonial leaders left the meeting and went home. They planned to meet again when they received news from the king and his parliament. Most importantly, the leaders from all the colonies had decided to work together. Being a proud American was becoming more important than being loyal to the king. These proud Americans were known as Patriots.
summary: In September, colonial leaders, including Samuel Adams and George Washington, convened in Philadelphia to draft a letter to King George III, expressing their grievances and demanding the removal of unfair laws and taxes. They warned that if their demands were not met, the colonies would cease purchasing British goods. Each leader signed the letter, signifying a unified front. After the meeting, they planned to await the King's response before reconvening. Crucially, this gathering solidified the leaders' commitment to collective action across all colonies. A new sense of American identity emerged, with loyalty to the American cause taking precedence over loyalty to the King, and these individuals became known as Patriots.

lesson_text: Like most colonists, Paul Revere hoped that the letter the colonial leaders had sent to the king would bring peace. Few people wanted to fight the British. And most Americans were not trained for war. But to be safe, many Patriots got ready to fight—just in case. In the town of Concord, near Boston, people hid cannonballs, gunpowder, weapons, and other things they might need. The British soldiers, or redcoats, found out about the hidden weapons and planned to go to Concord to take them away. Paul Revere decided to ride to Concord to warn the Patriots. Before he left Boston, he needed to know whether the redcoats were coming by land or across the Charles River. That night, he sent a Patriot up to the tower of Old North Church in Boston to give a signal. If the British were coming by land, the Patriot was to light one lantern. If they were coming across the river, he was to light two lanterns. Paul Revere got into a small boat in the dark waters around Boston. He kept a close eye on the church tower as he was rowed across the Charles River. Suddenly, a light appeared in the church tower. Just one light. But then he saw a second light. The redcoats were coming across the water! Quietly, Paul Revere was rowed to the shore. As soon as he got there, he jumped onto a waiting horse. Paul Revere raced through the countryside. “The regulars— the redcoats—are coming out!” he called. And as he passed each house, he saw windows and doors being thrown open, and candles being lit. The Patriots were getting ready for what was to come.
summary: Paul Revere, like many colonists, initially hoped for a peaceful resolution with Britain, but Patriots in Concord prepared for potential conflict by stockpiling weapons. When British redcoats discovered these hidden arms and planned to seize them, Revere resolved to warn the Patriots. To ascertain the British approach, he arranged a lantern signal from Boston’s Old North Church: one lantern for a land advance, two for a river crossing. As Revere was rowed across the Charles River, he observed two lights in the church tower, indicating the redcoats were advancing by water. Upon reaching shore, he mounted a horse and galloped through the countryside, shouting, “The regulars—the redcoats—are coming out!” This alarm spurred colonists to prepare for the imminent British arrival.

lesson_text: Paul Revere was arrested before he got to Concord. However, he had warned some people that the redcoats were coming. In the town of Lexington, near Concord, people woke to the sound of marching men. An army of redcoats had appeared! But the redcoats were not alone. A number of Patriots were there too. The Patriots in Concord and Lexington were called Minutemen because they could be ready to fight in a minute. The Minutemen and the British soldiers faced one another. A voice from the British side called out, “Throw down your guns.” But the Minutemen refused. The leader of the Minutemen told his men to stand their ground. Suddenly, a shot was fired, and then another. Soon the air was filled with smoke. When the smoke cleared, people could see that some of the Minutemen had been shot! The British soldiers still wanted the weapons that had been stored in Concord, so they set off to get them. But when they got to Concord, the weapons were gone. There was nothing they could do. But the Minutemen weren’t going to let the redcoats get away so easily. The Minutemen were good shots, and they forced the redcoats to retreat. The Americans had won the Battle of Concord.
summary: Though Paul Revere was arrested en route to Concord, his warnings reached Lexington, alerting Minutemen—Patriots ready for instant combat—to the approaching British redcoats. In Lexington, a confrontation ensued when Minutemen refused to disarm, leading to the first shots of the conflict and Minutemen casualties. The British then marched to Concord to seize hidden weapons, only to discover they had been moved. The Minutemen, demonstrating skilled marksmanship, engaged the British, forcing them to retreat and securing an American victory in the Battle of Concord, effectively initiating the American Revolution.

lesson_text: After the fighting at Lexington and Concord, there were more battles between the British and the Americans. While these battles were happening, the leaders of the colonies met again to decide what to do. They agreed they needed an American army. They also agreed to give Britain one last chance. The colonial leaders wrote another letter to King George III, asking him to be fair. The king and Parliament saw things differently. The colonists had fired shots, and so the king sent even more soldiers to America. Now the colonial leaders had to make a decision. Should they be ruled by Britain, or should they start a new nation that was completely free? They argued for a long time. They finally agreed to declare independence from Britain. Now they needed to put their decision in writing for the king— and the whole world—to read. Thomas Jefferson, a Virginian, was one of the youngest leaders. Yet, he was known as a wise person and an excellent writer. He was chosen to write what became known as the Declaration of Independence. But the Declaration of Independence was hard to write. Thomas Jefferson had the help of Benjamin Franklin and John Adams. It took them two weeks to get it just right. Thomas Jefferson wrote that if a government hurts people, then people have the right to start a new government. That was a shocking idea at the time. Today, most people accept this idea. He also wrote that people have the right to live, the right to be free, and the right to be happy. Thomas Jefferson wrote that “all men are created equal.” That means that everyone is born with equal rights. This is perhaps one of the most important ideas of all. The reason that the Fourth of July is our country’s birthday is because on that day, the Declaration of Independence was signed. The first person to sign the Declaration was John Hancock. His name was the largest of all because he wanted the king to notice it. For Americans, signing the Declaration of Independence was a brave thing to do, but to King George III, it was a crime called treason. Each of the other fifty-five men signed the paper. From that moment on, there were no longer thirteen colonies: there was a new nation instead—the United States of America. For most Americans, news of the Declaration of Independence was reason to celebrate. The American Revolution lasted for seven years, until finally the British were defeated. Not every American fought for independence. Some were Loyalists who fought on the side of the British. Today, we light fireworks on the Fourth of July to celebrate the day that Americans decided to be independent. We celebrate just as people did long ago!
summary: Following the skirmishes at Lexington and Concord and subsequent battles, colonial leaders convened again, agreeing on the necessity of an American army and sending a final letter to King George III seeking fairness. However, the King responded by dispatching more soldiers, forcing the leaders to decide on full independence from Britain. After extensive debate, they unanimously voted to declare independence. Thomas Jefferson, assisted by Benjamin Franklin and John Adams, then drafted the Declaration of Independence over two weeks. This pivotal document articulated revolutionary concepts, including the right of people to form a new government if the existing one harms them, and the fundamental rights to life, liberty, and happiness, asserting that 'all men are created equal.' On July 4th, the Declaration was signed by fifty-six men, including John Hancock, whose large signature was a defiant gesture to the King. This act transformed the thirteen colonies into the United States of America, though King George III considered it treason. The Declaration's announcement spurred celebrations, and after a seven-year struggle against the British (with some Loyalists siding with Britain), America achieved victory. Today, Americans commemorate their independence with fireworks on the Fourth of July.

lesson_text: At the time the American Revolution began, Benjamin Franklin was seventy years old. Benjamin Franklin had worked hard to become a successful printer. Besides printing books and newspapers, Franklin did many other important things. He set up Philadelphia’s first fire department. He even ran America’s first post office. And of course he helped Thomas Jefferson write the Declaration of Independence. Benjamin Franklin also invented things—such as a stove that keeps houses warm. We call it a Franklin stove. He invented a chair with an arm that is also a desk, as well as eyeglasses that let you see both near and far. And he invented something called a lightning rod that stops lightning from setting fire to houses. Benjamin Franklin also wrote a book that gave information about the seasons, and included wise sayings, such as, “Early to bed and early to rise, makes a man healthy, wealthy, and wise.” How did he do so much? He followed his own advice. He went to bed early and got up early. He did not believe in wasting time. One of his sayings was, “Lost time is never found again.”
summary: Benjamin Franklin, a successful printer, was seventy years old when the American Revolution began. His notable contributions extended beyond printing books and newspapers to establishing Philadelphia’s first fire department, running America’s first post office, and assisting Thomas Jefferson in drafting the Declaration of Independence. Franklin was also a prolific inventor, credited with the Franklin stove, a chair with an integrated desk, bifocal eyeglasses, and the lightning rod to prevent house fires. He authored a book featuring seasonal information and wise aphorisms, such as “Early to bed and early to rise, makes a man healthy, wealthy, and wise.” Franklin attributed his many achievements to his disciplined routine of early rising and his belief in not wasting time, famously stating, “Lost time is never found again.”

topic: George Washington and the Fight for America
lesson_text: When war broke out, George Washington was put in charge of the American army. The soldiers were brave but untrained. The army needed more weapons and won few battles. The British took the city of New York and chased the Americans south through New Jersey and across the Delaware River to Pennsylvania. Winter arrived, and George Washington’s men began to lose hope. They were cold and hungry, and some soldiers didn’t even have coats or shoes. George Washington needed a plan. It was Christmastime, and George knew that the redcoats in New Jersey would be celebrating on Christmas Day. If George made a surprise attack, he might win an important battle. On Christmas night, George Washington decided to take his army across the Delaware River to attack the British in New Jersey. Just as his soldiers were about to get into their boats to cross the river, a snowstorm began. Soon, it became difficult to see clearly. George Washington decided to cross the icy Delaware River first, to give his men courage. The storm gave George Washington the chance he needed to surprise the British. By the time the American soldiers got to the British camp in Trenton, New Jersey, it was morning. But they still took the redcoats by surprise. The British soldiers were not ready to fight the Americans. This was the victory George Washington and his men had hoped for. The war did not end with the victory at Trenton. Many more years of fighting followed. In the end, America defeated the British, and George Washington became the first president of the United States; and Martha Washington, his wife, became the First Lady.
summary: Upon the outbreak of war, George Washington assumed command of the American army. Despite their bravery, his untrained troops lacked weapons, frequently losing battles, which led to a British takeover of New York and a retreat through New Jersey to Pennsylvania. Facing a desolate winter, his soldiers were disheartened, cold, hungry, and ill-equipped. Washington devised a critical plan for a surprise attack on the British redcoats in New Jersey, who would be celebrating on Christmas Day. On Christmas night, despite a sudden snowstorm, Washington courageously led his troops across the icy Delaware River, inspiring his men. The storm provided ideal cover, allowing the Americans to surprise the unprepared British at Trenton, New Jersey, securing a crucial victory. Although the war continued for several more years, America ultimately triumphed, and George Washington became the first President of the United States, with Martha Washington serving as the first First Lady.

lesson_text: Every country needs a capital city. It was decided that the capital of the United States would be the District of Columbia. Plans were made to build a beautiful city with wide avenues and parks. There would also be a Capitol building—the place where the Congress of the United States would meet to make laws for the country. Plans were also made to build a house for the president and his family. The house would be called President’s Mansion. President’s Mansion eventually became known as the White House. George and Martha never got to live in the White House. The first president to do so was John Adams, along with his wife, Abigail. There is a story that George Washington asked Betsy Ross to make the first American flag, but no one knows for sure if this is true. What is true, though, is that Betsy Ross was a Patriot who lived in Philadelphia at the time. The first flag of the United States was a lot like the Stars and Stripes we use today, except that it had thirteen stars—one for each of the first states. Today, the American flag has fifty stars, one for each state, and thirteen stripes for the thirteen colonies. Another important American symbol is the Liberty Bell in Philadelphia. This great bell rang in Philadelphia to tell people that the Declaration of Independence had been sent to the king. People gathered to hear the declaration read out loud. From that moment on, the great bell has had a special meaning to all Americans. It became the Liberty Bell, the bell that told of America’s freedom. Have you ever seen this fancy eagle before? It is the American eagle, and it is on the Seal of the President of the United States. Around the eagle today there are fifty stars, one for each state. Do you see the branch in one of the eagle’s claws? It is an olive branch, a symbol of peace. The arrows in the other claw show strength. The American flag, the Liberty Bell, and the American eagle are three important symbols of the United States of America.
summary: The United States established its capital in the District of Columbia, with plans for a grand city featuring wide avenues, parks, and a Capitol building for Congress. The President's Mansion, eventually named the White House, was also conceived, though John and Abigail Adams were its first residents, not George and Martha Washington. While the anecdote of George Washington commissioning Betsy Ross to create the first American flag is unverified, Ross was a known Patriot. The original flag mirrored today's Stars and Stripes but featured thirteen stars for the initial states; current flags have fifty stars and thirteen stripes. The Liberty Bell in Philadelphia, which tolled to announce the Declaration of Independence, is a profound symbol of American freedom. The American eagle, prominently displayed on the Presidential Seal, further represents the nation, holding an olive branch for peace and arrows for strength. These three—the American flag, the Liberty Bell, and the American eagle—are vital national symbols.

lesson_text: Think Like a Scientist “It is eight o’clock. Time for bed!” Sofia’s dad says. “But the sun is still up. It’s still daytime!” Sofia replies. Sofia remembers other bedtimes when it was dark at eight o’clock. Sofia notices the world around her. She wonders about it. Observing the world around you is a part of science. Wondering is a part of science, too. 2 CHAPTER 1 Science can begin when you ask questions. How come my bedtime is sometimes before the sun sets? What does a wild bunny eat? Where does salt go when I mix it with water? Asking many questions means you are curious. Being curious is part of doing science! 3 Science also includes talking to others about your questions. You tell them what you observed. You ask them what they think the answers are. You ask, “How do we know?” 4 Science includes planning a way to find an answer to your question. You might write down what time the sun sets each day. You might put out three foods and watch which ones the bunny eats. You might mix a spoonful of salt in water and leave it for a few days. 5 6 Science includes comparing what you observed to what others observed. Do you all agree? Does anyone disagree? You can ask someone older to look up sunset times online. Do the times match your observations, or are they different? You can ask a neighbor what they see bunnies eat. Does your neighbor’s answer support what you found? You can ask a friend to try what you did with salt and water. Does your friend get the same results as you? People do science to learn how the world works. Scientists are curious people. They ask questions. They observe. They investigate. They know they might be wrong. So, they compare what they discover with others. Kids like you and Sofia can do these things. Then you are thinking like a scientist! Main Science Idea Science is a way to find out about things we are curious about. Science includes observing, asking questions, and investigating as a process for discovery. 7
summary: Science fundamentally involves observing the world and developing curiosity, leading to questions such as why sunset times vary or what animals eat. This scientific process extends to discussing observations and questions with others, collaboratively seeking answers. A crucial step is planning investigations to test hypotheses, which might involve tracking daily sunset times, observing an animal's feeding habits, or experimenting with dissolving salt in water. After conducting investigations, scientists compare their observations with those of others or existing information to validate findings. This comparison helps determine agreement or disagreement, allowing for the refinement of understanding, as scientists acknowledge the possibility of being mistaken. Engaging in observation, questioning, and investigation, and then comparing discoveries, embodies thinking like a scientist. Ultimately, science is a methodical approach to explore the unknown, driven by curiosity and structured investigation.

lesson_text: What Is Nature?What Is Nature? 8 CHAPTER 2 9 10 11 12 Main Science Idea Nature includes everything that exists or happens without people making it so. 13
summary: Nature is defined as encompassing all phenomena and entities that exist or occur independently, without any form of human intervention or creation. This definition distinguishes between elements and processes that are intrinsic to the natural world and those that are results of human design or influence. Therefore, anything that forms or takes place without being made or caused by people falls under the umbrella of nature.

lesson_text: What Is Measuring? Nia is visiting Grandma in the city. Grandma surprises Nia with a gift in a box. It is a scooter! Nia has fun riding her scooter in the city. She and Grandma go to a skate park where there are ramps. The wheels on the scooter turn easily. Nia hardly has to push hard going up the ramps. Rolling down the ramps takes no effort at all! CHAPTER 3 14 As the time to travel back home nears, Nia worries. “What if my scooter is too big for the bus?” “What if it is too long?” “What if it is too heavy?” “Don’t worry, Nia,” says Grandma. “You can measure to find out.” 15 Nia learns how to measure length. She uses a tape measure that has marks along it. Some marks have numbers. She can count them. For the marks in between, she can count them, too. Larger objects have higher measurements than smaller objects. 16 Nia and Grandma read the bus rules. Grandma gets her bathroom scale. “Put your suitcase on the scale. What is its weight?” she asks. Nia reads the numbers on the scale. “It says 16 pounds.” “Now, put your scooter in its box, and put the box on top of your suitcase,” says Grandma. Nia reads the scale again. “It is now 22 pounds.” Will Nia’s item meet the bus rules? 17 Grandma shows Nia how to figure out if the box will fit in the rack on the bus. They estimate the size of the box in inches. About how long is it? It is about as long as Nia’s arm. About 20 inches. About how wide is it? If they fold the handle, it is about 10 inches. “About how high is it?” “It is about the height of my hand. About 6 inches.” Will those measurements meet the bus rules? 18 “I think it will fit!” Nia says. “If you want to be sure, run and get the tape measure,” says Grandma. They measure the size of the box, and Nia smiles. Her new scooter gets to ride home on the bus with her! Main Science Idea Measurements let us know and describe the sizes of things. 19
summary: Measuring is a fundamental process that allows us to determine and describe the sizes and properties of objects, preventing issues like a scooter being too large for a bus. Nia's experience demonstrates how measuring helps understand an item's length, weight, and overall dimensions. Using tools like a tape measure, one can ascertain length by counting marked units, where larger objects naturally yield higher numerical measurements. Weight is measured using a scale, providing readings in units such as pounds. Before precise measurement, estimation can provide an approximate size, but accurate tools confirm whether an object meets specific size or weight regulations. Measurements are crucial for knowing and describing the various physical attributes of things.

lesson_text: Questions to Investigate Will the night sky look the same a month from now as it does tonight? Does the night sky look the same from all parts of Earth? These questions can be answered with science investigations. You can take a photo of the sky tonight at 8:00 p.m. Then wait a month. At 8:00 p.m., you take another picture from the exact same spot. You see that the stars seem to have moved in the sky. Which of the two questions about the night sky can you answer? CHAPTER 4 20 What kind of investigation would answer the other question? You could message your friend who lives far away. He could take a photo at 8:00 p.m. on the same day you do. Then you could compare the photos. Which question would this science investigation answer? You would find that the night sky looks different from different places on Earth. 21 Long ago, people drew pictures over the patterns of stars. They made up stories about the pictures. The stories helped them remember the patterns. They thought this group of stars looked like the tail and back of a bear. 22 Which of these star pictures of the Great Bear is the best one? Which one is your favorite? These are not questions that science investigations can answer. The answers are opinions. An opinion is not correct or incorrect. But you could ask, “Which star picture do the most people like?” That is a science question you could investigate. You could ask many people and count their answers. 23 Look at this picture of the daytime sky. Notice the clouds and the shadows within them. What do you think the clouds look like? Are the clouds pretty? These are not questions you could answer with a science investigation. The answers are opinions. They are just what you think, not something that can be proven. 24 Let’s ask some more questions. Do shadows always point in the same direction? How do the positions of the shadows change through the day? These are questions you could answer with science investigations. How would you investigate each question? Main Science Idea Some questions can be answered through science investigations, but science cannot answer all questions. 25
summary: Science investigations are powerful tools for answering questions about the observable world, such as how the night sky shifts over time or how it appears from different global locations. This involves empirical methods like taking comparative photographs of the sky at different times or from various places. However, scientific inquiry has limitations; it cannot provide answers to questions based on personal opinions, subjective preferences, or aesthetic judgments, such as determining the 'best' star picture or whether clouds are 'pretty.' While science cannot validate opinions, it can transform subjective inquiries into objective investigations by asking measurable questions, such as 'Which star picture do most people like?' by gathering data on preferences. Questions about consistent patterns, like the direction and changing positions of shadows throughout the day, are suitable for scientific investigation, demonstrating that science focuses on provable facts rather than unprovable opinions.

lesson_text: The Sun Queen People called scientist Mária Telkes the “Sun Queen.” Why? Because she invented so many ways to use sunlight. Each of her inventions began with a model. Models are used to explain ideas. Scientists use models to make things clear and simple. A model also can show something you want to build. There are many kinds of models. Drawings and diagrams can serve as models. So can objects that can be handled. CHAPTER 5 26 Mária Telkes thought about how people could use sunlight to cook food. First, she made a drawing of a solar oven to share her idea. Then, she built a working model. It could bake many foods, such as chicken and cookies. People still use her oven today! How is the drawn model like the working model oven? How are they different? 27 Mária Telkes also invented a device to make drinking water from salt water. It fit into a life raft. If someone was lost at sea, they could use the device to get unsalty water to stay alive. Mária Telkes made a drawing to show the parts. A plastic pouch lets sunlight in. It holds air and water, too. One tube helps fill the pouch with air and water. Another tube helps a person sip the unsalty water. The inside of the pouch contains mostly air. 28 Later, working models were built in a factory. The models were tested by sailors. It worked! It could save lives! A working model can change from the first design. That’s part of figuring out the best solution. 29 The Sun Queen even invented a house heated only by the sun. She figured out how to keep the house warm at night, when the sun was not shining. Her drawings showed a wall of very big glass windows. That wall would face the part of the sky that got the most sunlight. Cans of salt warm up during the day. They keep the house warm overnight. Big windows let a lot of sunlight in. 30 The model house was called the Dover Sun House. A little boy and his parents moved in. Curious people came to tour the house. They felt how warm it was inside, even when it was cold outside! What would you like to invent? How could a model help you share your ideas? Main Science Idea A model represents something else. In some ways, a model is like the real thing. In other ways, it differs. 31
summary: Mária Telkes, known as the 'Sun Queen,' innovated numerous ways to harness sunlight, with each invention beginning with a model. Models are crucial for clarifying and simplifying scientific ideas, serving as both explanatory tools and prototypes for construction, ranging from drawings and diagrams to tangible objects. Telkes's work on a solar oven began with a drawing to conceptualize the idea, followed by building a functional working model capable of baking food, which remains in use today. She also designed a solar-powered device for desalting water in life rafts, initially sketching its components and later developing working models that were factory-built and tested by sailors. These working models often evolve from their initial designs to optimize the solution. Furthermore, Telkes invented a solar-heated house, the Dover Sun House, utilizing large south-facing windows and salt cans to retain warmth, showcasing how models represent reality with both similarities and differences, helping people understand and implement new technologies.

lesson_text: Investigate! How do popcorn kernels sprout? Try this investigation at home to find out. 1 Ask an adult for ten popcorn kernels. 2 Spread out the kernels on a paper towel. 3 Spray or sprinkle the towel with water until it is damp but not too wet. 4 Fold the towel in half, slide it into a zipper plastic bag, and seal the bag. 5 Place the bag inside a cabinet or closet. 6 Observe the kernels each day. What changes do you notice? What parts sprout first—roots or stems? 32 CHAPTER 6 What do insects drink? Try this investigation with an adult to find out. 1 Put warm water in a small cup. 2 Add a spoonful of salt. Stir until the salt seems to disappear. 3 Pour a little salt water into a bottle cap. 4 Do Steps 1–3 again, but use sugar instead of salt. 5 Place the two caps next to each other on the ground outside. 6 Check the caps during the day to see if insects visit them. 33 Do plants sense sunlight? 1 Ask an adult to cut off the top of a carrot, leaving about 2 cm of the orange root. 2 Place a few pebbles in a small container. 3 Sit the carrot root on top of the pebbles. Add water halfway up the root. 4 Put the container near a sunny window. Check it each day, but do not turn the container. When the water gets low, add more. 5 Draw what you observe each day. 34 There are wildlife guides for cities and states but not for your neighborhood. You can solve this problem! How can you plan a wildlife trail for your neighborhood? 1 With an adult, walk around your neighborhood. 2 Look for wild animals. They can be small and on the ground, like worms or chipmunks. They can be large and in trees, like birds. 3 Draw a map to show where to walk to find wild animals. 4 Make an X at each place you can stop and observe animals. 5 Label your map to tell what to look or listen for at each stop. 6 Share your wildlife trail map with your family and friends. 35 You can carry out investigations to answer science questions. You can also solve problems with the help of investigations. Investigation steps tell what to do and in what order. They tell what materials to use. They tell when to record observations. 36 Main Science Idea Investigations follow a series of steps. You can also plan your own investigations. Write steps using numbers to show their order. After you try the investigation, give the steps to someone else. Then they can repeat the steps in the same order. You can talk and compare what they observed to what you observed. Look at these photos of an investigation. They are not in the correct order. How would you order them? 37
summary: Investigations are structured processes used to answer scientific questions or solve problems, requiring a defined sequence of steps, specific materials, and consistent recording of observations. Examples include an investigation into popcorn kernel sprouting, which involves dampening kernels on a paper towel, sealing them in a plastic bag, and observing daily changes in root and stem growth. Another investigation explores insect drinking preferences by offering separate caps of salt and sugar water outdoors and monitoring insect visits. To determine if plants sense sunlight, a carrot root is placed in water near a sunny window, with daily observations and drawings made. Investigations can also be practical, like planning a neighborhood wildlife trail by mapping animal sightings and labeling observation points. The method emphasizes clear, numbered steps for reproducibility, allowing others to repeat the investigation and compare their findings, fostering shared scientific understanding.

lesson_text: Dr. Fuertes explains where the data, or information, come from. Scientists pointed a tool at a sound maker. The tool measured the loudness of the sound. They wrote down each measurement. Then they arranged them on a line from softest to loudest. Dr. Fuertes explains that very loud sounds can harm people’s hearing. Data and Predictions Dr. Fuertes is visiting Riverside School today to talk about healthy hearing. She brings a diagram showing sounds that are softer and louder. CHAPTER 7 38 Predict where on the loudness graph your school’s cafeteria at lunchtime should be. To do this, think about the sounds on the diagram. Compare them to what you know about the loudness of your lunchtime cafeteria. Think about how your prediction could be checked. 39 The Wilson family is car camping. They set up their tent right next to their parked car. Mr. Wilson puts out the campfire at bedtime. But the kids want to read comic books before they go to sleep. It would be useful to know about light sources. Which sources of light are dimmest and brightest? 40 Think about the sources of light at the campground. Think about the brightness of light needed to read. Use the data in the diagram to compare. Predict which source would be best for reading comic books. How would you check your prediction? 41 This desert tortoise is only a couple of years old. It is about 3 inches in length. It will grow a little more each year, until it is an adult. The chart shows how many inches long this little fellow will be from ages 5 to 7 years. Age 5 Years 6 Years 7 Years 8 Years Inches 6 7 8 ? What length do you predict it will be at 8 years old? How did the data in the chart help you answer? 42 Main Science Idea Data are information. Data can help you predict some things. You can check to see if your prediction was correct. A tree grower sells young white oak trees for planting. The trees are 6 feet tall when they are sold to buyers. The chart shows how tall the tree will be in the first three years after it is planted. First Year Second Year Third Year Fourth Year Feet 6 8 10 ? How tall do you predict it will be after the fourth year? How do you know? 43
summary: Data, which refers to collected information, is essential for understanding phenomena and making informed predictions. Scientists gather data by using tools to measure observations, like the loudness of sounds, and then organize this information, such as on a scale from softest to loudest. This data allows for predictions, like estimating the noise level of a school cafeteria by comparing it to known sound levels. The accuracy of these predictions can then be verified through further observation or investigation. Data patterns, demonstrated through examples like the consistent growth of a desert tortoise or a white oak tree over several years, provide a basis for anticipating future outcomes. By analyzing sequential data, one can extrapolate trends and make educated guesses about future states, understanding that predictions are testable and can be confirmed or disproven.

lesson_text: How Much and How Many In science, we use numbers to measure. We can measure length, weight, time, and more. Think about things that can be measured. What’s the distance around a tree trunk? How long does it take to win a race? How many meercats are keeping watch? CHAPTER 8 44 Quantity means how much or how many of something. The number of units helps us tell sizes and amounts. How many people are in line? How tall is the plant? How much liquid is in the flask? 45 Some things cannot be measured with numbers. How something looks, tastes, or feels can’t be measured. How beautiful is a painting? How good does breakfast taste? Which stuffed animal feels nicest? 46 Some things about nature can be measured. Others cannot. We cannot measure how pretty a flower is. But we can measure how many bees collect nectar from it. 47 You can measure how bright each of these classrooms is. How close you must stand to see the poster in each light can be measured, too. But how nice this classroom looks with different types of light cannot be measured. 48 Let’s practice sorting things into groups. Which are details that can be measured? Which show details that cannot be measured? A thermometer can measure how hot it is. A scale can measure how heavy a puppy is. But you can’t measure how happy a person is. But we can’t measure how beautiful the sunset is. Main Science Idea Quantity means how much or how many of something. Some things can be counted or measured precisely. Other things cannot. 49
summary: In science, quantity refers to 'how much' or 'how many' of something, and numbers are used to measure these attributes. We can precisely measure various aspects such as length (e.g., a tree trunk's circumference), weight (e.g., a puppy's heaviness), or time (e.g., race duration), and count discrete items (e.g., meerkats, people in line). These measurements, expressed in units, allow us to determine sizes and amounts accurately, like a plant's height or a liquid's volume. However, many subjective qualities, such as beauty, taste, or feel, cannot be quantified numerically because they are matters of opinion rather than objective fact. For example, while one cannot measure a flower's prettiness or a classroom's aesthetic appeal, one can objectively count the number of bees visiting a flower or measure the brightness of a classroom. Therefore, distinguishing between precisely measurable quantities and unmeasurable subjective qualities is essential in scientific inquiry.

lesson_text: Super Solver! Inventor Kid is here to save the day! There’s no problem too big for me to solve! Oh no! My toy car keeps getting stuck under my bed! 50 CHAPTER 9 I made this Handy Helper to pick things up. Could I use it to save my car? I might need to change it a bit. If I add wheels and make it longer, it just might work! 51 Time to transform my Handy Helper into a Toy Rescuer! It works! This Toy Rescuer is a solution for the car stuck under my bed. 52 My Reach-O-Matic can reach high places. I wonder if it can also reach far underneath my bed. By making it shorter and adding a claw, it might just do the trick! 53 Oops! This version of the Reach-O-Matic didn’t work to rescue the car. That’s OK. Sometimes, inventions don’t work as planned. Time to think of another solution! 54 My remote-controlled truck zips around. Could it solve my toy car problem? Maybe if I add a magnetic attachment, the truck could save my toy car. Hooray! The changes to my remote-controlled truck worked, too! Inventor Kid saves the day! Main Science Idea People can design inventions to solve problems. 55
summary: People are capable of designing inventions to solve various problems, a process that frequently involves modifying existing tools and iterating on designs. For instance, to retrieve a toy car stuck under a bed, a 'Handy Helper' can be re-envisioned as a 'Toy Rescuer' by adding wheels and extending its reach. However, not all initial design modifications guarantee success; a different attempt to adapt a 'Reach-O-Matic' by shortening it and adding a claw might prove ineffective, illustrating that inventions sometimes fail to work as intended. Such setbacks necessitate devising new solutions. For example, transforming a remote-controlled truck by attaching a magnet can provide an alternative, successful method to rescue the car. This highlights that invention is an iterative problem-solving cycle of identifying issues, conceptualizing, modifying, testing, and refining until an effective solution is achieved.

lesson_text: Tulip Mystery Kai spent hours caring for his backyard garden. But one morning, he woke up to an unhappy surprise—his tulips were gone! They had disappeared during the night! Kai was curious. He needed to solve this backyard mystery. Kai spotted his friend Maya over the fence. He called, “Maya, I think bugs ate my tulips.” CHAPTER 10 56 Maya joined Kai’s investigation. They found holes where the tulip bulbs had been planted. But bugs couldn’t create such large holes They could not carry away an entire tulip bulb. “I don’t think the evidence supports my claim,” Kai admitted. “Maybe it wasn’t bugs that ate my tulips.” 57 Kai made a new claim. “I think rabbits are eating my tulips!” Maya asked, “What evidence do you have?” Kai pointed at the holes in the soil. “Look at these holes!” he replied. “Everyone knows rabbits love to nibble on things in gardens. They must have dug up my tulip bulbs!” 58 Kai and Maya looked for more evidence. Maya spotted soil on top of the fence. There were even a few pieces of tulip stem. Kai and Maya shared a look. Something had climbed the fence while carrying a tulip plant. Maya said, “Hold on! Rabbits don’t climb fences! Their paws aren’t the right shape.” 59 Kai and Maya thought carefully about all the evidence. “Hmm,” Maya said. “What other creatures around here can climb?” Kai exclaimed, “I’ve seen squirrels climb really well!” A spark lit up Maya’s eyes. “You’re right! Think about squirrel paws. They are built for climbing and digging!” 60 Main Science Idea Good evidence comes from facts. Strong evidence can help us see when we are wrong and make us change our minds about things. 61
summary: Solving a mystery, such as the disappearance of garden tulips, critically relies on gathering and evaluating factual evidence. Initially, a claim that bugs consumed the tulips is disproven by the size of the holes and the impracticality of bugs removing whole bulbs, demonstrating that initial hypotheses may lack supporting evidence. A subsequent claim, suggesting rabbits were responsible, is also challenged when new evidence emerges: soil and tulip stems found atop a fence. This indicates that the culprit must be capable of climbing, an ability rabbits lack due to their paw structure. This highlights the importance of strong, factual evidence in scientific investigation, which can compel a change in one's initial understanding. By carefully considering all evidence and identifying local creatures known for climbing and digging, like squirrels, a more accurate claim can be formulated and supported, ultimately solving the mystery.

lesson_text: 62 CHAPTER 11 Science Information Max is a boy who loves science. He also loves to visit the school library. He spots a rainbow poster on the library wall. April has arrived. Rainy days bring colorful surprises . . . like rainbows! Ms. Parker, the librarian, invites Max to a special learning station all about rainbows. A rainbow is a beautiful and colorful arch that appears in the sky after it rains. It happens when light from the sun shines through and bounces off raindrops in the air. Rainbows have different colors, including red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, and violet. Max gets a close look at the poster. It shows a rainbow stretching from the trees to the sky. He sees that the colors are next to one another. Max reads the poster’s caption to learn about rainbows. 63 Near the rainbow poster, another poster catches his eye. Its diagrams explain how light separates into colors. 64 When the sun comes out after it rains, something amazing happens. A prism is an object made of see-through material, like glass. When light passes through a prism, it bends. This makes the light split into different colors. 1. Sunlight enters the raindrops. 2. Raindrops are prisms that bend the light. 3. The sunlight separates into colors. 4. What we see is a rainbow! 65 Ms. Parker points out a video at the learning station. As Max watches it, he learns how sunlight and raindrops create rainbows in the sky. Colorful moving images help him see how light bounces, bends, and spreads out. The behavior of light can make beautiful rainbows in our world. Max still has one question. He knows he can ask Ms. Parker. “Why does a rainbow make a curved shape instead of a straight line?” Ms. Parker smiles. “That’s a great question, Max!” she replies. “The sun hits the water droplets in the air at different angles, from low in the air to high in the air.” 66 Max got details about rainbows from different places today. • He learned from posters with words and photos. • The posters had titles and drawings, too. • Max got information from a video. • He listened to the narrator speaking in the video. • He also got information from Ms. Parker. Max put all the pieces of information together. Now he understands much more about rainbows than he did before! Main Science Idea Information can come from printed words, pictures, and voices that we hear. Pictures can be diagrams, photos, or icons. We put all the information together to understand new things. 67
summary: Scientific information can be obtained from diverse sources, including printed words, various types of pictures (diagrams, photos, icons), and spoken explanations. For a comprehensive understanding of rainbows, one can consult posters with text and images detailing that a rainbow is a colorful arch formed when sunlight interacts with raindrops, splitting light into distinct colors like red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, and violet, similar to how a prism works. Diagrams can illustrate the process of light separating into colors. Videos, with their moving images and narration, further demonstrate how light bounces, bends, and spreads to create rainbows. Additionally, direct explanations from experts can clarify specific aspects, such as why rainbows appear curved due to sunlight hitting water droplets at different angles. By synthesizing information from these multiple modalities, a more complete understanding of scientific phenomena is achieved.

lesson_text: 68 CHAPTER 12 Learning from Patterns Have you ever noticed the spots on a ladybug’s back? The spots are arranged in a pattern on the bug’s body. One side of the bug’s body is a mirror image of the other. That’s a pattern. When things repeat or happen in the same way over and over again, that’s a pattern. What repeats in this pattern? Patterns can be found all over nature. You can find patterns by looking at plants and animals. You can find some patterns by listening. When we notice a pattern, we can figure out what will come next. Patterns helps scientists understand things better and make predictions. 69 Parts arranged in circles, around and around Yellow outlines around brown spots, from bottom to top Dark stripe then light stripe, over and over CROAK! (Then a quiet pause) CROAK! (Then quiet) TAP, TAP, TAP, TAP, TAP!!! Numbers can also make patterns. 70 How about the pattern in the orange numbers? Can you see the pattern in the pink numbers? 71 Have you ever seen a group of birds flying together in a V shape? That’s a pattern that birds use when they migrate. How would you describe the pattern? Humans follow patterns, too. How does the pattern help the jumper? Can you think of a pattern that helps you do something? 72 The jump rope makes a sound each time it hits the ground. SNAP, SNAP, SNAP!!! The watchers keep the rhythm. CLAP, CLAP, CLAP!!! Think about an activity you do every day, like brushing your teeth. You follow a pattern of steps. The steps happen in the same order every time you brush. 1. What do you do first? 2. What do you do next? 3. What do you do after that? 4. How do you finish the task? Main Science Idea Noticing and studying patterns can help you figure things out. 73
summary: Patterns involve repetitions or consistent occurrences, and they are pervasive throughout nature and human activities. They can be observed visually, such as the symmetrical spots on a ladybug or the arrangement of petals in a flower, and auditorily, like the repetitive croaking of a frog. Recognizing patterns allows individuals to anticipate future events and helps scientists gain a deeper understanding of phenomena and make predictions. Patterns are also evident in numerical sequences and in the structured behaviors of animals, such as birds migrating in a 'V' formation. Humans also follow patterns in daily routines, like the sequential steps of brushing teeth, or in activities like jump roping where rhythm is maintained. The ability to notice, study, and understand these patterns is a fundamental skill that aids in comprehending the world and problem-solving.

lesson_text: [IMAGE SPEC: CKSciLit_G1C13_SR_art_01: Illustration of a young female, about 7 years old, reaching in the full bathtub with a puzzled expression� The bathtub is filled with water� 74 CHAPTER 13 Demi’s Difficult Day Demi’s bathtub won’t drain. What causes this problem? Something must be clogging the drain. Demi is a curious kid. She loves to figure things out. Demi needs to find the cause so she can fix it. She reaches her hand into the bathwater. A sponge toy is stuck in the drain. That’s the cause of the problem! Demi pulls out the toy, and the water drains. Oh no! Next, Demi sees milk has spilled all over the table and floor. It’s easy enough to clean up the milk. But Demi is already thinking about the cause of the spill. What made it happen? The table tilts when she leans on it. The wobbly table is the cause of the spill. 75 Demi’s bike has a flat tire. There are so many problems to solve today! What is the cause of the flat tire? The tire has a nail in it. This problem is a little harder to fix. Demi will need the help of a grown-up. But she knows what caused the problem. 76 Demi is experiencing causes and effects today! Knowing the causes of things can be helpful. Spotting something that could cause a problem can help us keep the effect from happening. Demi notices nails on the driveway. Nails caused her flat bike tire! She uses a magnet to collect the nails before Mom gets home. Now Mom’s car won’t get a flat tire. 77 Demi thinks about other difficult parts of her day. She knows what caused her problems. Now she can change the outcomes for tomorrow. The next time Demi takes a bath, she will take her toys out of the tub. That way, the drain won’t get plugged. 78 The next time Demi puts a glass on the wobbly table, she won’t put it near the edge. Better yet, until she can figure out the cause of the wobble, she will put her glass on the counter where it won’t spill. Now to investigate the wobbly table! • What is the cause? • What is the effect? • How is that a problem? How can knowing the cause of the problem help Demi fix it? Main Science Idea Understanding causes and their effects can help with solving problems. 79
summary: Understanding the relationship between causes and their effects is crucial for effective problem-solving and prevention. When a bathtub doesn't drain, the cause is a clog, such as a toy in the drain. Similarly, a milk spill on a table can be attributed to a wobbly table, and a flat bike tire is caused by a nail. Identifying these causes not only enables immediate resolution but also empowers individuals to prevent future occurrences. For example, recognizing that nails caused a flat tire prompts action to collect nails from the driveway, preventing future tire damage for others. By proactively addressing causes, like removing toys from a tub or avoiding placing items on a wobbly table, one can alter future outcomes and mitigate potential problems. This ability to investigate and pinpoint causes allows for thoughtful solutions and improved management of everyday challenges.

lesson_text: 80 CHAPTER 14 Counting Quantities Counting is something we do every day. The number of something is its quantity. You can compare quantities. How many prairie dogs do you count? Are there more prairie dogs or alligators? Counting things can be useful. A farmer counts the baby chicks. She needs to know how many hatched. There are two baby chicks! All the chicks need to eat. Counting chicks tells the farmer how much food to buy. Counting helps the farmer, and the chicks get fed! Not everything needs to be counted, though. Counting how many spots are on the puppies doesn’t matter too much. But you can notice one puppy has more spots than another. It can help you tell them apart. 81 A young baker makes cookies. She must count how many cups of flour to add to the bowl. She must use the correct amount of flour. Adding more or less of an ingredient affects how a food turns out. Quantities matter in baking recipes. A scientist who is mixing chemicals must count. The quantity of one chemical must be exact. The quantity of another must be exact, too. Counting is not only helpful, but it also can be necessary. 82 To care for a plant, you must figure out how much water it needs. You can count the number of days that you water a plant in a week. You can keep track of the amount of water you pour over the plant. This will help you make sure the plant gets enough water and not too much. You could also count how many leaves grow on your plant. But is knowing that quantity useful for keeping the plant alive? 83 Scientists pay attention to quantities. They count and measure everything they study. Elephants are an endangered species.
