That means the number of living elephants is getting too low. There could end up being no elephants at all. Keeping track of the number of elephants is important. It lets scientists know if things people do to protect elephants are helping. It’s hard to know the exact quantity of elephants, though. They move around over vast areas 84 Main Science Idea Knowing quantities in science is helpful. It is not always important to know the exact numbers of things, though. This is an elephant nursery. The keepers care for orphaned elephants. The keepers count the elephants. They know exactly how many young elephants they need to feed. They know exactly how much food they feed each one. They keep track of how much the elephants grow. When the elephants have grown enough, they can survive on their own. They will go into the wild again. Saving the lives of elephants involves knowing how to count. 85
summary: Counting determines the quantity of something, indicating 'how much' or 'how many,' and is fundamental for comparing amounts, such as the populations of different animals. Counting is immensely useful in practical contexts: a farmer counts chicks to buy the correct amount of food, and a baker must precisely measure flour for a recipe to ensure the desired outcome. Similarly, scientists meticulously count and measure chemicals to ensure exact quantities for experiments, highlighting that counting can be not just helpful but necessary. In plant care, tracking watering frequency and volume is crucial for survival, whereas counting leaves, while a quantity, might not be as useful. Scientists utilize quantities to monitor endangered species like elephants, assessing conservation efforts, though precise numbers can be challenging to obtain for animals in vast wild areas. However, in controlled environments like an elephant nursery, keepers count and measure food and growth precisely to ensure the animals' survival and eventual return to the wild. While knowing quantities is helpful in science, it isn't always essential to know exact numbers in every situation.

lesson_text: CHAPTER 15 Systems Art Show STUDENT ART SHOW W E L C O M E to the student art show! You can see pictures that students worked on during the year. The theme of this year’s art show is systems. Each picture in the gallery is about a system. What is a system? A system is a set of parts that work together. The parts affect each other. E N J O Y T H E S H O W ! See what systems and their parts you can find along the way! 86 Theo Milbury Blooms Crayons on Paper This drawing shows a plant with its flower. The artist drew a stem, a leaf, and petals. The stem sends water from the roots to the rest of the plant. The leaves help the plant make food. Petals on the flower attract bees to spread pollen around. This helps plants make seeds to grow new plants. These parts work together as a system. They help the flower grow and survive. 87 Vanessa Valquez Hive City Colored Pencils on Paper Buzz, buzz, buzz. The bees in this picture are very busy. They are working in a beehive! A beehive is where bees live and work. Each bee plays an important part in the system. Some bees collect pollen to bring back to the hive. Other bees protect the hive and guard the queen. The queen bee lays eggs and makes new bees. All these bees work together. It’s a system 88 Luca Helman Far Out Crayons on Paper The solar system has eight planets. Some of them have moons. The planets move around the sun. Gravity keeps the planets and moons in place. 89 Story Miraldi See the Sea Watercolor This artist drew an aquarium. An aquarium is an underwater system designed by humans. It has parts that provide all the things aquatic animals need to live. These parts are meant to be like their natural habitats. The main part of an aquarium is water. Rocks or sand at the bottom of the aquarium give animals a place to rest or walk, just like in an ocean. Pretend plants and other objects give animals places to hide. Some aquariums have machines that keep the water at a good temperature. They are designed to imitate how the sun heats water in nature. Finally, fish, starfish, and all the creatures in the tank are part of an aquarium. 90 Main Science Idea Things that work together and affect each other form a system. There are many kinds of systems. 91 Dina Horowitz Jars of Green Colored Pencils on Paper A terrarium is like a self-contained garden. It is a system with living and nonliving parts. A terrarium is a closed container with soil, plants, and air in it. Water moves from the air to the soil and back again.
summary: A system is defined as a collection of interdependent parts that collaborate and influence each other. This concept is illustrated through various examples: a plant functions as a system where the stem, leaves, and petals work together for growth, food production, and reproduction through pollen spreading. A beehive represents a complex system where individual bees fulfill specific roles, such as collecting pollen, protecting the hive, or laying eggs, all contributing to the colony's overall function. The solar system is another natural system, with planets and moons orbiting the sun, held in place by gravity. Humans also design systems, such as aquariums, which are artificial underwater environments with components like water, substrate, and temperature control mechanisms designed to replicate natural habitats for aquatic animals. Similarly, a terrarium forms a self-contained system, integrating living plants with nonliving elements like soil and air, where water cycles internally. There are many types of systems, both natural and human-made, all characterized by interconnected parts working in unison.

lesson_text: CHAPTER 16 Fascinating Fasteners It’s show-and-tell day in Ms. Pei’s class! The students have been asked to bring in objects that use fasteners. A fastener is a small part that helps larger parts stay closed or connected. Nuts and bolts, nails, screws, and rivets are all fasteners. If you look carefully around you, you can almost always find some of these. Let’s see what some of the students brought to share with the class! 92 Ricardo is sharing a wooden birdhouse with the class. Several flat pieces of wood are held together with nails. Nails are pointy metal fasteners. They are hammered into place. Usually, nails are used to hold together wood parts. Many objects are built with nails. Emily brought in a picture frame to share. The corners of the picture frame are held together with tiny nails. They are smaller than the nails holding Ricardo’s birdhouse together. 93 Olga brought in a plastic flashlight to show the class. The outer parts of the flashlight are held together by screws. Bennett is sharing his eyeglasses. Eyeglasses use tiny screws to connect the parts of their frames. Screws are commonly found holding bigger parts together. They can be used with wooden, plastic, or metal materials. They twist into the parts instead of being banged in like nails. 94 Felix is showing the class his guitar. Some of its parts are held together with small screws. Now he plays the class a song! Strum, strum, strum. Coop brought her metal robot toy to show to the class. The metal body parts are connected by screws. They attach the head, arms, and legs to the robot’s torso. 95 Penny is sharing her toy car. The underside of the car uses rivets to hold the outer parts together. Rivets are small metal fasteners, too. They are often used in cars, planes, rockets, ships, and buildings. But they can also be used in smaller objects, too. A rivet is like a nail that isn’t pointy. It’s thin shape gets smashed to hold it in place and fasten materials together. 96 Theo rode his bicycle to school. He shows it to the class. Nuts and bolts hold the handlebars and pedals in place. They connect parts to the bike’s frame. Sonja shows the class her skateboard. The wheels are attached to the board using nuts and bolts. A bolt is like a screw without a pointy end. The nut is the part that twists onto the thin shaft. Main Science Idea One design for fastening materials together can be used in many different objects. 97 You can probably find these types of fasteners in the room you are in right now. Give it a try!
summary: Fasteners are small but essential components that connect or close larger parts of objects. Common types include nails, screws, rivets, and nuts and bolts, each designed for specific applications and materials. Nails are pointy metal fasteners hammered primarily into wood, used in structures like birdhouses and picture frames. Screws, conversely, twist into materials such as wood, plastic, or metal, securing parts in flashlights, eyeglasses, guitars, and robot toys. Rivets are small metal fasteners, similar to blunt nails, that are smashed to hold materials together, commonly found in larger constructions like cars and buildings, as well as smaller objects like toy cars. Nuts and bolts work together to fasten parts, with a nut twisting onto a bolt's shaft, typically used for stronger connections in items like bicycle handlebars and skateboard wheels. The underlying principle is that a single design for fastening materials can be versatile, applying across a wide array of objects.

topic: The Right Material for the Job
lesson_text: 98 CHAPTER 17 The Right Material for the Job Diego enjoys building things. Today he needs to design a space diorama for school. He looks through his craft closet for materials. Material is what an object is made of. Diego’s closet is filled with all kinds of materials! He is excited to pick out the best ones to use for his space diorama. Diego takes out his liquid materials first. Liquid does not hold its shape. A liquid will fill the space in a container. It will take the shape of the container. A few liquids can be used for his diorama. He can use liquid glue to stick other materials together and hold things in place. Liquid paint will be good for painting the planets, moons, and space scenery. When these materials dry, they won’t be liquids anymore. As water evaporates from the liquid, a solid will remain. 99 Diego sorts through his clay. Clay is tacky and thick. It can be shaped and molded to add thickness to the diorama’s landscape. He decides he will use clay to make textured surfaces like rocky terrain on the moon or the crust of planets. 100 Diego has a lot of solid materials. Solid materials hold their shapes. He can use them in many ways for his diorama. Cardboard is hard and sturdy. Diego can use it to make the bottom of the diorama. Paper wouldn’t be as good of a choice because paper folds and flops too much. He will also use cardboard tubes to make a rocket ship. Foam balls can be painted to look like planets and moons. They are of different sizes. 101 Diego has a box filled with scraps of fabric. Fabric is soft, even though it is a solid. It can be twisted, folded, cut, stitched, and glued! Diego thinks he can use gold fabric to cover his rocket ship. Then he can cut strips of orange fabric to use as the fire on his rocket’s engine. 102 Diego pulls out a box of wires and rubber bands. Wires are lightweight and flexible. Diego can use them to make antennae on satellites and connector parts for his rocket ship. Elastic rubber bands stretch and return to their original size. Diego decides to use elastic to make the astronauts in his diorama look like they are bouncing in space. With all of these materials, Diego feels ready to start building his diorama! Main Science Idea Describing materials can help you decide how they can be useful. 103
summary: Choosing the appropriate material for a task, such as constructing a space diorama, necessitates understanding the inherent properties of each material. Materials, which are what objects are composed of, come in diverse forms like liquids, solids, or flexible substances. Liquid materials, including glue and paint, conform to the shape of their container and are useful for bonding and coloring, transforming into solids upon drying as water evaporates. Tacky and thick clay is moldable, ideal for creating textured surfaces like lunar terrain or planetary crusts. Solid materials, maintaining their shape, serve various structural purposes; sturdy cardboard is excellent for diorama bases and rocket tubes, while foam balls can be painted into planets. Soft fabric, although a solid, can be manipulated by twisting, folding, cutting, stitching, and gluing for decorative elements like rocket coverings or flames. Lightweight, flexible wires are suitable for antennae, and elastic rubber bands, which stretch and return to their original size, can simulate bouncy movements. Describing these unique properties guides the decision-making process for their most effective utility.

lesson_text: When something changes, it means that it becomes different. You are taller now than you were when you were born. Your height changed as you got older. The height of the hills around where you live won’t naturally change much in your lifetime. Things that stay the same are stable. Hills are most often very stable. 104 CHAPTER 18 Things That Change Some things in nature change, and other things stay the same. Everything in motion has speed. Some motion seems very fast. Some motion is very slow. The runner and the tortoise can change speeds, too. They can go faster or slower. 105 This sandcastle at the beach was far away from the ocean water at the beginning of the day. After a few hours, the waves started washing the sandcastle away. What quickly changed? The tide came in. The ocean always has waves. In repeating cycles, the waves move higher onto the shore. The tide changed. And the castle changed, too. 106 This adult orangutan didn’t always look this way. When it was a baby, it was also much smaller. Its muscles were small. It didn’t have too much hair These are some of the physical traits that changed. There are also traits that stayed the same. The overall structure of the legs and arms never changed. Some things change a lot. Some things change less. 107 People have been growing food for a long time. We must eat to stay alive. Our need for food is something that never changes. People always need to do things to help them eat. Even the ancient Egyptians grew food to eat. But things change. Farming systems have changed to improve how food grows. Humans developed machines to do work. 108 Main Science Idea Many things are changing all the time. Here are a couple more examples of things that change in nature. Earth’s surface is always changing. Some changes happen too slowly to notice. When wind blows sand to the same area over time, it can form sand dunes. The formation of sand dunes is a slow change. But it is fast compared to the time it takes for a mountain to form. Clouds change in the sky. Their shapes change as they float by. Sometimes the sky is full of clouds. Other times there are no clouds in sight. 109
summary: Many things in nature are in a constant state of change, while others exhibit stability. Change implies a transformation or difference over time, exemplified by a person's growth in height as they age, contrasting with the relatively stable height of hills over a human lifetime. Motion, inherently tied to speed, can vary, with objects moving faster or slower. Environmental phenomena like tides demonstrate cyclical changes, causing sandcastles to erode as waves advance and retreat, while the presence of waves themselves remains constant. Organisms undergo significant physical changes during their lifespan, such as an orangutan's development from baby to adult, although fundamental anatomical structures typically remain consistent. Human practices, too, evolve; while the essential need for food is unwavering, farming systems and technologies continuously change to enhance food production. Earth's surface itself is dynamic, experiencing both gradual changes like the formation of sand dunes by wind and more rapid, observable shifts in cloud shapes and coverage in the sky. Some changes are fast, while others are very slow, highlighting the pervasive nature of transformation.

lesson_text: 110 CHAPTER 19 Invention and Discovery Step right up! Welcome to the Inventor’s Fair! Today you can learn about some scientists, engineers, and inventors. You can learn about how they made discoveries. Some inventors spent many years researching and testing their inventions. Others made accidental discoveries. There are different ways to discover things in science. Enjoy the fair! Meet Alexander Fleming. He’s a scientist. He accidentally discovered a type of mold that is now used as medicine. It is called penicillin. It kills some kinds of germs. It helps people feel better when they are sick. He was doing an experiment in his lab. When he checked on his experiment later, he found mold growing. And nothing else grew around it. He took a very close look at it. Was something in the mold killing germs? That is when he discovered that the mold could be used for medicine. It was a very surprising, and important, discovery. 111 Meet George de Mestral and his dog, Milka. After taking Milka for a walk one day, George noticed burrs stuck to her fur. He observed the burrs closely. They had tiny hooks in them. They could hook onto fur and fabric. This inspired George’s invention. What did he invent? Hook-and-loop fasteners. It was a solution to fastening shoes, clothing, and even backpacks. 112 Meet David Misell. He’s an inventor. Have you ever tried to see in the dark? If so, then maybe you’ve used his invention: the flashlight! It took him a long time to invent the flashlight. First, he had to produce light. In his day, that wasn’t so easy! Then, he had to research how to direct light waves. Sometimes his designs failed. It wasn’t easy, but he kept trying. He came up with many designs until he found the one that worked the best. 113 Meet Stephanie Kwolek. She’s an engineer. She invented an important material called Kevlar. Kevlar is a strong, lightweight fiber. It is five times stronger than steel but light enough to wear! Today we use it in things like body armor and helmets. It helps save lives. Stephanie discovered Kevlar by accident. She was working on an experiment for tires. When she mixed certain materials in the lab, she made this strong fiber. It was a very happy accident! 114 Meet George Washington Carver. He’s a scientist who works with plants. He spent long years researching different ways to use peanuts. And he kept discovering more and more along the way. He discovered something else in his research, too. It was how to keep farm soil healthy. He taught farmers how to rotate their crops. It helped their crops grow better. His solutions are still used in farming today. Main Science Idea Sometimes people work hard for a long time to solve a problem or invent something new. Sometimes they discover something new unexpectedly while they are working on something else. 115
summary: Scientific invention and discovery can manifest through both sustained, diligent research and unexpected accidental observations. For example, Alexander Fleming's discovery of penicillin, a mold capable of killing germs, occurred by chance during a lab experiment. George de Mestral's invention of hook-and-loop fasteners, used in clothing and backpacks, was inspired by observing the tiny hooks on burrs stuck to his dog's fur. In contrast, David Misell's invention of the flashlight was the culmination of extensive and persistent effort, involving research into light production and direction, and numerous design iterations despite initial failures. Stephanie Kwolek accidentally discovered Kevlar, a strong, lightweight fiber used in body armor, during an experiment for tire materials. Similarly, George Washington Carver dedicated many years to researching various uses for peanuts and also discovered methods for maintaining healthy farm soil through crop rotation. These examples highlight that breakthroughs can stem from purposeful, long-term problem-solving or unforeseen fortunate accidents during scientific work.

lesson_text: CHAPTER 20 How Do They Do That? Have you ever been to a movie theater? If so, you’ve experienced a sensation of light and sound! Seeing a film on a big screen is possible because of engineers. Engineers are people who study problems. They seek solutions. They figure out how to use materials and processes to make new things. 116 Where’s the popcorn? Engineers come up with designs. Designs are the plans for a solution. Engineers designed, or planned, a way to show movies on big screens. They used special materials for the screen. The screen reflects light. A certain coating makes sure the light is spread evenly. This lets you see the movie no matter where you sit. Sometimes engineers have to come up with a solution for making a gigantic screen. Engineers also design screens that can fit in smaller rooms and even in homes. 117 Popcorn, please. Some engineers design amusement park rides. They come up with ways for people to have safe but thrilling fun. Engineers think about speed. They design rides that are safe for going fast or safe for going slow. Engineers think about directions. They design rides that are safe for making twists, turns, or drops. 118 Wheeee!!! When designing amusement park rides, engineers also must think beyond the ride itself. Engineers think about what material to use. They have to test every part of the roller coaster to make it safe. 119 Safety first! Keeping animals safely in a zoo is a problem. When designing zoos, math helps engineers figure out how tall to make the enclosures. This way the animals will not escape. Problem solved! When designing roads, engineers use math to figure out how wide the roads should be and how to curve the roads so cars can turn one way or another. 120 Main Science Idea To design something means to make a plan for a solution. Engineers are people who study problems and figure out how to use materials and processes to make solutions. Engineering uses science. Engineers need to know how things work in the natural world. If the problem is how to fly safely in bad weather, an engineer can figure out a solution. Want to make a train without wheels? That is a problem that needs a solution. Knowing about magnets helps engineers design superfast trains that glide above their tracks. 121 Let’s travel!
summary: Engineers are professionals dedicated to solving problems by developing plans and utilizing materials and processes to create innovative solutions. Their work involves designing, which is the process of creating detailed plans. For instance, engineers designed movie projection systems, including screens with special light-reflective coatings that ensure even light distribution for optimal viewing. They also develop designs for diverse scales, from gigantic cinema screens to smaller home screens. In designing amusement park rides, engineers meticulously consider safety across various speeds, directions (twists, turns, drops), and material choices, conducting rigorous testing of every component. Engineering integrates scientific principles and mathematical calculations to address challenges, such as determining the appropriate height for zoo enclosures to prevent animal escapes or calculating road widths and curves for safe vehicle navigation. Their understanding of natural phenomena, like magnetism, enables them to design advanced solutions, such as superfast trains that glide above tracks, demonstrating engineering's role in advancing technology and safety across various fields.

lesson_text:
Religion is an important part of the lives of many people. Religion can show people how to live and behave. For some people, religion explains how the world was made. In this book, you will learn about three of the many different religions that people practice: Judaism, Christianity, and Islam.
What Is Religion?
2
CHAPTER
1
The Jewish people had a new kind of religion. They believed in only one god. Today, the belief in one god is the most important part of Judaism, Christianity, and Islam.
Long ago, the people of ancient Egypt and Mesopotamia worshipped many gods. Between three and four thousand years ago, a small group of people—the Jewish people—lived in the lands between Egypt and Mesopotamia. We now call these lands part of the Middle East.
3
summary: Religion significantly influences many lives, guiding behavior and offering explanations for the world's creation. This book focuses on Judaism, Christianity, and Islam. Historically, ancient Egyptians and Mesopotamians practiced polytheism, worshipping many gods. However, three to four thousand years ago, the Jewish people, originating between Egypt and Mesopotamia, introduced monotheism, the belief in one god. This belief remains a foundational principle for Judaism, Christianity, and Islam today.

topic: The History of Judaism: Moses and the Jewish People in Egypt
lesson_text:
The Torah, or holy book, tells the story of the Jewish people who had gone to live in Egypt. At first the Jews were happy there. They grew stronger as a group. But then an Egyptian pharaoh saw how strong they were becoming, and he did not like it. The pharaoh forced the Jewish people to become slaves. They had to work in the hot desert, building Egyptian cities.
The History of Judaism: Moses and
the Jewish People in Egypt
4
CHAPTER
2
Even though they were slaves, the Jews were not defeated. The pharaoh grew angry. He decided to kill all the Jewish baby boys by throwing them into the Nile River. One Jewish woman decided that the pharaoh would not kill her son. She made a basket and placed her baby inside. She sent the basket floating down the river. She told the baby’s sister, Miriam, to follow it.
5
After a while, the basket became tangled in reeds that grew close to the riverbank. A lady who was sitting on the riverbank saw the baby and rescued him. Miriam had followed her brother’s journey. Now she knew she had to be brave. The lady who had rescued her brother was the pharaoh’s own daughter.
6
“What a beautiful baby!” Miriam cried out, as she ran toward the pharaoh’s daughter. “I know a Jewish slave woman who could care for him.”
The woman Miriam spoke of was the baby’s real mother. The Egyptian princess thought for a moment, and then she said, “I will raise this baby as my own. His name will be Moses, and he will be a prince of Egypt! Bring me the slave woman. She can help me!” And so Moses’s real mother was allowed to care for him when he was a child.
7
Moses grew up as a royal prince in Egypt. One day he saw an Egyptian hurting a Jewish slave. Though Moses grew up as an Egyptian prince, he knew that he was Jewish. Moses was so angry, he killed the Egyptian. Moses was forced to run away. He escaped to the desert and became a shepherd.
8
Sometime later, Moses saw a very strange thing. He saw that a bush was on fire, and yet it was not burning up! As he moved toward the bush, a voice spoke to him.
“Moses,” the voice called, “I am the God of the Jews. You must lead them out of Egypt. Go back to the pharaoh and tell him to let my people go.”
9
Even though Moses was afraid, he did as God asked. But the pharaoh would not let the Jewish people go free. To punish the pharaoh and the Egyptians, God sent many terrible plagues upon them. Still the pharaoh refused to free the Jews.
10
summary: The Torah recounts the Jewish people's initial prosperity in Egypt, followed by their enslavement by a fearful pharaoh who mandated the killing of all Jewish baby boys. To save her son, Moses, a Jewish woman placed him in a basket on the Nile, where he was found and adopted by the pharaoh's daughter, with his birth mother hired to care for him. Moses was raised as an Egyptian prince but, after killing an Egyptian who was harming a Jewish slave, he fled to the desert and became a shepherd. Later, God spoke to Moses from a burning bush, instructing him to demand the pharaoh release the Jewish people. Moses obeyed, but the pharaoh's repeated refusals led God to inflict numerous plagues upon Egypt.

lesson_text:
The Flight from Egypt
Finally, Moses warned the pharaoh that God would kill the firstborn child in every Egyptian family if he did not free the Jews. Once again the pharaoh refused.
Then God told Moses to tell the Jewish people to mark their doors with blood so that the Angel of Death would know which homes to pass over, or not enter. The Jewish people did this, and their first-born children were spared. When the pharaoh’s own son was killed by the Angel of Death, the pharaoh finally let the Jewish people go.
CHAPTER
3
11
Moses and the Jewish people escaped from Egypt. This is known as the Exodus. The Jewish people had no time to get ready for the journey. All they had to eat along the way was flat bread.
12
The pharaoh changed his mind yet again. Just as the Jewish people reached Egypt’s border at the Red Sea, they saw his soldiers chasing after them. Moses held up his staff, or stick, and God separated the Red Sea into two giant walls of water. Moses led the Jewish people across the dry path in the middle. As soon as the Jewish people were safe, the walls of water fell onto the pharaoh’s soldiers, and they were drowned.
13
At last the Jewish people were free to begin their journey to the land God had promised them, the land of Israel. Along the way, God spoke to Moses and gave him the Ten Commandments, the laws the Jewish people must follow. Sadly, Moses never reached the land of Israel.
14
Today, Jewish people practice their religion by praying, going to a temple or synagogue, and reading or listening to stories from the Torah, which is part of the Jewish Bible. The Star of David is an important symbol of the Jewish faith.
Important Jewish holidays include Rosh Hashanah, or the Jewish New Year, Yom Kippur, or the Day of Forgiveness, and Passover. During Rosh Hashanah people eat apples and honey. Passover is the celebration of freedom from slavery in Egypt. During Passover, Jewish people eat flat bread and retell the story of the Exodus.
15
summary: Moses warned the pharaoh of the final plague: the death of the firstborn, instructing the Jewish people to mark their doors with blood to be spared. After his own son died, the pharaoh released them, initiating the Exodus from Egypt. As they fled, the pharaoh's army pursued them to the Red Sea, where God parted the waters, allowing the Jews to cross before closing the sea on the Egyptian soldiers. On their journey to the promised land of Israel, God gave Moses the Ten Commandments, though Moses never reached Israel. Modern Jewish practice includes prayer, synagogue attendance, Torah study, and observing holidays like Rosh Hashanah, Yom Kippur, and Passover, which commemorates the Exodus with flat bread.

lesson_text:
Christians also believe in one god. For Christians, their faith is linked to the teachings of Jesus of Nazareth. The Christian Bible, or holy book, tells of Jesus’s life and his teachings.
Jesus was born about two thousand years ago in Bethlehem, in Judaea, which was at the time part of the Roman Empire. Jesus was Jewish. The Romans made life difficult for the Jews in Judaea.
The History of Christianity
16
CHAPTER
4
The story of Jesus’s birth tells of a man named Joseph and his wife Mary, who were having a baby. Before the baby was born, Joseph and Mary traveled to Bethlehem. When they arrived there, the only place where they could stay was in a stable.
17
It was there in the stable that Mary gave birth to Jesus. Shepherds and travelers known as wise men learned about the birth of Jesus. They visited the baby Jesus in the stable and brought him gifts.
18
When Jesus grew up, he traveled through the area known as Galilee. He was a teacher. Jesus said that people were equal in the eyes of God and they should treat each other with kindness. Crowds often gathered to hear him speak. Those who followed Jesus believed he was the messiah, or the person they hoped would save them.
19
The Romans arrested and killed Jesus. Before he was arrested, Jesus asked twelve men, his first followers, to eat a last Passover meal with him. These followers are known as the Twelve Disciples. Today, Christians call this meal the Last Supper. After Jesus died, his teachings were carried by his followers across the Roman Empire.
20
During Easter, Christians remember the last days of Jesus’s life and his death on the cross. Christians believe that Jesus rose from the dead, and that is celebrated on Easter Sunday. The cross is an important Christian symbol.
Today, Christians practice their faith by praying, going to church, and reading the Bible. There are many Christian holidays, or celebrations, based on the life and teachings of Jesus. During the Christmas season, Christians celebrate the birth of Jesus.
21
summary: Christianity is a monotheistic faith rooted in the teachings of Jesus of Nazareth, as recorded in the Christian Bible. Jesus was born approximately two thousand years ago in Bethlehem to Mary and Joseph. As an adult teacher in Galilee, he advocated for equality and kindness, and his followers believed him to be the Messiah. The Romans arrested and crucified Jesus after he shared the Last Supper with his Twelve Disciples; his teachings subsequently spread across the Roman Empire. Christians observe Easter to commemorate Jesus's death and resurrection, and Christmas to celebrate his birth. Contemporary practices include prayer, church attendance, Bible reading, and recognizing the cross as a key symbol.

lesson_text:
The History of Islam
About six hundred years after Jesus lived, Muhammad, the prophet of Islam, was born in the city of Mecca in Arabia. The religion that Muhammad established is called Islam. People who practice it are called Muslims, and their holy book is the Koran.
22
CHAPTER
5
Muhammad was a merchant. He bought and sold things for a living. Because of his work, he traveled and met many people. The story of Muhammad tells us that one day, while he was in a cave, the angel Gabriel spoke to him. Muhammad left the cave and told his wife about the angel.
23
Sometime later, the angel spoke to Muhammad again, and Muhammad began to tell others about the messages he received from the angel. The angel said that there was only one god. The Arabic word for God is Allah.
Some people were angry with Muhammad because they worshipped many gods. And so Muhammad, along with his followers, left Mecca and escaped to a city called Medina.
24
In Medina people began following the teachings of Muhammad. Through these teachings they came to believe in one god. Then in 630 CE, Muhammad returned to Mecca with many of his followers. They destroyed the statues of gods the people there worshipped. Muhammad died two years after his return to Mecca. His followers carried his teachings across the Middle East and beyond.
25
Today, Muslims practice their faith by reading the Koran and praying. Sometimes they go to a mosque, or place of worship. The month of Ramadan is holy for Muslims, because during that month they remember the words Muhammad received from the angel. At the end of Ramadan, Muslims enjoy a special feast called Eid al-Fitr. The star and crescent are important symbols of Islam.
26
summary: Islam was founded by the Prophet Muhammad, born in Mecca, Arabia, approximately six hundred years after Jesus. Its adherents are called Muslims, and their holy book is the Koran. Muhammad, originally a merchant, received messages from the angel Gabriel in a cave, conveying the belief in one god, Allah. Facing opposition in Mecca for his monotheistic teachings, Muhammad and his followers migrated to Medina. In 630 CE, he returned to Mecca with many followers, destroying idolatrous statues. After his death, his teachings spread widely. Contemporary Muslim practices include reading the Koran, praying, attending mosques, observing Ramadan to commemorate revelations, and celebrating Eid al-Fitr. The star and crescent are significant Islamic symbols.

topic: A Trip to Old Time Farm
lesson_text:
A Trip to Old Time Farm
Ryan and Papa are doing something fun today. They
are visiting Old Time Farm! Ryan will look for horses,
cows, and chickens. He will see farmers growing fruits
and vegetables.
At the farm, Ryan asks Papa, “Will we see a tractor? Do
you think we can ride on one?”
“No way!” Papa says. “This farm does not have any tractors.
And the buildings do not have electricity for heat or light.”
Papa explains that Old Time Farm is a historical farm. The
farmers here raise crops and animals the way that pioneers did
a long time ago, before tractors were invented.
Ryan knows that farming is a lot of work. Farmers must dig
and plow earth to grow crops. They must haul food for their
animals. So much effort goes into being a farmer!
“It must be hard to farm without machines,” Ryan says to Papa.
“You might be surprised at the kinds of machines you can find
even at Old Time Farm,” Papa tells Ryan. “Let’s look for all the
things that these farmers use to help make their work easier.”
Ryan likes this idea. It will add a scavenger
hunt to find machines on Old Time Farm!
summary: Ryan and Papa visit Old Time Farm, a historical farm that operates without modern machinery like tractors or electricity. Ryan initially finds it hard to imagine farming without advanced machines, recognizing the significant effort required for tasks like digging, plowing, and hauling. However, Papa hints that Ryan might be surprised by the "machines" available at the farm. This sets up a scavenger hunt for Ryan to discover various tools that farmers use to simplify their work, introducing the concept of simple machines in a practical context.

lesson_text:
What Is a Ramp?
As soon as they enter the barnyard, Papa says, “I see
a machine!”
Ryan looks around. He doesn’t see any machines.
He sees only a big wooden barn. The barn is tall. It
has doors at the bottom in front. It also has doors on
the side that are much higher up. A stone wall slants
upward to the high side door.
“Do you see the stone wall on the side of the barn?” Papa asks
Ryan. “See how it slopes upward? That is a ramp,” he says. “A
ramp is a simple machine.”
“But Papa,” Ryan says, “that ramp doesn’t do anything. It
doesn’t move. How can it be a machine?” Ryan is a little
confused. The machines he knows about are things like
tractors and lawn mowers and kitchen mixers.
Papa explains. A machine doesn’t do a task itself. And it
doesn’t have to be made up of a bunch of moving parts. What
makes an object a simple machine is that it makes work easier.
When you push, pull, lift, or split something to move it, that
is work. Simple machines make work easier by changing how
you push or pull on something.
A machine can change how hard you push or pull a thing to
move it. A machine can change the direction that you push or
pull a thing to move it.
Papa says, “Imagine that barn without the ramp. Suppose
there was just a ladder to the high door. How would you
get things into the upstairs rooms of the barn? It would be
difficult, wouldn’t it?”
When you want to
move something
to a higher level,
how do you do it?
Some things you
can easily pick up
and lift to a higher
place. But what if
the object is too
heavy to lift? What if
the object is too big
to get ahold of?
You can slide or
roll a big or heavy
object up a ramp.
Moving the object
up a ramp is easier
than picking it up. In
the end, the object
has been lifted with
less effort.
When you move an object on a ramp, you move it a longer
distance. But the push or pull you use to move the object
does not have to be as strong. The distance is longer, but the
force of the push or pull is less. It’s easier!
summary: Papa identifies a slanting stone wall at the barn as a ramp, introducing Ryan to his first simple machine. Ryan is initially confused, expecting machines to be complex, moving devices. Papa clarifies that a simple machine, like a ramp, makes work easier by changing how force is applied, not by doing the task itself or necessarily having moving parts. Work involves pushing, pulling, lifting, or splitting to move something. Ramps ease work by allowing heavy or large objects to be slid or rolled to a higher level with less effort, even though the object travels a longer distance. The ramp reduces the required push or pull force, making the task easier than lifting directly.

topic: What Is a Wheel and Axle?
lesson_text:
What Is a Wheel and Axle?
Ryan wonders what the farmers might move up
the ramp to the upstairs rooms in the barn. Before
long, he thinks he has an idea. He spots a wagon
piled full of hay.
“That’s right,” Papa says. “You have also found your
second simple machine! That wagon has four wheels
on two axles. A wheel and axle make up another
simple machine.”
Ryan knows all about wheels! He has them on his bike, his
scooter, and his skates. There are wheels on Papa’s car and on
his lawn mower. Ryan’s school bus has wheels. So do the book
carts in the library and the grocery carts at the store.
Ryan thinks about the field of pumpkins at the farm. What
if he collected all the pumpkins into a box and slid it across
the ground? That would be hard! It is much easier to push a
load of pumpkins in a
wheelbarrow. It rolls
on a wheel! A simple
machine like a wheel
and axle makes the
effort easier.
Wheels on a wagon are not attached directly to the wagon.
The center of each wheel is fixed to a rod called an axle. The
wheel and axle move together. If you turn one of them, the
other turns with it.
Wheels and axles are useful in ways other than making things
roll, too. A doorknob is a wheel and axle. The knob part that
you turn with your hand is the wheel. That knob is attached
to an axle, a rod that goes through the door. The axle moves
parts inside the door when you turn the knob. It’s easier to
turn the knob than to turn the rod all by itself.
Ryan and Papa find another wheel and axle on the farm in an
unexpected place. The old water well has a bucket attached to
a chain. The chain is wrapped around an axle. When the wheel
is turned, the chain wraps around the axle and raises the
bucket full of water from the well. It’s a lot easier than pulling
the heavy bucket straight up.
summary: Papa reveals that a wagon with wheels and axles is another simple machine, helping Ryan understand how seemingly common objects are actually machines. Ryan is familiar with wheels from various personal and everyday items like bikes, scooters, cars, and carts. The wheel and axle system makes moving heavy loads, such as pumpkins in a wheelbarrow, significantly easier than sliding them directly. This simple machine consists of a wheel fixed to a central rod, the axle, with both components moving together. Beyond rolling, a wheel and axle also facilitates turning, as seen in a doorknob, where turning the larger knob (wheel) moves the smaller rod (axle) with less effort. Another application is found in an old water well, where turning a wheel wrapped with a chain around an axle makes it much easier to lift a heavy bucket of water than pulling it manually.

lesson_text:
What Is a Pulley?
Ryan spots another well. He looks for the wheel and
axle. He sees a wheel, but something about this well
is different. The bucket rope hangs over the grooved
wheel. But there is no way to turn the wheel.
Papa congratulates Ryan. He has found his third simple
machine! The wheel with the rope is called a pulley. Pulling
down on the rope across the wheel lifts the bucket.
Papa leads Ryan to another small barn on the farm to look for
more examples. Ryan spots another pulley right away.
Like the first barn they saw, this barn has a door high above
the ground. Papa explains that the upstairs area in a barn is
called a loft. Ryan figures out that farmers must use the pulley
to help them lift things into the loft.
Pulleys change the direction of a pulling force. They allow
people to lift objects upward by pulling downward.
Pulleys are used in many
places besides farms.
Pulleys are used to raise and
lower flags on flagpoles.
They are used to raise and
lower sails on sailboats.
They are even used when
exercising.
Roofers sometimes use
pulleys to lift shingles up
to a roof. A crane uses
pulleys to lift pieces into
place for the construction
of buildings. Elevators
inside tall buildings use
pulleys to lift people and
cargo from one floor
to another.
Often pulleys are used in sets. Two or more pulleys used
together with one rope make it much easier to lift a heavy
load. A system of two or more pulleys together is called a
block and tackle. This is not a simple machine though. It is
called a compound machine.
summary: Ryan discovers a pulley, his third simple machine, at a well where a rope hangs over a grooved wheel to lift a bucket, rather than turning the wheel itself like a wheel and axle. Papa explains that this setup, where pulling down on the rope lifts an object upward, defines a pulley. Pulleys primarily change the direction of a pulling force, making it easier to lift objects. Examples of pulleys in use extend beyond farms to flagpoles for raising and lowering flags, sailboats for sails, and even in exercise equipment. In construction, roofers use pulleys for shingles, cranes for heavy components, and elevators for lifting people and cargo. When multiple pulleys are combined with one rope to lift very heavy loads, this system is called a block and tackle, which is categorized as a compound machine rather than a simple machine.

lesson_text:
What Is a Lever?
A lot of work happens at the farm, but Ryan also
finds a place to play. “Look,” Ryan says. “It’s an old
wooden seesaw!”
Ryan climbs onto one end of the seesaw, and Papa
straddles the other end. When Papa sits down on his
end, Ryan is lifted high at the other end.
“This is also a machine!” Papa explains. “A seesaw is a
simple machine called a lever.”
A lever is made up of a board or rod that rocks back and forth.
It balances on a point called a fulcrum. The two sides of the
lever are called arms. When you push down on one arm of a
lever, the arm on the opposite side of the fulcrum moves up.
After a little fun on the seesaw, Ryan and Papa set out to see if
they can find more levers on the farm.
A lever makes it easier to lift a load or pry things apart.
Ryan and Papa find a fence gate that has a lever for a latch.
When Ryan pushes down on one arm of the latch, the
other arm lifts off of the plank to let the gate open. Where
is the fulcrum for the lever in this picture?
Ryan soon meets some volunteers working on the farm. He
learns that they are all using different types of levers!
One volunteer digs with
a shovel. The flat end is
one arm of a lever. The
handle end of the shovel
is the other arm. The
ground is the fulcrum.
When the volunteer
pushes down on the
handle arm, the spade
arm pushes dirt up to
leave a hole. Lifting the
dirt with a lever makes
the effort easier!
Another volunteer is
repairing the orchard
fence. She uses a lever
to pry a broken board
from the fence. The lever
pushes the board from
the fence rail the way the
shovel pulls dirt out of a
hole. Imagine how hard
this would be without
using a lever!
A volunteer is sweeping the kitchen porch with a broom.
The bristle end of the broom is the arm of a lever. The
broom moves dirt a greater distance for the person
sweeping the floor. It saves the person effort.
Inside Old Time Farm’s kitchen, Papa spots another lever.
It is a balance scale used to weigh foods such as fruit or
grains. When items on both arms of the scale weigh the
same, they balance equally on the fulcrum. Ryan says, “It’s
just like a seesaw!”
summary: Ryan discovers a seesaw, learning from Papa that it is a simple machine called a lever. A lever consists of a board or rod that pivots on a central point known as a fulcrum, with two opposing sides called arms. When force is applied to one arm, the other arm moves in the opposite direction. Levers are instrumental in making tasks like lifting loads or prying objects apart easier. Ryan and Papa find several examples on the farm: a fence latch operates as a lever to open the gate, and volunteers use various levers in their work. A shovel acts as a lever with the ground as a fulcrum to lift dirt, while another volunteer uses a lever to pry a broken board from a fence. A broom also functions as a lever, moving dirt a greater distance with less effort. Finally, a balance scale in the kitchen is identified as a lever, similar to a seesaw, used for weighing objects by balancing them on a fulcrum.

topic: What Are a Wedge and a Screw?
lesson_text:
What Are a Wedge and a Screw?
Outside the farm kitchen, Ryan and Papa meet a
farmer who is splitting big logs into firewood. He
uses an iron wedge. Ryan thinks its shape looks
like a slice of cake. Ryan learns that wedges are
simple machines, too.
To split the wood, the farmer puts the narrow end of the
wedge against the log and pounds the thick end of the wedge
with a mallet. Each time the farmer hits the wedge, the narrow
end drives deeper into the log. It makes the crack in the log
bigger until the wood splits apart. Using a wedge makes
splitting a log a lot easier than pulling it apart. “That would be
impossible!” Ryan says.
The head of an axe is also a wedge. A woodcutter can swing
the axe to split the wood. The axe is a wedge that makes the
effort easier.
Smaller wedges allow carpenters and wood-carvers to more
carefully shape wood. Wedges such as these are called chisels.
You can find wedges in your home, too. A knife is a wedge
that cuts food apart. A doorstop is a wedge, too. You push
the doorstop in under the door. The doorstop changes the
direction of the push. It pushes up against the door and down
against the floor. Those pushes hold the door in place.
A nail is a wedge, too. If you
look closely at a nail, you see
a skinny, pointy tip. The nail
gets wider from its pointy tip
the way a wedge gets wider
away from its skinny edge.
When you pound a nail against
a board, the point of the nail
pushes into the wood. It makes
the effort of putting a nail into
wood much easier than if the
nail did not have a point.
When two inclined planes are put
together, they form a wedge. If this
wedge is coiled around a cylinder, the
result is a screw. Can you spot the
curving wedge? When you rotate the
screw with a screwdriver, the spiral
wedge causes the screw to move
deep into the wood.
summary: Ryan and Papa encounter a farmer splitting logs with an iron wedge, introducing wedges as simple machines shaped like two inclined planes. The wedge works by concentrating force to drive into an object, progressively splitting it, making tasks like log splitting significantly easier than manual effort. An axe head is another common example of a wedge used for splitting. Smaller wedges, like chisels, are used by carpenters for detailed shaping. Wedges are also found in everyday items, such as knives for cutting food and doorstops that hold doors in place by applying opposing forces. Even a nail is a wedge, its pointy tip and widening body allowing it to be driven into wood with less effort. The text further explains that a screw is essentially a wedge coiled around a cylinder; rotating the screw causes its spiral wedge to penetrate deep into materials like wood, demonstrating how this simple machine is used for fastening.

lesson_text:
Science in Action
Meeting a Toolmaker
Ryan and Papa meet a blacksmith at Old Time
Farm. The blacksmith makes things out of iron
by heating the metal and then shaping it. She
makes all kinds of tools used on the farm. She
makes some simple machines. She makes axes and
wedges and iron bars for levers. Sometimes two or
more simple machines can be used together. Many
useful devices are combinations of two or more
simple machines working together.
Two or more simple machines combined in the same device
are called a compound machine. For example, remember the
shovel that Ryan learned is really a lever? The sharp edge of
the spade end of the shovel is a wedge. That edge pushes
earth apart when pushed into the ground. A shovel is made
of a lever and a wedge, so it is a compound machine.
The blacksmith shows Ryan some compound machines in her
workshop. She uses big pliers to hold hot metal as she shapes
it. Pliers are a compound machine. There are two levers. The
bolt that holds the two long pieces together is the fulcrum for
both levers.
Scissors are compound machines, too. Like pliers, they are two
levers attached in the middle at a fulcrum. The sharp cutting
edges of scissors are wedges.
Recently the blacksmith has repaired a plow. This plow is a farm
tool on wheels. It is pulled by a horse. The farmer walks behind
the plow to guide it. The plow has a wedge that cuts into the
earth. It pushes
the soil apart for
planting crops.
The plow has a
wheel and axle,
another simple
machine. Ryan
knows that a plow
is a compound
machine.
Archimedes
People have been inventing
ways to use and combine
simple machines for a
long time. Archimedes
lived over two
thousand years ago
in ancient Greece.
He observed and
described the ways
that levers, pulleys,
and screws work.
Archimedes was the first
person to write about
ways that machines
make tasks easier.
Archimedes invented
a way to use a screw
to lift water. The screw
fits snuggly inside a
pipe. Rotating a crank
at the top turns the
screw. The wedge that
spirals around the
screw pushes water
up through the pipe.
Turning the crank
is easier than lifting
many buckets of water
out of this river.
summary: Ryan and Papa visit a blacksmith who crafts tools, including simple machines like axes, wedges, and levers. This introduces the concept of compound machines, which are devices combining two or more simple machines to perform work. Examples of compound machines include a shovel, which is a combination of a lever (the handle) and a wedge (the spade edge), allowing it to dig and push earth apart. Pliers and scissors are also compound machines, each utilizing two levers joined at a fulcrum, with scissors further incorporating wedges for cutting edges. A farm plow is identified as a compound machine, featuring a wedge for cutting soil and a wheel and axle for movement. The text also highlights the historical significance of simple machines, referencing Archimedes, an ancient Greek who, over two millennia ago, observed, described, and even invented practical applications for levers, pulleys, and screws, notably developing a water-lifting screw, demonstrating how machines make tasks easier.

lesson_text:
Long, long ago
people all over the
world found food
by hunting and
gathering. This meant
they moved from
place to place as they
followed animals and
gathered plants, nuts, and berries. Some people
walked great distances hunting and gathering as they
went. Others traveled in small boats, following the
coastlines until they found a place to hunt and gather.

Some of the people
who had found
themselves in North
America followed herds
of large animals known
as woolly mammoths.
Woolly mammoths
looked like African
elephants, though their
ears were smaller and
their tusks were longer!
Animals such as
woolly mammoths
not only provided
these people with
food, they also gave
them fur, skin, and
bones that were used
to make clothing,
tools, and simple,
warm homes.

At certain times of
the year across North
America, people
were able to gather
fruits, berries, and
plants. They used
these foods during
the winter months.
They even gathered
a sweet syrup
from the trees in
the forests and
woodlands. And
they fished in the
oceans, rivers, and
streams too!
summary: Long ago, people globally survived by hunting animals and gathering plants, nuts, and berries, necessitating a nomadic lifestyle, often moving great distances or using boats along coastlines. In North America, these hunter-gatherers followed woolly mammoths, which provided essential food, fur, skin, and bones for clothing, tools, and homes. They also gathered seasonal fruits, berries, plants, and sweet syrup, storing some for winter, and fished in various waterways.

lesson_text:
Over many years people kept on
moving across North America.
This movement of people also
happened in Central and South
America. Then there came a time
when some people became
quite good at farming.
They took wild plants that they had eaten for hundreds
of years, and by experimenting with these plants, they
developed a new crop called corn.

The development of farming created more food for people
to eat. This meant that more people could live in one place.
Some people continued to travel in search of food. But many
settled and stayed in places where they could raise food crops
and hunt on land near their farms.
summary: After extensive movement across the Americas, some populations transitioned from nomadic hunting and gathering to farming. Through experimentation with wild plants, they developed corn, a new crop that significantly increased food availability. This agricultural advancement allowed more people to settle in one location, leading many to establish permanent communities where they could cultivate crops and hunt nearby, though some continued to travel for food.

lesson_text:
The Maya were one of several
groups of people who lived
and farmed in the Americas. The Maya became expert
farmers. They made canals, or channels dug into the
earth, to carry water to areas of farmland that were dry.
They farmed on mountainsides and in the forests. They
hunted and fished too.
Successful farming led to
the growth of a great Maya
civilization. The Maya built
great cities. The cities and
their surrounding lands
were ruled by kings and
queens. Farmers grew the
crops that fed the increasing
Maya population.

The Maya built pyramids that were used
to worship their gods. They believed their
gods controlled the world. For example, the
Maya believed in a god of mountains and
earthquakes, a god of thunder, and a god of
the sky. Maya priests were in charge of the
many religious ceremonies that were part
of everyday life.

Maya priests were also
doctors and astronomers.
The astronomer priests
carefully watched the
movements of the stars.
They learned about the
movement of the sun and
the changing of the seasons.
The Maya did this without
any tools or instruments, just
with the naked eye!
By studying the night
sky, the Maya priests were
able to create a calendar
that recorded the change
of the seasons, and the
number of days in a
year. The Maya came up
with 365 days too! Maya
farmers used the calendar
to tell them when to
plant and harvest their
crops. They also planned
their celebrations around
this calendar!

The Maya developed a number
system made up of lines, circles,
dots, and ovals. Numbers were
used to record information about
such things as crops and goods.
The Maya also had a system of
writing made up of symbols
called glyphs. The sons and some
daughters of important people
learned to read and write. When they were older, some became
scribes and wrote down important information on paper made
from tree bark. They also carved messages
on stone walls and on buildings.

The Maya played a popular ball game. The game had a different
name depending on where it was played. Almost every
Maya city had a ball court as big as a modern football field.
The ball used in this game was a heavy, rubber ball. Players
had to keep the ball in the air using only their knees, hips,
shoulders, and forearms. Players scored points by passing the
ball through stone hoops. The team with the most points won.
summary: The Maya were expert farmers, employing canals and farming on mountainsides and in forests, also hunting and fishing. Their agricultural success fostered a great civilization with cities ruled by kings and queens. They built pyramids to worship multiple gods, believed to control the world, with priests leading religious ceremonies. These priests also served as doctors and astronomers, observing celestial movements without instruments to develop a 365-day calendar crucial for farming and celebrations. The Maya created a number system using lines, circles, dots, and ovals, and a writing system of glyphs, with scribes recording information. A popular rubber ball game, played in large courts, required players to use knees, hips, shoulders, and forearms to pass the ball through stone hoops.

lesson_text:
Hundreds of years ago, in
the Americas, a group of
people set off in search
of a home. These people
became the creators of
the Aztec Empire. As the
story goes, the Aztec
believed that their sun
god had told them to search for an eagle eating a snake,
while sitting on a prickly pear cactus. When they found
such a thing, they were to settle in that place.

According to the story,
they found an island
in the middle of a
beautiful lake in central
Mexico. And on the
island they spotted an
eagle perched on a
cactus—and yes, it was
eating a snake! It was on
that island that the Aztec built the most amazing city called
Tenochtitlán, which means “the place of the prickly pear.” The
island and the city are now modern-day Mexico City.
This is the modern flag of Mexico. On it you can see the eagle,
the snake, and the cactus. This Aztec story is an important part
of Mexican culture.

The Aztec built bridges
from their island city
to the shore of the
lake. Because the lake
contained salt water, the
Aztec used clay pipes to
bring in fresh water from
the mainland nearby.
The water was used for
drinking and cooking.
They built canals, or
waterways, and moved
about the city in canoes.
They farmed on the island
too by creating gardens
on raised beds. The Aztec
did this by digging up
mud from the bottom of
the lake and piling it up.
Then they shaped the
piles into long, narrow
gardens and planted such
crops as maize, beans,
and squash. They also
grew flowers.

Tenochtitlán also had streets and tall buildings. At the very
center of the city was the Great Temple. The Aztec emperor,
or ruler, and the priests who were in charge of all religious
practices lived in grand palaces in the city. The Aztec believed
in many gods, but the sun god and the rain god were among
the most important. The Great Temple was used for the
worship of Aztec gods.

More than two hundred
thousand people lived in
the city of Tenochtitlán.
It was one of the biggest
cities in the world at the
time. The city had busy
marketplaces where
many people traded
goods. Farmers brought their food crops to the city from the
gardens and fields nearby. They traded food crops for things
they needed. People also traded gold and silver jewelry, tools,
clay pots, clothing, feathers, and seashells.

The Aztec were strong and skillful
warriors. They conquered other people
and took their land. They created
an empire. The Aztec emperor
was the most powerful
person in the empire. One of
the greatest Aztec emperors
was Moctezuma II. He was
so powerful, when he entered a
room, people threw themselves
on the floor.
Some Aztec boys learned to
read and write. The priests
were their teachers. Some
were also taught medicine and
astronomy. Others learned to
be craftsmen or
farmers. All boys
trained from an
early age to be
warriors. Girls
learned other skills,
including pottery
and weaving.
summary: The Aztec Empire began with a people searching for a home, guided by their sun god to find an eagle eating a snake on a prickly pear cactus. This led them to an island in a central Mexican lake, where they built Tenochtitlán, an incredible city now modern-day Mexico City and featured on the Mexican flag. They engineered bridges, used clay pipes for fresh water, navigated canals by canoe, and created fertile raised-bed gardens for crops like maize, beans, and squash. Tenochtitlán was a large city with streets, tall buildings, and the Great Temple at its heart, dedicated to gods like the sun and rain god. The emperor, like Moctezuma II, and priests resided in grand palaces. The city’s bustling marketplaces facilitated trade of food, jewelry, tools, and more. The Aztec were powerful warriors who built an empire, with boys trained as warriors and educated by priests in subjects like reading, writing, medicine, and astronomy, while girls learned pottery and weaving.

lesson_text:
The Aztec created a great empire,
but the Inca built an even bigger
one that stretched all along the
western coast of South America.
Today that empire would include
large parts of the modern-day
countries of Peru, Colombia,
Ecuador, Bolivia, Chile, and Argentina. At the head of
this amazing empire, the man in charge of millions of
people, was the all-powerful Sapa Inca.

The Inca were expert road builders. They built a road called
the Royal Road, which stretched for two thousand miles. For a
time it was the longest road in the world. Inca soldiers could
move quickly along the road if they were needed. And farmers
could easily move from place to place to trade their crops, which
included cocoa and many different kinds of potatoes.

The Inca also used a chain of speedy messengers who ran along
the Royal Road taking important news from place to place. The
Inca did not have a written language, so each runner had to
remember their message so they could tell it to the next runner.
However, the Inca did have their
own way of counting and recording
information. They used a quipu. A quipu
was a group of different colored strings
with knots tied in a certain way. The
strings and knots might show numbers
of soldiers, or give information about
farmers’ crops.

Like the Maya and the Aztec, the Inca worshipped different
gods. Of special importance to them was the sun god. Here, the
Inca sun god is shown wearing the sun as his crown. He is also
shown crying precious raindrops, which is a sign that he has the
power to bring rain to the farmers’ crops. The sun god holds a
thunderbolt in his hand to show his strength and power!

The Inca also built great cities with temples and palaces. Perhaps
one of the most remarkable cities ever built is the Inca city of
Machu Picchu, which sits high up in the Andes Mountains of
modern-day Peru. The stones used to build the city were so
carefully cut that they fit together like jigsaw pieces. The city
was built for a powerful Inca king.
summary: The Inca established a vast empire along the western coast of South America, encompassing parts of modern Peru, Colombia, Ecuador, Bolivia, Chile, and Argentina, led by the powerful Sapa Inca. They were expert road builders, constructing the 2000-mile Royal Road for rapid troop movement and crop trade, including cocoa and potatoes. Without a written language, they relied on speedy messengers to transmit oral messages along this road. For counting and recording, the Inca used quipu—knotted, colored strings conveying information like soldier numbers or crop data. They worshipped various gods, with the sun god being paramount, depicted with a sun crown, life-giving raindrops, and a thunderbolt. The Inca also built magnificent cities like Machu Picchu in the Andes Mountains of Peru, known for its precisely cut, interlocking stone architecture, constructed for a powerful king.

lesson_text:
The people of these early civilizations
often wondered how the world
was created, or made. Their
religions helped them to make
sense of this mystery and, for
some, provided answers. The
Maya had their own story
about the creation of Earth.
Maya storytellers passed
this story from
one generation
to the next—
all the way
down to today.
This is the Maya story
of how Earth and its
people came to be.

In the beginning there was no
Earth. There was only darkness.
But then the gods created a place
between the sea and the sky. This
happened when two of the gods,
Tepew and Q’uk’umatz, shouted
out the name “Earth.” Suddenly
Earth appeared. Mountains rose
up, and plains appeared.
Trees and plants grew
across the land.

However, Earth was silent until
the gods filled it with animals
of every kind. Suddenly there
were jaguars, pumas, snakes,
deer, and antelope on the
land. The gods filled the
oceans with animals too.

But soon the gods realized that they needed people. They began
by making clay people. The clay people looked good, but they
could not move. They could not walk about. And when the sun
shone bright, they began to melt!

The gods knew they must start again. So they decided to make
wooden people. The wooden people were stronger. They did
not melt in the warm sun. But the wooden people were not
quite right. For one thing, they could not think for themselves.

The gods tried one last
time to create the people
they wanted to live on
Earth. They asked the
animals to help them. The
animals showed the gods
a perfect place for people
to live. In this place grew
yellow and white corn.
The gods created humans
from that corn.
The first humans
could hear, see,
and think. The
humans thanked
the gods and built
great temples in
their honor. These
humans were
exactly what the
gods had hoped
for, and they
were happy.
summary: Early civilizations, like the Maya, used religion to explain the world's creation, passing their stories orally. The Maya creation story begins with only darkness before two gods, Tepew and Q’uk’umatz, created Earth by shouting its name, causing mountains, plains, trees, and plants to appear. Earth remained silent until the gods populated it with diverse animals, both on land and in the oceans. Subsequently, the gods attempted to create people. Their first attempt, clay people, failed as they couldn't move and melted in the sun. Wooden people, their second attempt, were stronger but lacked the ability to think independently. Finally, with the help of animals who revealed a place with yellow and white corn, the gods successfully created humans from corn. These first humans possessed the ability to hear, see, and think, expressed gratitude by building temples, and fulfilled the gods' expectations.

topic: The Maya, Aztec, and Inca Today
lesson_text:
At least six million
Maya still live in
Central America.
Many speak the
languages of their
ancestors, follow
their traditions,
and, as you have
heard, listen to their stories. They weave cloth, grow
the same crops, and eat the same food. But they also
go to school, watch TV, and play games just like you do!

In Mexico, descendants of the Aztec enjoy celebrating their
culture. Many people speak Nahuatl, the language of the
people who made their home on the island in the lake. They
perform Aztec dances and wear traditional dress. And just as
their ancestors did, the Aztec people of today love flowers,
which are a big part of their holidays and celebrations.

If you were to travel up into the Andes Mountains of Peru, you
would meet the descendants of the Inca. You would meet
people in brightly colored clothing walking on mountain paths
with llamas at their side. You would hear Quechua, the language
of the people who built Machu Picchu. You would most likely
be invited to taste the different kinds of potatoes that the Inca
people love to eat. And you would be able to watch the sun set
over the beautiful Andes Mountains.
summary: Millions of Maya descendants continue to live in Central America, maintaining ancestral languages, traditions, stories, crafts like weaving, and growing/eating traditional foods, while also engaging in modern activities like schooling and television. In Mexico, Aztec descendants celebrate their culture, speaking Nahuatl, performing dances in traditional attire, and incorporating flowers prominently in their festivities, just as their ancestors did. In the Peruvian Andes, Inca descendants can be found, speaking Quechua, wearing vibrant clothing, often accompanied by llamas, and preserving their culinary traditions, including a love for diverse potatoes.

lesson_text: Grace is looking forward to school today. She gets to wear her gymnastics clothes. Today at school is show-and-tell day. On show-and-tell day, students each get to share something with the class. They can bring an object from home to show. Or they can tell something that they know how to do. Last month for show-and-tell, Grace brought a big seashell she found at the beach. Today, instead of bringing an object to school, she shows something she can do. Grace does a backbend! Grace learned to do a backbend in her gymnastics class. She has taken gymnastics lessons since she was small. She practices every day so she will be ready to compete soon. Her practice makes her body strong and flexible. Mr. Brown asks, “Grace, what is the hardest gymnastics skill you have learned?” Grace answers right away, but she does not use words. Instead, she shows everyone. She does a handstand. Grace returns to her feet. “It is harder to hold your body up on your arms than it is on your legs,” she explains. “Arms are not as strong as legs.” Mr. Brown asks the class to think about how Grace’s body is working while she does a handstand.
summary: Grace participates in show-and-tell, showcasing her gymnastics skills by performing a backbend and a handstand. She has been taking gymnastics since she was small, practicing daily to develop a strong and flexible body for competition. Grace demonstrates that holding her body in a handstand is more challenging than standing on her legs, explaining that arms are generally not as strong as legs. This introduces the concept of how the body works during physical activity.

lesson_text: Grace performed a backbend and handstand at show-and-tell. The skills took many tries for her to learn. When Grace learns new gymnastics skills, she moves her body in ways that are hard at first. Many of the movements she can do take a lot of practice. She exercises to get stronger. She stretches to become more flexible. Though Grace is very flexible, her body can only bend in certain ways. Your body can only bend at joints. Joints are the places where bones are connected together. Bones themselves do not bend. Your body has over two hundred bones. The bones make up your skeleton. Your skeleton is your body’s frame. Separate parts that work together are called a system. Your bones make up your skeletal system. You have bones in your head. You have bones in your arms and hands. You have bones in your torso and back. You have bones in your legs and feet. All the bones in your head form your skull. Your hard skull protects your soft brain. Your rib cage is a set of bones that protects your heart and lungs. Bend and straighten your fingers. Can you count how many bones each finger has? To grow and stay healthy, bones need nutrients from your diet. Calcium is a nutrient in certain foods, especially in dairy, spinach, and kale. It is important to get enough calcium in your diet, especially while your bones are growing. Bones do not bend, but they can break. A doctor uses an X-ray picture to see if a bone is broken. A broken bone takes a long time to heal. The bone must be held in place the whole time it is healing so that it does not bend at the broken spot. The hard bandage that protects a broken bone is called a cast.
summary: The human body moves by bending at joints, which are connections between bones, as bones themselves are inflexible. Over 200 bones comprise the skeletal system, providing the body's essential framework. Key bones include the skull, which safeguards the brain, and the rib cage, protecting the heart and lungs. Maintaining healthy bones, especially during growth, necessitates a diet rich in calcium, found in foods like dairy and leafy greens. Bones, while rigid, are susceptible to fractures, which are diagnosed via X-ray and require a cast to immobilize the bone during the long healing process.

lesson_text: Gymnastics involves body movements. Grace can do many different kinds of movements. The parts of her body that produce motion are muscles. Grace’s gymnastics coach teaches her exercises to make her muscles stronger. She learns to stretch to make her muscles more flexible. Your muscles make up your muscular system. Some of your muscles are called skeletal muscles. These are muscles that attach to your bones. They also attach to each other. Muscles make your body bend and straighten at the joints. Muscle is soft body tissue. You have muscles in your face. You have muscles in your arms and hands. You have muscles in your legs and feet. You have muscles in your torso and back. Muscles work by contracting and relaxing. Contracting means shortening. Relaxing means lengthening. Any time you bend or straighten part of your body at a joint, muscles are contracting or relaxing to move your bones. Contracting a muscle is also called flexing. When you bend your leg, some muscles contract to bend it. Then others contract to make your leg straight again. Exercising muscles until they are tired makes them stronger when they rest and recover. Repeated exercise can build strong muscles. Push-ups are good exercise for arm muscles. Leg lifts are good exercise for abdominal muscles. Running is good exercise for leg muscles. Some other kinds of muscles aren’t attached to bones. Your heart is a muscle. When you feel your heartbeat, you are feeling your heart muscle contract. Exercise that makes your heart beat fast for a short time is good for your heart muscle. It helps keep you fit and healthy. Growing and building strong muscles requires a diet of healthful foods in addition to exercise. Over time, after lifting a certain amount of weight, muscles become stronger and can lift more. Also over time, after repeating a motion, muscles can stretch farther. Muscles can get hurt if we stretch them too far or too fast. A pulled muscle can be very painful. To be able to do something like splits, Grace needed to move toward the position again and again, gently and gradually.
summary: Muscles are soft tissues that generate body motion, forming the muscular system. Skeletal muscles attach to bones and enable movement at joints through contraction (shortening) and relaxation (lengthening). Repeated exercise strengthens muscles, like push-ups for arms or running for legs, and helps them recover and grow. Beyond skeletal muscles, the heart is also a muscle, and exercise beneficial for it contributes to overall fitness. Building strong muscles also requires a diet of healthy foods. Muscles can become more flexible with gradual stretching but can be injured if stretched too far or too quickly.

lesson_text: After demonstrating several gymnastics skills for her class, Grace is breathing hard and fast. Her chest rises and falls. It is hard for her to speak for a few minutes. As she sits still and rests, her breathing slows down. When she is breathing normally again, it is easier to talk. Your body needs air to stay alive. Breathing is the body’s process of taking in air. Your body breathes automatically, whether you think about it or not. Breathing continues when you are not aware of it. You breathe the whole time you are asleep. When you are awake, you can notice your breathing and partially control it. You can temporarily hold your breath. Take a deep breath, and let it out. Breathing in is called inhaling. When you breathe in, you inhale. Breathing out is called exhaling. When you breathe out, you exhale. Notice how your chest swells when you inhale. Your lungs inside your chest are filling with air. Notice how your chest and belly shrink back in when you exhale. Your lungs push the old air out. You take fresh air in again with your next breath. Your body parts that take in and release air make up your respiratory system. You breathe air in through your nose and mouth. Your lungs are in your chest. A muscle beneath your lungs controls your breathing. While you are active, your body needs more air. You breathe faster and more heavily. While you are resting, your body needs less air. You breathe slower and less deeply. Your lungs need clean, fresh air. Even though you can’t see it, air can be dirty and contain harmful particles or germs.
